\uline{in which}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $V$ \uline{is a Zariski open subset of an affine space over} $\Q$
\item \uline{the geometric fibers of} $p$ \uline{are irreducible}, \uline{and} $W$ \uline{is reduced}.
\item $f$ \uline{is quasi-finite and dominant}.
\end{enumerate}
\uline{Then}, \uline{for every open set} $U\subset V(\R)$ (\uline{in the usual topology}) \uline{and every extension} $F$ \uline{of} $E$, \uline{there exists} $v\in V(\Q)\cap U$ \uline{such that} $f^{-1}(v)$ \uline{is the spectrum of an extension} \uline{of} $E$ \uline{linearly disjoint from} $F$.

Let $W'=W\otimes_EF$. The hypotheses of 4.12 are again satisfied for $W'/F$ and $f':W'\longrightarrow W\longrightarrow V$, and one must construct $v\in V(\Q)\cap U$ such that $f'^{-1}(v)=f^{-1}(v)\otimes_EF$ is the spectrum of a field. This reduces us to the case $E=F$, which follows from Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (cf. Lang, \emph{Diophantine Geometry}, Chap. VIII).

\noindent \uline{Proposition} 5.2.\quad \uline{For} $x\in\MC(G,h)$ \uline{and} $K$ \uline{compact open in} $G(\Af)$, \uline{the image} \uline{in} ${}_K\MC(G,h)$ \uline{of} $G(\Af)\cdot x\subset\MC(G,h)$ \uline{is dense}.

This is a consequence of (0.4). The reader will verify:

\noindent \uline{Proposition} 5.3.\quad \uline{Let} $E$ \uline{be a field endowed with a complex embedding} $\rho$, $X$ \uline{a scheme over} $E$, \uline{and} $Y$ \uline{a reduced closed subscheme of} $X_{\C}$. \uline{Suppose there exist} \uline{finite extensions} $E_i$ \uline{of} $E$ \uline{in} $\C$, \uline{schemes} $M_{i,\alpha}/E_i$ \uline{and} $E_i$-\uline{morphisms} $v_{i,\alpha}:M_{i,\alpha}\longrightarrow X\otimes_EE_i$, \uline{or} $v_i:\coprod_{\alpha} M_{i,\alpha}\longrightarrow X\otimes_EE_i$, \uline{such that} $E=\bigcap_i E_i$, \uline{that} $v_i(\coprod_{\alpha} M_{i,\alpha}\otimes_{E_i}\C)\subset Y$ \uline{and that} $v_i(\coprod_{\alpha} M_{i,\alpha}\otimes_{E_i}\C)$ \uline{is dense in} $Y$. \uline{Then} $Y$ \uline{is defined over} $E$.

\noindent \uline{Corollary} 5.4.\quad \uline{Let} $u:(G^1,h^1)\longrightarrow(G^2,h^2)$ \uline{be as in} 1.14. \uline{Let} $M_E(G^1,h^1)$ \uline{and} $M_E(G^2,h^2)$ \uline{be weakly canonical models of the} $\MC(G^i,h^i)$ \uline{over} \uline{a number field} $E$ ($E(G^i,h^i)\subset E\subset\C$). \uline{Then} $v:\MC(G^1,h^1)\longrightarrow\MC(G^2,h^2)$ \uline{is defined over} $E$ (cf. 3.12)
% D008 authority physical page 33 EOF

Let $K^i\subset G^i(\Af)$ be compact open subgroups such that $v(K^1)\subset K^2$. We prove that $v(K^1,K^2):{}_{K^1}\MC(G^1,h^1)\longrightarrow{}_{K^2}\MC(G^2,h^2)$ is defined over $E$. Let $u:(H,h')\to(G^1,h^1)$ be as in 3.13 and set $F=E\cdot E(H,h')$. For $g\in G^1(\Af)$, one has $F$-morphisms
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(g):\quad M_F(H,h')&\longrightarrow M_F(G^1,h^1)
 \xrightarrow{\ g\ } M_F(G^1,h^1)
 \longrightarrow {}_{K^1}M_F(G^1,h^1),\\
b(g):\quad M_F(H,h')&\longrightarrow M_F(G^2,h^2)
 \xrightarrow{\ v(g)\ } M_F(G^2,h^2)
 \longrightarrow {}_{K^2}M_F(G^2,h^2),
\end{aligned}
\]
and, after extension of scalars to $\C$, $v(K^1,K^2)\circ a(g)=b(g)$.

By 5.1 and 5.2, one can apply 5.3 to $X={}_{K^1}M_E(G^1,h^1)\times{}_{K^2}M_E(G^2,h^2)$, to the graph $Y$ of $v$, to the $E_i=E\cdot E(H,h')$ for variable $(H,h',u)$, and to $(a(g),b(g)):M_{E_i}(H,h')\longrightarrow X_{E_i}$: it follows that the graph of $v$ is defined over $E$.

In the special case $(G^1,h^1)=(G^2,h^2)$ and $u=\Id$, 5.4 says:

\noindent \uline{Corollary} 5.5.\quad \uline{Up to (unique) isomorphism, there exists at most one weakly canonical model of} $\MC(G,h)$ \uline{over} $E$ ($E(G,h)\subset E\subset\C$).

\noindent \uline{Corollary} 5.6.\quad \uline{If} $G'$ \uline{is simply connected,} \uline{the reciprocity law of a weakly canonical model of} $\MC(G,h)$ \uline{over} $E$ ($E(G,h)\subset E\subset\C$) \uline{is given by} 3.9.1.

The proof is the same as in the special case $v:(G,h)\to(T,vh)$ of 5.4.

\noindent \uline{Corollary} 5.7.\quad \uline{Let} $v:(G^1,h^1)\hookrightarrow(G^2,h^2)$ \uline{be as in} 1.15. \uline{If} $\MC(G^2,h^2)$ \uline{admits a weakly canonical model over} $E$, \uline{with} $E(G^2,h^2)\subset E(G^1,h^1)\subset E\subset\C$, \uline{then} $\MC(G^1,h^1)$ \uline{admits a weakly canonical model over} $E$.

Let $K^i$ be a compact open subgroup of $G^i(\Af)$. Using 1.15, we are reduced to showing only that if $v(K^1)\subset K^2$ and ${}_{K^1}\MC(G^1,h^1)\hookrightarrow{}_{K^2}\MC(G^2,h^2)$, then the subscheme ${}_{K^1}\MC(G^1,h^1)$ of ${}_{K^2}\MC(G^2,h^2)={}_{K^2}M_E(G^2,h^2)\otimes_E\C$ is defined over $E$.
% D008 authority physical page 34 EOF

Let $u:(H,h')\to(G^1,h^1)$ be as in 3.13, and for $g\in G^1(\Af)$ let $a(g)$ be the composite homomorphism defined over $F=E\cdot E(H,h')$:
\[
a(g):M_F(H,h')\longrightarrow M_F(G^1,h^1)
 \xrightarrow{\ v(g)\ } M_F(G^2,h^2)
 \longrightarrow{}_{K^2}M_F(G^2,h^2).
\]
By 5.1 and 5.2, one concludes by applying 5.3 to $X={}_{K^2}M_E(G^2,h^2)$, to $Y={}_{K^1}\MC(G^1,h^1)$, to the $E_i=E\cdot E(H,h')$ for variable $(H,h',u)$, and to $a(g):M_{E_i}(H,h')\longrightarrow X_{E_i}$.

\noindent \uline{Example} 5.8.\quad For $(G,h_0)$ as in 4.9, one constructs, by 5.7 and 4.21, a canonical model $M(G^{\circ},h_0)\subset M(\Gp(V,\psi),h_0)\otimes_{\Q}E(G^{\circ},h^{\circ})$.

\noindent \uline{Variant} 5.9.\quad Let $(G_1,h_0)$ be such that, with the notation of 4.22, there exists $u:(G_1,h_0)\hookrightarrow(\Gp_{2g}^{(F)},h_0)$ (for example $(G_1^{\circ},h_0)$ with $(G_1,h_0)$ as in 4.13). An application of 5.7 yields a canonical model of $M(G_1,h_0)$.

\noindent \uline{Proposition} 5.10.\quad \uline{Let} $(G,h)$ \uline{be as in} 3.13, \uline{let the} $E_i:E(G,h)\subset E_i\subset\C$ \uline{be number fields}, \uline{let} $E$ \uline{be the intersection of the} $E_i$, \uline{and let} $M_{E_i}(G,h)$ \uline{be a weakly canonical model of} $\MC(G,h)$ \uline{over} $E_i$. \uline{Then there exists a unique model} $M_E(G,h)$ \uline{of} $\MC(G,h)$ \uline{over} $E$, \uline{such that for every} $i$ \uline{the model} $M_E(G,h)\otimes_EE_i$ \uline{over} $E_i$ \uline{is isomorphic to} $M_{E_i}(G,h)$.

In view of the uniqueness assertion, one may suppose the $E_i$ finite in number. Let $F$ be the extension of $E$ in $\C$ generated by them, and let $\mathfrak E$ be the set of subextensions of $F$ containing one of the $E_i$. Using 5.5, one obtains for every $F'\in\mathfrak E$ a model $M_{F'}(G,h)$, and for every inclusion $F'\subset F''$ ($F',F''\in\mathfrak E$) an isomorphism of models $\alpha(F'',F'):M_{F'}(G,h)\otimes_{F'}F''\longrightarrow M_{F''}(G,h)$.

Let $u:(H,h')\to(G,h)$ be as in 3.13, with $E(H,h')$ linearly disjoint from $F$ over $E(G,h)$ (5.1). Put $E_1=E(H,h')\cdot E$ and $F'_1=E_1\cdot F'=E(H,h')\cdot F'$ ($F'\in\mathfrak E$).

Let $g\in G(\Af)$ and let $K\subset G(\Af)$ be a compact open subgroup. Since $M_{F'}(G,h)$ is weakly canonical, one has an $F'_1$-morphism
% D008 authority physical page 35 EOF
\[
a'(g):M_{F'_1}(H,h')\longrightarrow M_{F'_1}(G,h)
 \xrightarrow{\ g\ } M_{F'_1}(G,h)
 \longrightarrow {}_K M_{F'_1}(G,h).
\]
Since $F'_1=E_1\otimes_EF'$, one may ``interpret'' this as a morphism of $F'$-schemes
\[
a(g):M_{E_1}(H,h')\otimes_EF'\longrightarrow {}_K M_{F'}(G,h).
\]
The $a(g)$ satisfy $\alpha(F'',F')\,a(g)_{F''}=a(g)$. One concludes by 5.2 and the following lemma, applied to $X^1=\coprod_{g\in G(\Af)}M_{E_1}(H,h')$. Its proof is left to the reader as an exercise.

\noindent \uline{Lemma} 5.10.1.\quad \uline{Let} $F/E$ \uline{be a finite extension of fields and let} $\mathfrak E$ \uline{be a set of subfields of} $F$, \uline{whose intersection is reduced to} $E$, \uline{such that}
\[
F\in\mathfrak E\text{ and }F'\subset F''\subset F\Longrightarrow F''\in\mathfrak E.
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \uline{The functor that sends a scheme} $X/E$ \uline{to the system} $\mathcal X$ \uline{of schemes} $X_{F'}/F'$ $(F'\in\mathfrak E)$ \uline{and the isomorphisms} $(X_{F'})\otimes_{F'}F''\xrightarrow{\sim}X_{F''}$ $(F'\subset F'',\ F',F''\in\mathfrak E)$ \uline{is fully faithful}.
\item \uline{For a system} $\mathcal X=\{X(F')/F'\ (F'\in\mathfrak E);\allowbreak\ \alpha(F'',F'):X(F')\otimes_{F'}F''\xrightarrow{\sim}X(F'')\allowbreak\ (F'\subset F'',\ F',F''\in\mathfrak E)\}$ \uline{to come from a scheme} $X/E$, \uline{it is enough that the} $X(F')/F'$ \uline{be quasi-projective and that there exist a scheme} $X^1/E$ \uline{and a morphism} $u:X^1_{\mathfrak E}\longrightarrow\mathcal X$ \uline{such that the} $u(F'):X^1_{F'}\longrightarrow X(F')$ \uline{have dense image}.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent \uline{Remark} 5.10.2.\quad Under the hypotheses of 5.10, for $u:(H,h')\hookrightarrow(G,h)$ as in 3.13, the field of definition of $u:\MC(H,h')\longrightarrow\MC(G,h)$ is contained in the extension $\bigcap_i E(H,h')\cdot E_i$ of $E(H,h')\cdot E$.

\noindent \uline{Proposition} 5.11.\quad \uline{Let} $h:\bS\longrightarrow G_{\R}$ \uline{be as in} 3.13 \uline{and let} $\delta:\bS\longrightarrow C^\circ_{\R}$ ($C$ \uline{the center of} $G$). \uline{If} $E(G,h),E(C,\delta)\subset E\subset\C$ \uline{and if} $\MC(G,h)$ \uline{admits a weakly canonical model over} $E$, \uline{then} $\MC(G,h.\delta)$ \uline{does as well}.

Let $K$ be a compact open subgroup of $G(\Af)$ and let $L=K\cap C^{\circ}(\Af)$. Over $\C$, the morphism
\[
u:(G\times C^{\circ},(h,\delta))\longrightarrow(G,h\delta):(g,c)\longmapsto gc
\]
% D008 authority physical page 36 EOF
induces morphisms
\[
u_K:{}_K\MC(G,h)\times {}_L\MC(C^{\circ},\delta)
 \longrightarrow {}_K\MC(G,h\delta).
\]
Let $d$ be the morphism $d:C^{\circ}\longrightarrow G\times C^{\circ}:c\longmapsto(c,c^{-1})$. The subgroup $d(C^{\circ}(\Af))$ of $G\times C^{\circ}(\Af)$ acts on $\MC(G,h)\times\MC(C^{\circ},\delta)$ through the quotient $\pi_0(C^{\circ}(\A))$ of $C^{\circ}(\Af)$, and $u_K$ induces an isomorphism
\[
\bar u_K:\bigl({}_K\MC(G,h)\times{}_L\MC(C^{\circ},\delta)\bigr)/
\bigl(L\backslash\pi_0(C^{\circ}(\A))\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\sim}{}_K\MC(G,h\delta).
\]
Define ${}_K M_E(G,h\delta)$ to be the quotient
\[
{}_K M_E(G,h)\times{}_L M_E(C^{\circ},\delta)/
\bigl(L\backslash\pi_0(C^{\circ}(\A))\bigr)
\]
and one verifies that this gives a weakly canonical model. By construction, one has\begingroup\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true\makeatother
\begin{align}
M_E(G,h)\times_E M_E(C^{\circ},\delta)&\longrightarrow M_E(G,h\delta). \tag{5.11.1}
\end{align}\endgroup

\noindent \uline{Conjecture} 5.12.\quad \uline{For every} $(G,h_0)$ \uline{as in} 3.13, \uline{there exists a canonical model of} $\MC(G,h_0)$.

Suppose---this is a typical case---that $G$ is $\Q$-simple and adjoint. Let $\widetilde G$ be the universal covering of $G$ and let $\omega$ be a weight of $\widetilde G_{\C}$. If, with the notation of 3.7, the conjugacy class of $h_0r$ is described by integers $(n_i)_{i\in|\Delta|}$, and if $\omega=\sum m_i\alpha_i$, put $\langle\omega,h_0r\rangle=\sum n_i m_i$. So far, it has only been possible to attack 5.12 when $\widetilde G$ admits a nontrivial representation $V$ such that all irreducible components $V'$ of $V_{\C}$ satisfy:

\noindent $(*)$\quad as $\omega$ runs through the weights of $V'$, $\langle\omega,h_0r\rangle$ takes at most two values.

Let $\sigma$ be the opposition involution. Condition $(*)$ also means that the dominant weight $\omega$ of $V'$ satisfies $\langle\omega,h_0r\rangle+\langle\sigma\omega,h_0r\rangle=0$ or 1. There is no such representation $V$ if $G$ is exceptional (the noncompact factors of $G_{\R}$ are then of type $E_{6(-14)}$ or $E_{7(-25)}$), or of trialitarian type $D_4$, nor if $G$ is of type $D_n$ and $G_{\R}$ has noncompact factors of both types $D_n^{\mathbb H}$ and $D_n^{\mathbb R,2}$.
% D008 authority physical page 37 EOF

\noindent \S\ 6. \uline{Strange models}.\par\vspace{0.9em}

\noindent 6.1.\quad Let $F$ be a totally real number field, and let
\begingroup
\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true
\makeatother
\begin{align}
{}_F\Sigma:\quad 0\longrightarrow {}_FG'&\longrightarrow {}_FG
 \longrightarrow \Gm\longrightarrow0 \tag{6.1.1}
\end{align}
\endgroup
be a form over $F$ of the exact sequence
\begingroup
\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true
\makeatother
\begin{align}
{}_F\Sigma_0:\quad 0\longrightarrow\Sp_{2n}&\longrightarrow\Gp_{2n}
 \xrightarrow{\ \mu\ }\Gm\longrightarrow0, \tag{6.1.2}
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\Gp$ denotes a group of symplectic similitudes.

Assume that, for every real place $\tau$ of $F$, $\Sigma\otimes_{F,\tau}\R$ is of one of the following types:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item ${}_F\Sigma\otimes_{F,\tau}\R$ is isomorphic to ${}_F\Sigma_0\otimes_{F,\tau}\R$, or
\item $G'\otimes_{F,\tau}\R$ is compact.
\end{enumerate}
Let $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_g$ denote the real places of $F$, and suppose that the places of type (a) are $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_r$, \uline{with} $r>0$.

\noindent 6.2.\quad The group ${}_FG$ may be described as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Choose a quaternion algebra $B$ over $F$, indefinite at the places $\tau_i$ for $i\le r$, and definite for $i>r$. Let $x\mapsto\overline{x}$ denote its canonical involution.
\item Choose a free $B$-module $V$, endowed with a nondegenerate $F$-bilinear form $\Phi$, \uline{symmetric} and such that
\[
\Phi(bx,y)=\Phi(x,\overline b\,y).
\]
\item Assume that, for $i>r$, the form deduced from $\Phi$ by extension of scalars through $\tau_i:F\to\R$ is positive definite.
\item Take ${}_FG$ to be the group of $B$-linear similitudes of $\Phi$; in other words, the elements $g\in G(\Q)$ are the $g\in\GL_B(V)$ for which there exists $\mu(g)\in F^*$ satisfying
\[
\Phi(gx,gy)=\mu(g)\Phi(x,y).
\]
\end{enumerate}
% D008 authority physical page 38 EOF
\noindent 6.3.\quad Let
\[
\Sigma:\quad 0\longrightarrow G'\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow F^*\longrightarrow0
\]
denote the exact sequence of algebraic groups over $\Q$ deduced from ${}_F\Sigma$ by Weil restriction of scalars from $F$ to $\Q$. We have
\begingroup
\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true
\makeatother
\begin{align}
G_{\R}&=\prod_{\tau}{}_FG\otimes_{F,\tau}\R
\qquad(\tau\text{ a real place}). \tag{6.3.1}
\end{align}
\endgroup
A morphism $h:\bS\to G_{\R}$ is defined by its coordinates $h_i:\bS\longrightarrow {}_FG\otimes_{F,\tau_i}\R$.
By 1.6, there exists a unique conjugacy class of morphisms $h$ such that, for $i\le r$, $h_i$ is of type 1.6, and for $i>r$, $h_i$ is trivial. Let $h_0$ be in this class.

The field $E(G,h_0)$ is the totally real subfield of $\C$ generated by the elements $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^r\tau_i(f)$ for $f\in F$.

\noindent \uline{Theorem} 6.4.\quad \uline{With the preceding notation,} $\MC(G,h_0)$ \uline{admits a canonical model} $M(G,h_0)$.

Let $Z$ be a totally imaginary quadratic extension of $F$. Let $V'=V\otimes_F Z$, $L=B\otimes_F Z$, and let $G'$ be the algebraic subgroup of $\GL_L(V')$ generated by $G$ and $Z^*$:
\begingroup
\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true
\makeatother
\begin{align}
0\longrightarrow F^*&\xrightarrow{\ (f,f^{-1})\ }G\times Z^*
 \xrightarrow{\ q\ }G'\longrightarrow0. \tag{6.4.1}
\end{align}
\endgroup
Let $x\mapsto\widetilde x$ be the involution of $L$ given by the tensor product of the involutions of $B$ and $Z$. Up to a factor in $F$, there exists on $Z$ a unique alternating $F$-bilinear form $\psi_Z$. If ${}_F\psi$ is the alternating $F$-bilinear form on $V'$ which is the tensor product of $\Phi$ and $\psi_Z$, then
\[
{}_F\psi(\ell x,y)={}_F\psi(x,\widetilde{\ell}\,y).
\]
Put $\psi(x,y)=\Tr_{F/\Q}\bigl({}_F\psi(x,y)\bigr)$.

Choose, for every real place of $F$, a complex embedding of $Z$
% D008 authority physical page 39 EOF
inducing it. Then $\displaystyle Z^*(\R)\simeq\prod_{i=1}^g \C^*$. Let $h_Z$ be the homomorphism from $\bS$ into $Z^*_{\R}$ with coordinates $h_i:\bS(\R)=\C^*\longrightarrow\C^*$ $(1\le i\le g)$ equal to $(z\mapsto1)$ for $i\le r$, and to $(z\mapsto z^{-1})$ for $i>r$.

For every $h:\bS\to G_{\R}$ as in 6.3, put $h'=q\circ(h\times h_Z):\bS\longrightarrow G'_{\R}$.

\noindent \uline{Lemma} 6.4.2.\quad \uline{There exists} $b\in L$ \uline{such that, for a suitable choice of} $\psi_Z$, \uline{the form}
\[
\psi\bigl(x,b\,h'_0(i)y\bigr)\qquad\text{\uline{on}}\quad V'\otimes_{\Q}\R
\]
\uline{is symmetric and positive definite}.

This is verified after extension of scalars from $\Q$ to $\R$.

This lemma and 5.9 make it possible to construct a canonical model of $M(G',h'_0)$ (since $G'$ is contained in the group of symplectic similitudes of ${}_F\psi(x,by)$). Applying 5.11 and 5.7, one obtains a weakly canonical model of $\MC(G,h_0)$ over the extension $E(Z^*,h_Z)$ of $E(G,h_0)$. The conclusion follows from 5.10, 5.10.2 and the following lemma, which can be deduced from 5.13.

\noindent \uline{Lemma} 6.5.\quad \uline{Let} $F$ \uline{be a totally real number field, endowed with a set} $S$ \uline{of real embeddings}. \uline{Let} $F^{\ast}$ \uline{be the number field corresponding to the subgroup of} $\Gal(\overline{\Q}/\Q)$ \uline{which stabilizes} $S$. \uline{For} $Z$ \uline{a totally imaginary quadratic extension of} $F$, \uline{endowed with a set} $T$ \uline{of complex embeddings, one above each element of} $S$, \uline{let likewise} $Z^{\ast}\supset F^{\ast}$ \uline{be the field of invariants of the stabilizer of} $T$. \uline{Then, for every extension} $E$ \uline{of} $F^{\ast}$, \uline{there exist} $Z$ \uline{and} $T$ \uline{such that} $Z^{\ast}$ \uline{is linearly disjoint from} $E$.

\noindent \uline{Remark} 6.6.\quad The canonical map 1.13, 1.14
\begingroup
\makeatletter
\tagsleft@true
\makeatother
\begin{align}
\MC(G,h_0)\times\MC(Z^*,h_Z)&\longrightarrow\MC(G',h'_0) \tag{6.6.1}
\end{align}
\endgroup
is interpreted as follows. Each conjugate of $h$ defines on $V_{\C}$ a
% D008 authority physical page 40 EOF
Hodge bigrading \uline{invariant} under $F$:
\[
V_{\C}=V^{-1,0}\oplus V^{0,-1}\oplus V^{0,0}
\qquad(\overline{V^{pq}}=V^{qp}).
\]
One should beware that the grading (by weight) of $V_{\C}$ by the
$\displaystyle V^n=\sum_{p+q=n}V^{pq}$ is not defined over $\Q$ if $r\ne g$.

Similarly, $Z_{\C}$ is bigraded:
\[
Z_{\C}=Z^{-1,0}\oplus Z^{0,-1}\oplus Z^{0,0}.
\]
The miracle is that the $\Q$-vector space $V'=V\otimes_F Z$, endowed with the tensor-product Hodge bigrading
$\displaystyle V'_{\C}=V_{\C}^{\prime -1,0}\oplus V_{\C}^{\prime 0,-1}\quad(!)$, is the $H_1$ of an abelian variety.

% D008 authority physical page 41 EOF

\begin{center}
{\small Actes, Congrès intern. math., 1970. Volume 1, pp. 425--430.}\\[4em]
{\Large\bfseries HODGE THEORY I}\\[1.6em]
{\large by PIERRE DELIGNE}
\end{center}

We propose to give a heuristic dictionary between statements in $\ell$-adic cohomology and statements in Hodge theory. This dictionary draws in particular on [3] and on Grothendieck's conjectural theory of motives [2]. So far it has mainly served to formulate conjectures in Hodge theory, and has sometimes suggested proofs of them.

\paragraph{Definition 1.1.} A mixed Hodge structure $H$ consists of
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item a finitely generated $\Z$-module $H_{\Z}$ (the ``integral lattice'');
\item a finite increasing filtration $W$ on $H_{\Q}=H_{\Z}\otimes\Q$ (the ``weight filtration'');
\item a finite decreasing filtration $F$ on $H_{\C}=H_{\Z}\otimes\C$ (the ``Hodge filtration'').
\end{enumerate}
These data are subject to the axiom:

There exists on $\Gr_W(H_{\C})$ a (unique) bigrading by subspaces $H^{p,q}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item
\[
\Gr_W^n(H_{\C})=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q};
\]
\item the filtration $F$ induces on $\Gr_W(H_{\C})$ the filtration
\[
\Gr_W(F)^p=\bigoplus_{p'\ge p}H^{p',q'};
\]
\item $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$.
\end{enumerate}
A morphism $f:H\to H'$ is a homomorphism $f_{\Z}:H_{\Z}\to H'_{\Z}$ such that $f_{\Q}:H_{\Q}\to H'_{\Q}$ and $f_{\C}:H_{\C}\to H'_{\C}$ are respectively compatible with the filtrations $W$ and $F$.

The Hodge numbers of $H$ are the integers
\[
\tag{1.2}
h^{pq}=\dim H^{p,q}=h^{qp}.
\]
One says that $H$ is pure of weight $n$ if $h^{pq}=0$ for $p+q\ne n$ (i.e. if $\Gr_W^i(H)=0$ for $i\ne n$). One also says that $H$ is a Hodge structure of weight $n$.

The Tate Hodge structure $\Z(1)$ is the Hodge structure of weight $-2$, purely of type $(-1,-1)$, for which $\Z(1)_{\C}=\C$ and $\Z(1)_{\Z}=2\pi i\Z=\Ker(\exp:\C\to\C^*)\subset\C$. Put $\Z(n)=\Z(1)^{\otimes n}$.

One can show that mixed Hodge structures form an abelian category. If $f:H\to H'$ is a morphism, then $f_{\Q}$ and $f_{\C}$ are strictly compatible with the filtrations $W$ and $F$ ([1], 2.3.5).

\paragraph{2.} Let $A$ be a normal integral domain of finite type over $\Z$, let $K$ be its field of fractions, and let $\barK$ be an algebraic closure of $K$. Let $K_{nr}$ be the largest subextension of $\barK$ unramified at every prime ideal of $A$. It is known---or one may take this as the definition---that
\[
\pi_1(\Spec(A),\barK)=\Gal(K_{nr}/K).
\]
For every closed point $x$ of $\Spec(A)$, defined by a maximal ideal $m_x$ of $A$, the residue field $k_x=A/m_x$ is finite; the point $x$ defines a conjugacy class of ``Frobenius substitutions'' $\varphi_x\in\pi_1(\Spec(A),\barK)$. Put $q_x=\#k_x$ and $F_x=\varphi_x^{-1}$.

Let $K$ be a field of finite type over the prime field of characteristic $p$, let $\barK$ be an algebraic closure of $K$, let $\ell$ be a prime number $\ne p$, and let $H$ be a finitely generated $\Zl$-module (or $\Ql$-module) endowed with a continuous action $\rho$ of $\Gal(\barK/K)$. In what follows we shall always suppose that there exists $A$ as above, with $\ell$ invertible in $A$, such that $\rho$ factors through
\[
\pi_1(\Spec(A),\barK)=\Gal(K_{nr}/K).
\]
We shall say that $H$ is pure of weight $n$ if, for every closed point $x$ of a nonempty open subset of $\Spec(A)$, the eigenvalues $\alpha$ of $F_x$ acting on $H$ are algebraic integers all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value
\[
|\alpha|=q_x^{n/2}.
\]

\paragraph{Principle 2.1.} If the Galois module $H$ ``comes from algebraic geometry'', there exists on $H_{\Ql}=H\otimes_{\Zl}\Ql$ a (unique) increasing filtration $W$ (the ``weight filtration''), invariant under Galois, such that $\Gr_n^W(H)$ is pure of weight $n$.

One may think that $\Gr_n^W(H)$ is moreover semisimple.

When resolution of singularities is available, one can often give a conjectural definition of $W$, whose correctness follows from the Weil conjectures [5] (cf. 6).

Let $\mu$ be the subgroup of $\barK^*$ formed by the roots of unity. The Tate module $\Zl(1)$, defined by
\[
\Zl(1)=\Hom(\Ql/\Zl,\mu),
\]
is pure of weight $-2$. Put $\Zl(n)=\Zl(1)^{\otimes n}$.

It is trivial that every morphism $f:H\to H'$ is strictly compatible with the weight filtration.

Principle 2.1 agrees with the fact that every extension of $\Gm$ (``weight $-2$'') by an abelian variety (``weight $-1>-2$'') is trivial.

\paragraph{3. Translation.} The Galois modules which appear in $\ell$-adic cohomology have, over $\C$, mixed Hodge structures as analogues. In addition one has the dictionary
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\quad\vrule\quad}l}
\text{pure module of weight }n & \text{Hodge structure of weight }n\\
\text{weight filtration} & \text{weight filtration}\\
\text{Galois-equivariant homomorphism} & \text{morphism}\\
\text{Tate module }\Zl(1) & \text{Tate Hodge structure }\Z(1).
\end{array}
\]

\paragraph{4.} Let $X$ be a complex algebraic variety (= a scheme of finite type over $\C$, which we shall suppose separated). There exists a subfield $K$ of $\C$, of finite type over $\Q$, such that $X$ can be defined over $K$ (i.e. arises by extension of scalars from $K$ to $\C$ from a $K$-scheme $X'$). Let $\barK$ be the algebraic closure of $K$ in $\C$. The Galois group $\Gal(\barK/K)$ then acts on the $\ell$-adic cohomology groups $H^*(X,\Zl)$; one has
\[
H^*(X(\C),\Z)\otimes\Zl=H^*(X,\Zl)=H^*(X'_{\barK},\Zl).
\]

According to 3, one should expect the cohomology groups $H^n(X(\C),\Z)$ to carry natural mixed Hodge structures. This can be proved (see [1], 3.2.5, for the case where $X$ is smooth; the proof is algebraic, starting from classical Hodge theory [6]). For $X$ projective and smooth, the Weil conjectures imply that $H^n(X,\Zl)$ is pure of weight $n$, while classical Hodge theory endows $H^n(X,\Z)$ with a Hodge structure of weight $n$. For every morphism $f:X\to Y$ and for $K$ large enough, $f^*:H^*(Y,\Zl)\to H^*(X,\Zl)$ commutes with Galois (by transport of structure); likewise, $f^*:H^*(Y,\Z)\to H^*(X,\Z)$ is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures. For $X$ smooth, the cohomology class in $H^{2n}(X,\Zl(n))$ of an algebraic cycle of codimension $n$, $Z$, defined over $K$, is Galois-invariant, i.e. defines
\[
c(Z)\in\Hom_{\Gal}(\Zl(-n),H^{2n}(X,\Zl)).
\]
Similarly, the cohomology class $c(Z)\in H^{2n}(X(\C),\Z)$ is purely of type $(n,n)$, i.e. corresponds to
\[
c(Z)\in\Hom_{\mathrm{H.M.}}(\Z(-n),H^{2n}(X(\C),\Z)).
\]

\paragraph{5.} If $f:H\to H'$ is a Galois-compatible morphism between $\Ql$-vector spaces of different weights, then $f=0$. Likewise, if $f:H\to H'$ is a morphism of pure mixed Hodge structures of different weights, then $f$ is torsion. A more useful remark is the following.

\paragraph{Scholium 5.1.} Let $H$ and $H'$ be Hodge structures of weights $n$ and $n'$, with $n>n'$. Let $f:H_{\Q}\to H'_{\Q}$ be a homomorphism such that $f:H_{\C}\to H'_{\C}$ respects $F$. Then $f=0$.

\paragraph{6.} Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\C$, let $D=\sum_{i=1}^nD_i$ be a normal-crossings divisor in $X$, a sum of smooth divisors, and let $j$ be the inclusion into $X$ of $U=X-D$. For $Q\subset[1,n]$, put
\[
D_Q=\bigcap_{i\in Q}D_i.
\]
In $\ell$-adic cohomology, one has canonically
\[
\tag{6.1}
R^qj_*\Zl=\bigoplus_{\#Q=q}\Zl(-q)_{D_Q},
\]
and the Leray spectral sequence for $j$ is
\[
\tag{6.2}
E_2^{pq}=\bigoplus_{\#Q=q}H^p(D_Q,\Ql)\otimes\Zl(-q)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(U,\Ql).
\]
According to the Weil conjectures [5], $H^p(D_Q,\Ql)$ is pure of weight $p$, so that $E_2^{pq}$ is pure of weight $p+2q$. As a quotient of a subobject of $E_2^{pq}$, $E_r^{pq}$ is also pure of weight $p+2q$. By 5, $d_r=0$ for $r\ge3$, since the weights $p+2q$ and $p+2q-r+2$ of $E_r^{pq}$ and $E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}$ are different. Hence $E_3^{pq}=E_{\infty}^{pq}$. Up to reindexing, the weight filtration of $H^*(U,\Ql)$ is the abutment of (6.2):
\[
\tag{6.3}
\Gr_n^W(H^k(U,\Ql))=E_3^{2k-n,n-k}.
\]

\paragraph{7.} In integral cohomology, for the usual topology, the Leray spectral sequence for $j$ is
\[
\tag{7.1}
{}'E_2^{pq}=\bigoplus_{\#Q=q}H^p(D_Q,\Z)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(U,\Z).
\]
Since every $D_Q$ is a nonsingular projective variety, ${}'E_2^{pq}$ is endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $p$. Put $E_2^{pq}={}'E_2^{pq}\otimes\Z(-q)$ (a Hodge structure of weight $p+2q$). As an abelian group, $E_2^{pq}={}'E_2^{pq}$; it is useful to regard (7.1) as a spectral sequence with initial term $E_2^{pq}$. According to 3, one should expect
\[
d_2:E_2^{pq}\to E_2^{p+2,q-1}
\]
to be a morphism of Hodge structures. This is proved by interpreting $d_2$ as a Gysin morphism. Thus $E_3^{pq}$ is endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $p+2q$. According to 3, one expects that, modulo torsion, the spectral sequence (6.4)\footnote{The printed text refers to (6.4); the intended reference appears to be (7.1).} degenerates at $E_3$ ($E_3=E_{\infty}$), and that the vanishing of the $d_r$ ($r\ge3$) is an application of 5.1. This program is carried out in [1] 3.2. There the weight filtration of $H^*(U,\Q)$ is defined as the abutment of (7.1), up to the reindexing (6.3).

In fact, in order to endow cohomology groups $H^*$ with a mixed Hodge structure, the key point up to now has always been to find a spectral sequence $E$ abutting to $H^*$ such that the $\ell$-adic analogue of $E_2^{pq}$ is conjecturally pure (of weight $p+2q$); $E_2^{pq}$ must then carry a natural Hodge structure (of weight $p+2q$), and the filtration $W$ is the abutment of $E$.

\paragraph{8.} Let $\Spec(V)$ be the spectrum of a henselian discrete valuation ring (a henselian trait), with fraction field $K$ and residue field $k$ of finite type over the prime field of characteristic $p$. Let $\barK$ be an algebraic closure of $K$ and let $H$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\Ql$ ($\ell\ne p$), on which $\Gal(\barK/K)$ acts continuously. According to Grothendieck, it is known ([4], appendix) that a finite-index subgroup of the inertia group $I$ acts unipotently. Replacing $V$ by a finite extension, one reduces to the case in which the action of all of $I$ is unipotent (the semistable case); it then factors through the largest pro-$\ell$ quotient $I_{\ell}$ of $I$, canonically isomorphic to $\Zl(1)$.

\paragraph{Principle 8.1.} In the semistable case, if the Galois module $H$ ``comes from algebraic geometry'', there exists a (unique) increasing filtration $W$ of $H$ (the ``weight filtration'') such that $I$ acts trivially on $\Gr_n^W(H)$ and such that $\Gr_n^W(H)$, as a Galois module under $\Gal(\bar k/k)\simeq\Gal(\barK/K)/I$, is pure of weight $n$.

Compare 2.1 and the appendix of [4].

When resolution of singularities is available, one can sometimes give a conjectural definition of $W$, whose validity follows from the Weil conjectures. With the help of resolution and Weil, it is often easy to show that in any case $H$ has a filtration whose successive quotients are pure Galois modules under $\Gal(\bar k/k)$.

Suppose $H$ is semistable. For $T\in I_{\ell}$, define $\log T$ as the finite sum
\[
-\sum_{n>0}(\Id-T)^n/n.
\]
The map $(T,x)\mapsto\log T(x)$ is identified with a homomorphism
\[
\tag{8.2}
M:\Zl(1)\otimes H\longrightarrow H.
\]
Since $\Zl(1)$ has weight $-2$, one necessarily has (cf. 5)
\[
\tag{8.3}
M(\Zl(1)\otimes W_n(H))\subset W_{n-2}(H)
\]
and $M$ induces
\[
\tag{8.4}
\Gr(M):\Zl(1)\otimes\Gr_n^W(H)\longrightarrow\Gr_{n-2}^W(H).
\]

\paragraph{8.5.} If $X$ is a nonsingular projective variety over an algebraically closed field $k_0$, define
\[
L:\Zl(-1)\otimes H^*(X,\Zl)\longrightarrow H^*(X,\Zl)
\]
to be cup product with the cohomology class of a hyperplane section. One will note a formal analogy between $L$ and $M$: just as $M$ is defined by an action of $\Zl(1)$, one may regard $L$ as defined by an action of $\Zl(-1)$; $L$ raises degree by $2$, and $\Gr M$ (8.4) lowers it by $2$.

\paragraph{9.} Let $D$ be the unit disk, $D^*=D-\{0\}$, and let $X$
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X&\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow&\mathbb P^r(\C)\times D\\[-0.2em]
{}^{f}\searrow&&\swarrow^{\pr_2}\\[-0.2em]
& D&
\end{array}
\]
be a family of projective varieties parametrized by $D$, with $f$ proper and $f|D^*$ smooth. Keep the notation of 8, and recall that in the analogy between a henselian trait and a small neighborhood of $0$ in the complex line, one has the following dictionary (note that the spectrum of the ring of germs of holomorphic functions at $0$ is a henselian trait):
\[
\tag{9.1}
\begin{array}{r@{\quad\vrule\quad}l}
D & \Spec(V)\\
D^* & \Spec(K)\\
\text{a universal covering }\wt D^*\text{ of }D^* & \Spec(\barK)\\
\text{fundamental group }\pi_1(D^*) & \text{inertia group }I\\
\text{(with }\pi_1(D^*)=\Z\simeq\Z(1)_{\Z}\text{)} & \text{(with }I_{\ell}=\Zl(1)\text{)}\\
X & \text{projective scheme }X\text{ over }\Spec(V)\\
X^*=f^{-1}(D^*) & X_K\\
\wt X=X\times_D\wt D^* & X_{\barK}\\
\text{local system }R^if_*\Z|D^* & \text{Galois module }H^i(X_{\barK},\Zl)\\
H^i(\wt X,\Z) & H^i(X_{\barK},\Zl).
\end{array}
\]
Note that $\wt X$ is homotopy equivalent to each of the fibers $X_t=f^{-1}(t)$ ($t\in D^*$): $H^i(X_{\barK},\Zl)$ again has $H^i(X_t,\Z)$ as analogue, and the action of $I$ corresponds to the monodromy transformation $T$.

Here again, it is known that a finite-index subgroup of $\pi_1(D^*)$ acts unipotently on $H^i(\wt X,\Q)=H^i(X_t,\Q)$. Assume we are in the semistable case where all of $\pi_1(D^*)$ acts unipotently (this amounts to replacing $D$ by a finite covering), and let $T$ be the action of the canonical generator of $\pi_1(D^*)$.

By 3 and 8, one expects $H^i(\wt X,\Q)\simeq H^i(X_t,\Q)$ to be endowed with an increasing filtration $W$, $\Gr_n^W(H^i(\wt X,\Q))$ to be endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $n$, $\log T(W_n)\subset W_{n-2}$, and $\log T$ to induce a morphism of Hodge structures
\[
M_n:\Z(-1)\otimes\Gr_n^W(H^i)\longrightarrow\Gr_{n-2}^W(H^i).
\]
One would moreover like (8.2), and not only (8.3) and (8.4), to have an analogue.

In fact, for each vector $u$ in the tangent space to $D$ at $0$, one can define a mixed Hodge structure $\calH_u$ on $H^i(\wt X,\Z)$. The filtration $W$ and the Hodge structures on the $\Gr_n^W(H^i)$ are independent of $u$, and the dependence of $\calH_u$ on $u$ is expressed simply in terms of $T$. In analogy with (8.2), one finds that, for every $u$, $\log T$ induces a homomorphism of mixed Hodge structures
\[
M:\Z(1)\otimes H^i(\wt X,\Z)\longrightarrow H^i(\wt X,\Z).
\]
Finally, the analogy 8.5 is not misleading (but here the fact that $f|D^*$ is supposed proper and smooth is no doubt essential). One proves that
\[
(\log T)^k:\Gr_{n+k}^W(H^n(\wt X,\Q))\longrightarrow\Gr_{n-k}^W(H^n(\wt X,\Q))
\]
is an isomorphism for every $k$ (cf. [6], IV 6, cor. to th. 5). This characterizes the filtration $W$. Up to now, an analogue of Hodge's positivity theorem (cf. [6], IV 7, cor. to th. 7) is available only in very special cases. One hopes that the mixed structures $\calH_u$ determine, as $t\to0$, the asymptotic behavior of the family of pure structures $H^i(X_t,\Z)$ ($t\in D^*$).

\section*{Introduction}

According to Hodge, the cohomology space $H^n(X,\C)$ of a compact Kähler variety $X$ is endowed with a \emph{Hodge structure} of weight $n$, that is, with a natural bigrading
\[
H^n(X,\C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{pq}
\]
satisfying $\overline{H^{pq}}=H^{qp}$. We show here that the complex cohomology of a nonsingular algebraic variety, not necessarily compact, is endowed with a somewhat more general kind of structure, which presents $H^n(X,\C)$ as a successive extension of Hodge structures of decreasing weights, lying between $2n$ and $n$, whose Hodge numbers $h^{pq}=\dim H^{pq}$ are zero for $p>n$ or $q>n$.

The reader will find in [14] an exposition of the yoga underlying this construction.

The proof, essentially algebraic, rests on the one hand on Hodge theory and on the other hand on Hironaka's resolution of singularities, which permits one, via a spectral sequence, to \emph{express} the cohomology of a nonsingular quasi-projective algebraic variety in terms of the cohomology of nonsingular projective varieties.

Section 1 contains, besides a few elementary facts about filtrations collected for the reader's convenience, two key results:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Theorem (1.2.10), which will be used only through its corollary (2.3.5), giving the fundamental properties of mixed Hodge structures;
\item the \emph{lemma on two filtrations} (1.3.16).
\end{enumerate}
Section 2 recalls Hodge theory and introduces mixed Hodge structures. The heart of the paper is no. 3.2, which defines the mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(X,\C)$ and establishes certain degeneracies of spectral sequences.

Section 4 gives various applications, all deduced from (4.1.1) and from the theory of the $(K/k)$-trace for Hodge structures which follows from it (4.1.2). The principal ones are (4.2.6) and (4.4.15).

\section*{1. Filtrations}
\subsection*{1.1. Filtered objects}

\paragraph{(1.1.1)} Let $\calA$ be an abelian category. We shall have to consider filtrations of type $\Z$, usually finite, on the objects of $\calA$.

\paragraph{Definition (1.1.2).} A decreasing, respectively increasing, filtration $F$ of an object $A$ of $\calA$ is a family $(F^n(A))_{n\in\Z}$, respectively $(F_n(A))_{n\in\Z}$, of subobjects of $A$, satisfying
\[
\forall n,m\qquad n\le m\Rightarrow F^n(A)\supset F^m(A)
\]
(resp. $\forall n,m\quad n\le m\Rightarrow F_n(A)\subset F_m(A)$).

A filtered object is an object endowed with a filtration. When no confusion is possible, the same letter will often denote filtrations on different objects of $\calA$.

If $F$ is a decreasing, respectively increasing, filtration on $A$, put $F^{\infty}(A)=0$ and $F^{-\infty}(A)=A$ (resp. $F_{-\infty}(A)=0$ and $F_{\infty}(A)=A$).

The shifted filtrations of a decreasing filtration $W$ are defined by
\[
W[n]^p(A)=W^{n+p}(A).
\]

\paragraph{(1.1.3)} If $F$ is a decreasing, respectively increasing, filtration of $A$, then the $F_n(A)=F^{-n}(A)$, respectively the $F^n(A)=F_{-n}(A)$, form an increasing, respectively decreasing, filtration of $A$. Thus in principle it is enough to consider decreasing filtrations; unless explicitly stated otherwise, the word \emph{filtration} will henceforth mean \emph{decreasing filtration}.

\paragraph{(1.1.4)} A filtration $F$ of $A$ is called finite if there exist $n$ and $m$ such that $F^n(A)=A$ and $F^m(A)=0$.

\paragraph{(1.1.5)} A morphism from a filtered object $(A,F)$ to a filtered object $(B,F)$ is a morphism $f$ from $A$ to $B$ satisfying
\[
f(F^n(A))\subset F^n(B)\qquad\text{for }n\in\Z.
\]
The filtered objects (respectively, the objects with finite filtrations) of $\calA$ form an additive category in which finite inductive and projective limits exist (and hence so do the kernels, cokernels, images, and coimages of a morphism).

A morphism $f:(A,F)\to(B,F)$ is called strict, or strictly compatible with the filtrations, if the canonical arrow from $\Coim(f)$ to $\Imop(f)$ is an isomorphism of filtered objects (cf. (1.1.11)).

\paragraph{(1.1.6)} Let ${}^{\circ}$ be the contravariant identity functor from $\calA$ to the dual category $\calA^{\circ}$. If $(A,F)$ is a filtered object of $\calA$, the objects $(A/F^{1-n}(A))^{\circ}$ are identified with subobjects of $A^{\circ}$. The filtration on $A^{\circ}$ dual to $F$ is defined by
\[
F^n(A^{\circ})=(A/F^{1-n}(A))^{\circ}.
\]
The bidual of $(A,F)$ is identified with $(A,F)$. This construction identifies the dual of the category of filtered objects of $\calA$ with the category of filtered objects of $\calA^{\circ}$.

\paragraph{(1.1.7)} If $(A,F)$ is a filtered object of $\calA$, its associated graded object is the object of $\calA^{\Z}$ defined by
\[
\Gr^n(A)=F^n(A)/F^{n+1}(A).
\]
The convention (1.1.6) is justified by the simple formula
\[
\Gr^n(A^{\circ})=\Gr^{-n}(A)^{\circ},
\]
which is verified on the autodual diagram
\begin{equation}\tag{1.1.7.1}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.2em,row sep=1.0em]
& A/F^n(A) & A/F^{n+1}(A) \arrow[l] & 0 \\
& & A \arrow[ul] \arrow[u] & \Gr^n(A) \arrow[ul] \arrow[u] \\
& F^{n+1}(A) \arrow[r] \arrow[ur] & F^n(A) \arrow[u] \arrow[ur] & & 0 \arrow[ul]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{(1.1.8)} Let $(A,F)$ be a filtered object and let $j:X\hookrightarrow A$ be a subobject of $A$. The filtration induced on $X$ by $F$ is the unique filtration on $X$ such that $j$ is strictly compatible with the filtrations; one has
\[
F^n(X)=j^{-1}(F^n(A))=X\cap F^n(A).
\]
Dually, the quotient filtration on $A/X$, the unique filtration such that $p:A\to A/X$ is strictly compatible with the filtrations, is given by
\[
F^n(A/X)=p(F^n(A))\simeq (X+F^n(A))/X\simeq F^n(A)/(X\cap F^n(A)).
\]

\paragraph{Lemma (1.1.9).} If $X$ and $Y$ are two subobjects of $A$, with $X\subset Y$, then on $Y/X\simeq\Ker(A/X\to A/Y)$ the quotient filtration from $Y$ coincides with the filtration induced from $A/X$. In the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.3em,row sep=1.0em]
A/Y && A/X \arrow[ll] & \\
& A \arrow[ul] \arrow[ur] && Y/X \arrow[ul] \\
X \arrow[ur] \arrow[rr] && Y \arrow[ul] \arrow[uu] \arrow[ur] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
the arrows are strict.

\paragraph{(1.1.10)} The filtration of (1.1.9) on $Y/X$ will be called the filtration induced by that of $A$. By (1.1.9), its definition is autodual.

In particular, if $\Sigma:A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C$ is a $0$-sequence and if $B$ is filtered, then
\[
H(\Sigma)=\Ker(g)/\Imop(f)=\Ker(\Coker(f)\to\Coim(g))
\]
is endowed with a canonical induced filtration.

The reader will verify the following.

\paragraph{Proposition (1.1.11).} \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Let $f:(A,F)\to(B,F)$ be a morphism of finitely filtered objects. For $f$ to be strict, it is necessary and sufficient that the sequence
\[
0\to\Gr(\Ker(f))\to\Gr(A)\to\Gr(B)\to\Gr(\Coker(f))\to0
\]
be exact.
\item Let $\Sigma:(A,F)\to(B,F)\to(C,F)$ be a $0$-sequence of strict morphisms. Then one has canonically
\[
H(\Gr(\Sigma))\simeq\Gr(H(\Sigma)).
\]
In particular, if $\Sigma$ is exact in $\calA$, then $\Gr(\Sigma)$ is exact in $\calA^{\Z}$.
\end{enumerate}

In a category of modules, to say that a morphism $f:(A,F)\to(B,F)$ is strict means that every $b\in B$ of filtration $\ge n$ ($b\in F^n(B)$) which is in the image of $A$ is already in the image of $F^n(A)$:
\[
f(F^n(A))=f(A)\cap F^n(B).
\]

\paragraph{(1.1.12)} If $\otimes:\calA_1\times\cdots\times\calA_n\to\calB$ is a multiadditive right exact functor, and if $A_i$ is a finitely filtered object of $\calA_i$ ($1\le i\le n$), one defines a filtration on $\bigotimes_{i=1}^nA_i$ by
\[
F^k\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i\right)=\sum_{\sum k_i=k}\Imop\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n F^{k_i}(A_i)\to\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i\right)
\]
(sum of subobjects).

Dually, if $H$ is left exact, put
\[
F^k(H(A_i))=\bigcap_{\sum k_i=k}\Ker\left(H(A_i)\to H(A_i/F^{k_i}(A_i))\right).
\]

For exact $H$, the two definitions are equivalent. These definitions are extended to functors contravariant in certain variables by (1.1.6). In particular, for the left exact functor $\Hom$, one puts
\[
F^k(\Hom(A,B))=\{f:A\to B\mid \forall n,\ f(F^n(A))\subset F^{n+k}(B)\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\Hom((A,F),(B,F))=F^0(\Hom(A,B)).
\]

Under the preceding hypotheses, one has evident morphisms
\[
\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\Gr(A_i)\to \Gr\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^nA_i\right)
\]
and
\[
\Gr H(A_i)\to H(\Gr(A_i)).
\]
For exact $H$, these are mutually inverse isomorphisms.

These constructions are compatible with the composition of functors, in a sense which we leave to the reader not to make explicit.

\subsection*{1.2. Opposite filtrations}

\paragraph{(1.2.1)} Let $A$ be an object of $\calA$ endowed with two filtrations $F$ and $G$. By definition, $\Gr_F^m(A)$ is a quotient of a subobject of $A$, and as such is endowed with a filtration induced by $G$ (1.1.10). Passing to the associated graded object, one defines a bigraded object $(\Gr_G^n\Gr_F^m(A))_{n,m\in\Z}$. By a lemma of Zassenhaus, $\Gr_G^n\Gr_F^m(A)$ and $\Gr_F^m\Gr_G^n(A)$ are canonically isomorphic: if one defines the induced filtrations (1.1.10) as quotient filtrations of filtrations induced on a subobject, one has
\[
\begin{array}{rcc}
\Gr_G^n\Gr_F^m(A)&\approx&
(F^m(A)\cap G^n(A))/((F^{m+1}(A)\cap G^n(A))+(F^m(A)\cap G^{n+1}(A)))\\
&&\Big\Vert\\
\Gr_F^m\Gr_G^n(A)&\approx&
(G^n(A)\cap F^m(A))/((G^{n+1}(A)\cap F^m(A))+(G^n(A)\cap F^{m+1}(A))).
\end{array}
\]

\paragraph{(1.2.2)} Let $H$ be a third filtration of $A$. It induces a filtration on $\Gr_F(A)$, and hence on $\Gr_G\Gr_F(A)$. It also induces a filtration on $\Gr_F\Gr_G(A)$. One should note that these filtrations do not in general correspond under the isomorphism (1.2.1). In the expression $\Gr_H\Gr_G\Gr_F(A)$, therefore, $G$ and $H$ play symmetric roles, but $F$ and $G$ do not.

\paragraph{Definition (1.2.3).} Two finite filtrations $F$ and $\overline F$ on $A$ are called $n$-opposite if
\[
\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}(A)=0\qquad\text{for }p+q\ne n.
\]

\paragraph{(1.2.4)} If $A^{p,q}$ is a bigraded object of $\calA$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item $A^{p,q}=0$ except for finitely many pairs $(p,q)$;
\item $A^{p,q}=0$ for $p+q\ne n$,
\end{enumerate}
then one defines two finite $n$-opposite filtrations of $A=\sum_{p,q}A^{p,q}$ by putting
\begin{align}
F^p(A)&=\sum_{p'\ge p} A^{p',q'}, \tag{1.2.4.1}\\
\overline F^q(A)&=\sum_{q'\ge q} A^{p',q'}. \tag{1.2.4.2}
\end{align}
One has
\[
\tag{1.2.4.3}
\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}(A)=A^{p,q}.
\]
Conversely:

\paragraph{Proposition (1.2.5).} \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Let $F$ and $\overline F$ be two finite filtrations on $A$. For $F$ and $\overline F$ to be $n$-opposite, it is necessary and sufficient that
\[
\forall p,q\qquad p+q=n+1\Rightarrow F^p(A)\oplus\overline F^q(A)\iso A.
\]
\item If $F$ and $\overline F$ are $n$-opposite, and if one puts
\[
\begin{cases}
A^{p,q}=0 & \text{for }p+q\ne n,\\
A^{p,q}=F^p(A)\cap\overline F^q(A) & \text{for }p+q=n,
\end{cases}
\]
then $A$ is the direct sum of the $A^{p,q}$, and $F$ and $\overline F$ are deduced from the bigrading $A^{p,q}$ of $A$ by the procedure (1.2.4).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Proof.} (i) The condition $\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^q(A)=0$ for $p+q>n$ means that
\[
F^p\cap\overline F^q=(F^{p+1}\cap\overline F^q)+(F^p\cap\overline F^{q+1})\qquad(p+q>n).
\]
By hypothesis, $F^p\cap\overline F^q$ is zero for $p+q$ sufficiently large; by descending induction one deduces that the condition $\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^q(A)=0$ for $p+q>n$ is equivalent to the condition $F^p(A)\cap\overline F^q(A)=0$ for $p+q>n$. Dually ((1.1.6), (1.1.7), (1.1.10)) the condition $\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^q(A)=0$ for $p+q<n$ is equivalent to $A=F^p(A)+\overline F^q(A)$ for $(1-p)+(1-q)>-n$, that is, for $p+q\le n+1$, and (i) follows.

(ii) If $F$ and $\overline F$ are $n$-opposite, we prove by descending induction on $p$ that
\[
\tag{1.2.5.1}
\bigoplus_{p'\ge p} A^{p',q'}\iso F^p(A).
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item For $F^p(A)=0$, the assertion is evident.
\item The decomposition $A=F^{p+1}(A)\oplus\overline F^{n-p}(A)$ induces on $F^p(A)\supset F^{p+1}(A)$ a decomposition
\[
F^p(A)=F^{p+1}(A)\oplus(F^p(A)\cap\overline F^{n-p}(A)),
\]
and the induction concludes the proof. For $p$ sufficiently small, $F^p(A)=A$. By (1.2.5.1), the $A^{p,q}$ therefore form a bigrading of $A$, and $F$ satisfies (1.2.4.1). That $\overline F$ satisfies (1.2.4.2) follows by symmetry.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{(1.2.6)} The constructions (1.2.4) and (1.2.5) establish quasi-inverse equivalences of categories between objects of $\calA$ endowed with two finite $n$-opposite filtrations and bigraded objects of $\calA$ of the type considered in (1.2.4).

\paragraph{Definition (1.2.7).} Three finite filtrations $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$ on an object $A$ of $\calA$ are called opposite if
\[
\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}\Gr_W^n(A)=0\qquad\text{for }p+q+n\ne0.
\]
This condition is symmetric in $F$ and $\overline F$. It means that $F$ and $\overline F$ induce on $W^n(A)/W^{n+1}(A)$ two $(-n)$-opposite filtrations. Put
\[
A^{p,q}=\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}\Gr_W^{-p-q}(A),
\]
whence decompositions (1.2.4), (1.2.5)
\[
\tag{1.2.7.1}
W^n(A)/W^{n+1}(A)=\bigoplus_{p+q=-n}A^{p,q}
\]
which make $\Gr_W(A)$ into a bigraded object.

\paragraph{Lemma (1.2.8).} Let $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$ be three finite opposite filtrations on $A$, and let $\sigma$ be a sequence $(p_i,q_i)_{i\ge0}$ of pairs of integers satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item $p_i\le p_j$ and $q_i\le q_j$ for $i\ge j$;
\item For $i>0$, $p_i+q_i=p_0+q_0-i+1$.
\end{enumerate}
Put $p=p_0$, $q=q_0$, $n=-p-q$, and
\[
A_{\sigma}=\left(\sum_{0\le i} (W^{n+i}(A)\cap F^{p_i}(A))\right)
\cap
\left(\sum_{0\le i} (W^{n+i}(A)\cap \overline F^{q_i}(A))\right).
\]
Then the projection from $W^n(A)$ to $\Gr_W^n(A)$ induces an isomorphism
\[
A_{\sigma}\iso A^{p,q}\subset\Gr_W^n(A).
\]

We prove by induction on $k$ the following assertion:

\noindent $(*_k)$ The projection from $W^n(A)/W^{n+k}(A)$ to $\Gr_W^n(A)$ induces an isomorphism from
\[
(((\sum_{i<k}(W^{n+i}(A)\cap F^{p_i}(A)))+W^{n+k}(A))
\cap
((\sum_{i<k}(W^{n+i}(A)\cap\overline F^{q_i}(A)))+W^{n+k}(A)))/W^{n+k}(A)
\]
to $A^{p,q}\subset\Gr_W^n(A)$.

For $k=1$, this is exactly the definition of $A^{p,q}$. By (1.2.5)(i), one has
\[
\tag{1.2.8.1}
F^{p_k}(\Gr_W^{n+k}(A))\oplus \overline F^{q_k}(\Gr_W^{n+k}(A))\iso \Gr_W^{n+k}(A).
\]
Put
\begin{align*}
B&=\sum_{i<k}(W^{n+i}(A)\cap F^{p_i}(A))\\
C&=\sum_{i<k}(W^{n+i}(A)\cap\overline F^{q_i}(A))\\
B'&=(W^{n+k}(A)\cap F^{p_k}(A))+W^{n+k+1}(A)\\
C'&=(W^{n+k}(A)\cap\overline F^{q_k}(A))+W^{n+k+1}(A)\\
D&=W^{n+k}(A)\\
E&=W^{n+k+1}(A).
\end{align*}
Formula (1.2.8.1) becomes
\[
B'+C'=D,
\]
and
\[
B'\cap C'=E.
\]
Moreover, since $p_k\le p_i$ $(i\le k)$,
\[
B\cap D\subset F^{p_k}(A)\cap W^{n+k}(A)\subset B'
\]
and since $q_k\le q_i$ $(i\le k)$,
\[
C\cap D\subset \overline F^{q_k}(A)\cap W^{n+k}(A)\subset C'.
\]
The assertion $(*_{k+1})$ therefore follows from $(*_k)$ and from the following lemma.

\paragraph{Lemma (1.2.9).} Let $B$, $C$, $B'$, $C'$, $D$, and $E$ be subobjects of $A$. Assume that
\[
B'+C'=D,
\qquad
B'\cap C'=E,
\]
\[
B\cap D\subset B',
\qquad
C\cap D\subset C'.
\]
Then,
\[
((B+B')\cap(C+C'))/E\iso((B+D)\cap(C+D))/D.
\]
To prove surjectivity, one writes
\begin{align*}
((B+B')\cap(C+C'))+D
&=(((B+B')\cap(C+C'))+B')+C'\\
&=((B+B')\cap(C+C'+B'))+C'\\
&=(B+B'+C')\cap(C+C'+B')\\
&=(B+D)\cap(C+D).
\end{align*}
To prove injectivity, one writes
\[
(B+B')\cap(C+C')\cap D=((B+B')\cap D)\cap((C+C')\cap D).
\]
Since $B'\subset D$, one has
\[
(B+B')\cap D=(B\cap D)+B'=B';
\]
similarly,
\[
(C+C')\cap D=C',
\]
and
\[
(B+B')\cap(C+C')\cap D=B'\cap C'=E.
\]
Finally, the proof of (1.2.8) is completed by observing that (1.2.8) is equivalent to $(*_k)$ for large $k$.

\paragraph{Theorem (1.2.10).} Let $\calA$ be an abelian category, and provisionally denote by $\calA'$ the category of objects of $\calA$ endowed with three opposite filtrations $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$. The morphisms in $\calA'$ are the morphisms in $\calA$ compatible with the three filtrations.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\calA'$ is an abelian category.
\item The kernel (respectively, the cokernel) of an arrow $f:A\to B$ in $\calA'$ is the kernel (respectively, the cokernel) of $f$ in $\calA$, endowed with the filtrations induced from those of $A$ (respectively, the quotient filtrations induced from those of $B$).
\item Every morphism $f:A\to B$ in $\calA'$ is strictly compatible with the filtrations $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$; the morphism $\Gr_W(f)$ is compatible with the bigradings of $\Gr_W(A)$ and $\Gr_W(B)$; the morphisms $\Gr_F(f)$ and $\Gr_{\overline F}(f)$ are strictly compatible with the filtration induced by $W$.
\item The functors \emph{forget the filtrations}, $\Gr_W$, $\Gr_F$, $\Gr_{\overline F}$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Gr_W\Gr_F&\simeq\Gr_F\Gr_W\simeq\Gr_{\overline F}\Gr_F\Gr_W\\
&\simeq\Gr_{\overline F}\Gr_W\simeq\Gr_W\Gr_{\overline F}
\end{aligned}
\]
from $\calA'$ to $\calA$ are exact.
\end{enumerate}

Let $\sigma_0(p,q)$ and $\sigma_1(p,q)$ denote the sequences
\[
\sigma_0(p,q)=(p,q),(p,q),(p,q-1),(p,q-2),(p,q-3),\ldots
\]
\[
\sigma_1(p,q)=(p,q),(p,q),(p-1,q),(p-2,q),(p-3,q),\ldots
\]
and, with the notation of (1.2.8), put
\[
A_i^{p,q}=A_{\sigma_i(p,q)}\qquad(i=0,1).
\]
If $f:A\to B$ is compatible with $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$, then
\[
\tag{1.2.10.1}
f(A_i^{p,q})\subset B_i^{p,q}\qquad(i=0,1).
\]
Assertion (iii) therefore follows from the following lemma.

\paragraph{Lemma (1.2.11).} The $A_i^{p,q}$ form a bigrading of $A$. One has
\[
\tag{1.2.11.1}
W^n(A)=\sum_{n+p+q\le0} A_i^{p,q}\qquad(i=0,1),
\]
\[
\tag{1.2.11.2}
F^p(A)=\sum_{p'\ge p} A_0^{p',q'},
\]
\[
\tag{1.2.11.3}
\overline F^q(A)=\sum_{q'\ge q} A_1^{p',q'}.
\]

By symmetry, it is enough to prove the assertions for $i=0$. Put $A_0=\bigoplus A_0^{p,q}$, and define on $A_0$ filtrations $W$ and $F$ by the formulae of (1.2.11). The canonical map $i$ from $A_0$ to $A$ is compatible with the filtrations $W$ and $F$. Moreover, by (1.2.8), $\Gr_W(i)$ is an isomorphism, and it induces isomorphisms of graded objects
\[
\tag{1.2.11.4}
\sum_{p+q=n} A_0^{p,q}\iso \Gr_W^{-n}(A)=\sum_{p+q=n}A^{p,q}.
\]
The morphism $i$ is therefore an isomorphism, and the $A_0^{p,q}$ form a bigrading of $A$. Formula (1.2.11.1) then expresses that $\Gr_W(i)$ is an isomorphism. By (1.2.11.4), $\Gr_F\Gr_W(i)$ is an isomorphism, hence so are $\Gr_W\Gr_F(i)$ and $\Gr_F(i)$. Formula (1.2.11.2) follows.

\paragraph{(1.2.12)} We prove (1.2.10). Let $f:A\to B$ be in $\calA'$ and endow $K=\Ker(f)$ with the filtrations induced from those of $A$. By (1.2.11), $\Gr_W(K)\hookrightarrow\Gr_W(A)$; moreover, the filtration $F$ (respectively, $\overline F$) of $K$ induces on $\Gr_W(K)$ the inverse-image filtration of the filtration $F$ on $\Gr_W(A)$. Finally, the subobject $\Gr_W(K)$ of $\Gr_W(A)$ is compatible with the bigrading of $\Gr_W(A)$:
\[
\Gr_W(K)=\bigoplus_{p,q}(\Gr_W(K)\cap A^{p,q}).
\]
It follows that
\[
\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}\Gr_W^n(K)\hookrightarrow \Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^{q}\Gr_W^n(A);
\]
the filtrations $W$, $F$, and $\overline F$ of $K$ are therefore opposite, and $K$ is a kernel of $f$ in $\calA'$. Together with the dual result, this proves (ii).

If $f$ is an arrow of $\calA'$, the canonical morphism from $\Coim(f)$ to $\Imop(f)$ is an isomorphism in $\calA$; by (iii), it is also an isomorphism in $\calA'$, which is therefore abelian.

The functor \emph{forget the filtrations} is exact by (ii). The exactness of the other functors in (iv) follows at once from (ii), (iii), and (1.1.11)(i) or (ii).

\paragraph{(1.2.13)} Let $A$ be an object of $\calA$ endowed with a finite increasing filtration $W$, and with two finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\overline F$. The construction (1.1.3) associates to $W_{\bullet}$ a decreasing filtration $W^{\bullet}$. We shall say that the filtrations $W_{\bullet}$, $F$, and $\overline F$ are opposite if the filtrations $W^{\bullet}$, $F$, and $\overline F$ are opposite, that is, if for every $n$ the filtrations induced by $F$ and $\overline F$ on
\[
\Gr_n^W(A)=W_n(A)/W_{n-1}(A)
\]
are $n$-opposite.

Theorem (1.2.10) carries over trivially to this variant.

\subsection*{1.3. The lemma on two filtrations}

\paragraph{(1.3.1)} Let $K$ be a differential complex of objects of $\calA$, endowed with a filtration $F$. This filtration is called biregular if it induces on each component of $K$ a finite filtration. Recall the definition of the terms $E_r^{pq}(K,F)$, or simply $E_r^{pq}$, of the spectral sequence defined by $F$. Put
\[
Z_r^{pq}=\Ker\left(d:F^p(K^{p+q})\to K^{p+q+1}/F^{p+r}(K^{p+q+1})\right),
\]
and define $B_r^{pq}$ dually by the formula
\[
K^{p+q}/B_r^{pq}=\coker\left(d:F^{p-r+1}(K^{p+q-1})\to K^{p+q}/F^{p+1}(K^{p+q})\right).
\]
These formulae still make sense for $r=\infty$.

One should note that the use made here of the notation $B_r^{pq}$ is different from that of Godement [TF].

By definition one has:
\begin{align}
E_r^{pq}&=\Imop\left(Z_r^{pq}\to K^{p+q}/B_r^{pq}\right) \tag{1.3.1.1}\\
&=Z_r^{pq}/(B_r^{pq}\cap Z_r^{pq}) \tag{1.3.1.2}\\
&=\Ker\left(K^{p+q}/B_r^{pq}\to K^{p+q}/(Z_r^{pq}+B_r^{pq})\right). \tag{1.3.1.3}
\end{align}
One can also write
\begin{align}
B_r^{p*}\cap Z_r^{p*}
&\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=}(dF^{p-r+1}+F^{p+1})\cap(d^{-1}F^{p+r}\cap F^p) \notag\\
&=(dF^{p-r+1}\cap F^p)+(F^{p+1}\cap d^{-1}F^{p+r}), \tag{1.3.1.4}
\end{align}
since $dF^{p-r+1}\subset d^{-1}F^{p+r}$ and $F^{p+1}\subset F^p$.


For $r<\infty$, the $E_r$ form a complex graded by the degree $p-r(p+q)$, and $E_{r+1}$ is expressed as the cohomology of this complex:
\[
\tag{1.3.1.5}
E_{r+1}^{p,q}=H\bigl(E_r^{p-r,q+r-1}\xrightarrow{d_r}E_r^{p,q}\xrightarrow{d_r}E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\bigr).
\]
For $r=0$ one has
\[
\tag{1.3.1.6}
E_0^{**}=\Gr_F^*(K^*).
\]

\paragraph{Proposition (1.3.2).} Let $K$ be a complex endowed with a biregular filtration $F$. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the spectral sequence defined by $F$ degenerates ($E_1=E_{\infty}$).
\item the morphisms $d:K^i\to K^{i+1}$ are strictly compatible with the filtrations.
\end{enumerate}
We check this when $\calA$ is a category of modules. For fixed $p$ and $q$, the hypothesis that the arrows $d_r$ with source $E_r^{p,q}$ are zero for $r\geq1$ means that, if $x\in F^p(K^{p+q})$ satisfies $dx\in F^{p+1}(K^{p+q+1})$, then there exists $y$ in $K^{p+q}$ such that $dy=0$ and such that $x$ and $y$ have the same image in $E_1^{p,q}$. Modifying $y$ by a boundary and putting $z=x-y$, one obtains
\[
\forall x\in F^p(K^{p+q})\;\bigl(dx\in F^{p+1}(K^{p+q+1})\Rightarrow
\exists z\in F^{p+1}(K^{p+q}),\ dz=dx\bigr)
\]
or, in other words,
\[
\tag{1}
F^{p+1}(K^{p+q+1})\cap dF^p(K^{p+q})=dF^{p+1}(K^{p+q}).
\]
If this condition holds for all $p$ and $q$, then by induction on $r$ one has
\[
F^{p+r}\cap dF^p=dF^{p+r},
\]
which, for $p+r$ large, becomes
\[
\tag{2}
F^p\cap dK=dF^p.
\]
Assertion (2) trivially implies (i), and is equivalent to (ii). This proves (1.3.2).

\paragraph{(1.3.3)} If $(K,F)$ is a filtered complex, we shall denote by $\Dec(K)$ the complex $K$ endowed with the shifted filtration
\[
\Dec(F)^pK^n=Z_1^{p+n,-p}.
\]
This filtration is compatible with the differentials:
\[
dZ_1^{p+n,-p}\subset F^{p+n+1}(K^{n+1})\cap\Ker(d)
       \subset Z_{\infty}^{p+n+1,-p}\subset Z_1^{p+n+1,-p}.
\]
Since
\[
\tag{1.3.3.1}
Z_1^{p+1+n,-p-1}\subset F^{p+1+n}(K^n)\subset B_1^{p+n,-p}\subset Z_1^{p+n,-p},
\]
the evident map from $Z_1^{p+n,-p}/Z_1^{p+1+n,-p-1}$ to $Z_1^{p+n,-p}/B_1^{p+n,-p}$ is a morphism
\[
\tag{1.3.3.2}
u:E_0^{p,n-p}(\Dec K)\longrightarrow E_1^{p+n,-p}(K).
\]

\paragraph{Proposition (1.3.4).}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The morphisms (1.3.3.2) form a morphism of graded complexes from $E_0(\Dec K)$ to $E_1(K)$.
\item This morphism induces an isomorphism on cohomology.
\item Step by step, via (1.3.1.5), it induces isomorphisms of graded complexes
\[
E_r(\Dec(K))\iso E_{r+1}(K)\qquad(r\ge1).
\]
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Proof.} Let $F'$ be the filtration of $K$ defined by
\[
F'^p(K^n)=\Dec(F)^{p-n}(K^n)=Z_1^{p,n-p}.
\]
There are trivial isomorphisms, compatible with the $d_r$ and with (1.3.1.5),
\[
\tag{1.3.4.1}
E_r^{p,n-p}(\Dec K)=E_{r+1}^{p+n,-p}(K,F').
\]
The map $u$ is deduced from (1.3.4.1) and from the identity morphism
\[
(K,F')\longrightarrow(K,F).
\]
This proves (i), and it remains to verify that for $r\ge2$,
\[
E_r^{p,q}(K,F')\simeq E_r^{p,q}(K,F).
\]
Indeed one has
\[
Z_r^{p,q}(K,F')=Z_r^{p,q}(K,F)\qquad(r\ge1),
\]
and
\[
Z_r^{p,q}(K,F')\cap B_r^{p,q}(K,F')=Z_r^{p,q}(K,F)\cap B_r^{p,q}(K,F)\qquad(r\ge2),
\]
and then applies (1.3.1.2).

\paragraph{(1.3.5)} The construction (1.3.3) is not self-dual. The dual construction consists in defining
\[
\Dec^*(F)^pK^n=B_1^{p+n-1,-p+1}.
\]
One then has morphisms
\[
E_0^{p,n-p}(\Dec K)\longrightarrow E_1^{p+n,p}(K)\longrightarrow E_0^{p,n-p}(\Dec^*K)
\]
and, for $r\ge1$, isomorphisms
\[
E_r^{p,n-p}(\Dec K)\iso E_{r+1}^{p+n,p}(K)\iso E_r^{p,n-p}(\Dec^*K).
\]
Recall that a morphism of complexes is called a quasi-isomorphism if it induces an isomorphism on cohomology.

\paragraph{Definition (1.3.6).}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item A morphism $f:(K,F)\to(K',F')$ of filtered complexes with biregular filtration is a filtered quasi-isomorphism if $\Gr_F(f)$ is a quasi-isomorphism, i.e. if the $E_1^{p,q}(f)$ are isomorphisms.
\item A morphism $f:(K,F,W)\to(K',F',W')$ between biregular bifiltered complexes is a bifiltered quasi-isomorphism if $\Gr_F\Gr_W(f)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{(1.3.7)} Let $K$ be a differential complex of objects of $\calA$, endowed with two filtrations $F$ and $W$. Let $E_r^{p,q}$ be the spectral sequence defined by $W$. The filtration $F$ induces several filtrations on the $E_r^{p,q}$, which we shall compare.

\paragraph{(1.3.8)} Formula (1.3.1.2) identifies $E_r^{p,q}$ with a quotient of a subobject of $K^{p+q}$. Thus the term $E_r^{p,q}$ receives a filtration $F_d$ induced by $F$, called the first direct filtration.

\paragraph{(1.3.9)} Dually, formula (1.3.1.3) identifies $E_r^{p,q}$ with a subobject of a quotient of $K^{p+q}$, and hence gives a new filtration $F_{d*}$ induced by $F$, the second direct filtration.

\paragraph{Lemma (1.3.10).} On $E_0$ and $E_1$ one has $F_d=F_{d*}$. For $r=0$ or $1$, one has $B_r^{p,q}\subset Z_r^{p,q}$, and one applies (1.1.9).

\paragraph{(1.3.11)} Formula (1.3.1.5) identifies $E_{r+1}^{p,q}$ with a quotient of a subobject of $E_r^{p,q}$. The recurrent filtration $F_r$ of the $E_r^{p,q}$ is defined by the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item on $E_0^{p,q}$, $F_r=F_d=F_{d*}$.
\item on $E_{r+1}^{p,q}$, the recurrent filtration is the one induced by the recurrent filtration of $E_r^{p,q}$.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{(1.3.12)} The definitions (1.3.8) and (1.3.9) still make sense for $r=\infty$. If the filtration of $K$ is biregular, the direct filtrations of $E_{\infty}^{p,q}$ coincide with those of $E_r^{p,q}=E_{\infty}^{p,q}$ for $r$ large enough, and the recurrent filtration of $E_{\infty}^{p,q}$ is defined by requiring it to coincide with that of $E_r^{p,q}$ for $r$ large enough.

The filtrations $F$ and $W$ each induce a filtration of $H^*(K)$, and $E_{\infty}^{**}=\Gr_W^*(H^*(K))$. The filtration $F$ of $H^*(K)$ therefore induces a new filtration on $E_{\infty}^{p,q}$.

\paragraph{Proposition (1.3.13).}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For the first direct filtration, the morphisms $d_r$ are compatible with filtrations. If $E_{r+1}^{p,q}$ is regarded as a quotient of a subobject of $E_r^{p,q}$, then the first direct filtration on $E_{r+1}^{p,q}$ is finer than the filtration $F'$ induced by the first direct filtration on $E_r^{p,q}$; one has $F_d(E_{r+1}^{p,q})\subset F'(E_{r+1}^{p,q})$.
\item Dually, the morphisms $d_r$ are compatible with the second direct filtration, and the second direct filtration on $E_{r+1}^{p,q}$ is less fine than the filtration induced by that of $E_r^{p,q}$.
\item $F_d(E_r^{p,q})\subset F_r(E_r^{p,q})\subset F_{d*}(E_r^{p,q})$.
\item On $E_{\infty}^{p,q}$, the filtration induced by the filtration $F$ of $H^*(K)$ (1.3.12) is finer than the first direct filtration and less fine than the second.
\end{enumerate}
(i) is evident, (ii) is its dual, and (iii) follows by induction. The first assertion of (iv) is easy to check, and the second is dual to it.

\paragraph{(1.3.14)} Denote by $\Dec(K)$, respectively by $\Dec^*(K)$, the complex $K$ endowed with the filtrations $\Dec(W)$ and $F$, respectively $\Dec^*(W)$ and $F$.

It is clear from (1.3.4.1) that the isomorphism (1.3.4) transforms the first direct filtration of $E_r(\Dec K)$ into the first direct filtration of $E_{r+1}(K)$, for $r\ge1$. The dual isomorphism (1.3.5) transforms the second direct filtration of $E_r(\Dec^*K)$ into the second direct filtration of $E_{r+1}(K)$.

\paragraph{Lemma (1.3.15).} If the filtration $F$ is biregular, and if, on the $\Gr_W^p(K)$, the morphisms $d$ are strictly compatible with the filtration induced by $F$, then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the morphism (1.3.3.2) of graded complexes filtered by $F$
\[
u:\Gr_{\Dec(W)}(K)\longrightarrow E_1(K,W)
\]
is a filtered quasi-isomorphism;
\item dually, the morphism (1.3.5)
\[
u:E_1(K,W)\longrightarrow \Gr_{\Dec^*(W)}(K)
\]
is a filtered quasi-isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
By duality it is enough to prove (i). By (1.3.3) and (1.3.4), the complex $E_1(K,W)$, filtered by $F$, is a quotient of the filtered complex $\Gr_{\Dec(W)}(K)$. Let $U$ be the filtered kernel complex; it is acyclic by (1.3.4) (ii). The long exact cohomology sequence associated with the exact sequence of complexes
\[
0\to\Gr_F(U)\to\Gr_F(\Gr_{\Dec(W)}(K))\to\Gr_F(E_1(K,W))\to0
\]
shows that $u$ is a filtered quasi-isomorphism if and only if $\Gr_F(U)$ is an acyclic complex. By (1.3.2), and because $U$ is acyclic, this amounts to requiring that the differentials of $U$ be strictly compatible with the filtration $F$. From (1.3.3.1) one obtains that $U$ is the sum, over $p$, of the complexes
\[
(U^p)^n=B_1^{p+n,-p}/Z_1^{p+1+n,-p-1},
\]
endowed with the filtration induced by $F$.

Each differential $d$ of each of the complexes $U^p$ is included in a commutative diagram of filtered objects of the following type, where, for simplicity, the total or complementary degree has been omitted:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.2em,row sep=1.4em]
B^p/Z^{p+1} \arrow[rrrr,"d"] \arrow[dr]
  & & & & B^{p+1}/Z^{p+1} \arrow[dl] \arrow[dd] \\
  & \Coim(d) \arrow[rr,"{\text{\textcircled{\scriptsize 5}}}"]
  & & \Imop(d) \arrow[ur] \arrow[dr] & \\
W^{p+1}/Z^{p+1} \arrow[uu] \arrow[ur] \arrow[rrrr,"{\text{\textcircled{\scriptsize 3}}}" near start]
  & & {\text{\raisebox{1.2em}{\textcircled{\scriptsize 4}}}} & & B^{p+1}/W^{p+2} \arrow[dd] \\
  & & {\text{\textcircled{\scriptsize 2}}} & & \\
W^{p+1}/W^{p+2} \arrow[uu] \arrow[rrrr,"{\text{\textcircled{\scriptsize 1}}}"]
  & & & & W^{p+1}/W^{p+2}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
By hypothesis, the morphism (1) is strict. Since the square (2) is just the canonical decomposition of (1), the arrow (3) is a filtered isomorphism. The arrows of the trapezium (4) are isomorphisms; hence they are filtered isomorphisms, because (3) is one. That (5) is a filtered isomorphism means that $d$ is strict. This proves (1.3.15).

\paragraph{Theorem (1.3.16).} Let $K$ be a complex endowed with two filtrations $W$ and $F$, with $F$ biregular. Let $r_0\ge0$ be an integer, and suppose that, for $0\le r<r_0$, the differentials of the graded complex $E_r(K,W)$ are strictly compatible with the filtration $F_r$. Then, for $r\le r_0+1$, one has
\[
F_d=F_r=F_{d*}\quad\text{on }E_r^{p,q}.
\]
The theorem is proved by induction on $r_0$. For $r_0=0$ the hypothesis is empty, and one applies (1.3.10) and (1.3.13), (iii). For $r_0\ge1$, by the induction hypothesis, one has $F_d=F_r=F_{d*}$ on $E_r^{p,q}$ for $r\le r_0$.

By (1.3.15), the morphism $u:E_0(\Dec K)\to E_1(K)$ is a filtered quasi-isomorphism. It therefore induces a filtered isomorphism from $H^*(\Dec K)$ to $H^*(E_1(K))$:
\[
u:(E_1(\Dec K),F_r)\iso(E_2(K),F_r).
\]
Step by step, it follows that the canonical isomorphism from $E_s(\Dec K)$ to $E_{s+1}(K)$ ($s\ge1$) is a filtered isomorphism for the recurrent filtration. On $E_1(\Dec(K))$, $F_r=F_d$ (1.3.10), and we already know (1.3.14) that $u'$ is a filtered isomorphism
\[
u':(E_1(\Dec K),F_d)\iso(E_2(K),F_d).
\]
Thus on $E_2(K)$ one has $F_d=F_r$. Together with the dual result, this proves (1.3.16) for $r_0=1$.

Assume now that $r_0\ge2$. Then the arrows $d_1$ of $E_1(K)$ are strictly compatible with the filtrations; hence so are the arrows $d_0$ of $E_0(\Dec K)$ (indeed, $u$ induces an isomorphism of spectral sequences, and one applies the criterion (1.3.2)).

For $0<s<r_0-1$, the isomorphism $(E_s(\Dec K),F_r)\simeq(E_{s+1}(K),F_r)$ shows that the $d_s$ are strictly compatible with the recurrent filtrations. By the induction hypothesis one therefore has $F_d=F_r$ on $E_s(\Dec K)$ for $s\le r_0$. The isomorphism $(E_s(\Dec K),F_d)\simeq(E_{s+1}(K),F_d)$ (1.3.13) then shows that $F_d=F_r$ on $E_r(K)$ for $r\le r_0+1$. Together with the dual result, this proves (1.3.16).

\paragraph{Corollary (1.3.17).} Under the general hypotheses of (1.3.16), suppose that, for every $r$, the differentials $d_r$ are strictly compatible with the recurrent filtrations of the $E_r$. Then, on $E_{\infty}$, the filtrations $F_d$, $F_r$, and $F_{d*}$ coincide, and coincide with the filtration induced by the filtration $F$ of $H^*(K)$.

This follows at once from (1.3.16) and (1.3.13) (iv).

\subsection*{1.4. Hypercohomology of filtered complexes.}

In this section we recall some standard constructions in hypercohomology. We do not use the language of derived categories, which would be the most natural here.

\emph{Throughout this section, by a ``complex'' we shall mean a ``complex bounded below''.}

\paragraph{(1.4.1)} Let $T$ be a left exact functor from an abelian category $\calA$ to an abelian category $\calB$. Assume that every object of $\calA$ injects into an injective object; the derived functors $R^iT:\calA\to\calB$ are therefore defined. An object $A$ of $\calA$ will be called acyclic for $T$ if $R^iT(A)=0$ for $i>0$.

\paragraph{(1.4.2)} Let $(A,F)$ be a filtered object with a finite filtration, and let $TF$ be the filtration of $TA$ by its subobjects $TF^pA$ (these are subobjects because $T$ is left exact). If $\Gr_F(A)$ is $T$-acyclic, then the $F^p(A)$ are $T$-acyclic as successive extensions of $T$-acyclic objects. The image under $T$ of the sequence
\[
0\to F^{p+1}(A)\to F^p(A)\to\Gr^p(A)\to0
\]
is therefore exact, and
\[
\tag{1.4.2.1}
\Gr_{TF}TA\iso T\Gr_FA.
\]

\paragraph{(1.4.3)} Let $A$ be an object with two finite filtrations $F$ and $W$ such that $\Gr_F\Gr_WA$ is $T$-acyclic. The objects $\Gr_FA$ and $\Gr_WA$ are then $T$-acyclic, as are the $F^q(A)\cap W^p(A)$. The sequences
\[
0\to T(F^q\cap W^{p+1})\to T(F^q\cap W^p)\to T\bigl((F^q\cap W^p)/(F^q\cap W^{p+1})\bigr)\to0
\]
are therefore exact, and $T(F^q(\Gr_W^p(A)))$ is the image in $T(\Gr_W^p(A))$ of $T(F^p\cap W^q)$. The diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
T(F^q\cap W^p) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & T(F^q\Gr_W^pA) \arrow[r] & T\Gr_W^pA \arrow[d]\\
TF^q\cap TW^p \arrow[rr] && \Gr_{TW}^pTA
\end{tikzcd}
\]
then shows that the isomorphism (1.4.2.1) relative to $W$ carries the filtration $\Gr_{TW}(TF)$ to the filtration $T(\Gr_W(F))$.

\paragraph{(1.4.4)} Let $K$ be a complex of objects of $\calA$. The \emph{hypercohomology objects} $R^iT(K)$ are computed as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Choose a quasi-isomorphism $i:K\to K'$ such that the components of $K'$ are acyclic for $T$. For example, one may take for $K'$ the simple complex associated with a Cartan--Eilenberg injective resolution of $K$.
\item Put
\[
R^iT(K)=H^i(T(K')).
\]
\end{enumerate}
One checks that $R^iT(K)$ does not depend on the choice of $K'$, depends functorially on $K$, and that a quasi-isomorphism $f:K_1\to K_2$ induces \emph{isomorphisms}
\[
R^iT(f):R^iT(K_1)\longrightarrow R^iT(K_2).
\]

\paragraph{(1.4.5)} Let $F$ be a biregular filtration of $K$. A \emph{filtered $T$-acyclic resolution} of $K$ is a filtered quasi-isomorphism $i:K\to K'$ from $K$ to a biregular filtered complex such that the $\Gr^p(K'^n)$ are acyclic for $T$. If $K'$ is such a resolution, the $K'^n$ are acyclic for $T$ and the filtered complex (cf. (1.4.2)) $T(K')$ defines a spectral sequence
\[
E_1^{p,q}=R^{p+q}T(\Gr^pK)\Rightarrow R^{p+q}T(K).
\]
This is independent of the choice of $K'$. It is called the \emph{hypercohomology spectral sequence of the filtered complex $K$}. It depends functorially on $K$, and a filtered quasi-isomorphism induces an isomorphism of spectral sequences.

The differentials $d_1$ of this spectral sequence are the connecting morphisms defined by the short exact sequences
\[
0\to\Gr^{p+1}K\to F^pK/F^{p+2}K\to\Gr^pK\to0.
\]

\paragraph{(1.4.6)} Let $K$ be a complex. Denote by $\tau_{\le p}(K)$ the following subcomplex:
\[
\tau_{\le p}(K)^n=\begin{cases}
K^n& \text{for }n<p\\
\Ker(d)& \text{for }n=p\\
0& \text{for }n>p.
\end{cases}
\]
The \emph{filtration}, called \emph{canonical}, of $K$ by the $\tau_{\le p}(K)$ is obtained by shifting the trivial filtration $G$ for which $G^0(K)=K$ and $G^1(K)=0$. For the canonical filtration one has
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_1^{p,q}&=0 &&\text{if }p+q\ne-p\\
H^{-p} &&&\text{if }p+q=-p.
\end{aligned}
\]
A quasi-isomorphism $f:K\to K'$ is automatically a filtered quasi-isomorphism for the canonical filtrations.

\paragraph{(1.4.7)} The subcomplexes $\sigma_{\ge p}(K)$ of $K$:
\[
\sigma_{\ge p}(K)^n=\begin{cases}
0& \text{if }n<p\\
K^n& \text{if }n\ge p
\end{cases}
\]
define a biregular filtration, the \emph{stupid filtration} of $K$.

The hypercohomology spectral sequences attached to the stupid or canonical filtrations of $K$ are the two \emph{hypercohomology spectral sequences} of $K$.

\paragraph{Example (1.4.8). ---} Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map between topological spaces, and let $\calF$ be an abelian sheaf on $X$. Let $\calF^*$ be a resolution of $\calF$ by $f_*$-acyclic sheaves. Then $R^if_*\calF\simeq\calH^i(f_*\calF^*)$. Take as $T$ the functor $\Gamma(Y,\cdot)$. The hypercohomology spectral sequence of the complex $f_*\calF^*$, endowed with its canonical filtration (1.4.6),
\[
E_1^{p,q}=H^{2p+q}(Y,R^{-p}f_*\calF)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,\calF)
\]
is, up to the renumbering $E_r^{p,q}\mapsto E_{r+1}^{2p+q,-p}$, the \emph{Leray spectral sequence} for $f$ and $\calF$.

\paragraph{(1.4.9)} Let $(K,W,F)$ be a biregular bifiltered complex. To this complex one associates:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item A spectral sequence
\[
{}_WE_1^{p,n-p}=H^n(\Gr_W^p(K))\Rightarrow H^n(K),
\]
whose differentials ${}_Wd_1$ are the connecting morphisms deduced from the short exact sequences
\[
0\to\Gr_W^{p+1}(K)\to W^p(K)/W^{p+2}(K)\to\Gr_W^p(K)\to0;
\]
\item An analogous spectral sequence for the filtration $F$;
\item Exact squares
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small,row sep=large]
& 0 \arrow[d] & 0 \arrow[d] & 0 \arrow[d] & \\
0 \arrow[r] & \Gr_F^{p+1}\Gr_W^{q+1}K \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & F^p/F^{p+2}(\Gr_W^{q+1}K) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \Gr_F^{p}\Gr_W^{q+1}K \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & 0\\
0 \arrow[r] & \Gr_F^{p+1}(W^q/W^{q+2}(K)) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & F^p/F^{p+2}(W^q/W^{q+2}(K)) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \Gr_F^{p}(W^q/W^{q+2}(K)) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & 0\\
0 \arrow[r] & \Gr_F^{p+1}\Gr_W^{q}K \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & F^p/F^{p+2}\Gr_W^{q}K \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \Gr_F^{p}\Gr_W^{q}K \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & 0\\
& 0 & 0 & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The exterior rows and columns of this square define connecting morphisms
\[
{}_{F,W}d_1:H^n\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK\longrightarrow H^{n+1}\Gr_F^{p+1}\Gr_W^qK,
\]
\[
{}_{W,F}d_1:H^n\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK\longrightarrow H^{n+1}\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^{q+1}K.
\]
These morphisms satisfy
\[
\begin{gathered}
{}_{FW}d_1\circ{}_{WF}d_1+{}_{WF}d_1\circ{}_{FW}d_1=0\\
{}_{FW}d_1^2=0\qquad {}_{WF}d_1^2=0.
\end{gathered}
\]
The morphisms ${}_{FW}d_1$ are the $d_1$ morphisms of the spectral sequences $E^{(q)}$, with term $E_1^{(q)p,n-p}$ equal to
\[
\tag{1.4.9.1}
E_1^{p,q,n-p-q}\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=}H^n(\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK)\Rightarrow H^n(\Gr_W^qK)={}_WE_1^{q,n-q},
\]
defined by the filtered complex $\Gr_W^q(K)$. This spectral sequence abuts to the filtration induced by $F$ on $H^*\Gr_W^qK$. Similarly, the ${}_{WF}d_1$ are the $d_1$ of spectral sequences with the same initial terms
\[
\tag{1.4.9.2}
E_1^{p,q,n-p-q}=H^n(\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK)\Rightarrow H^n(\Gr_F^pK).
\]
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5.2em,row sep=3.2em]
& H^n\Gr_W^qK
  \arrow[dr,shift left=1.2pt,"{\scriptstyle({}_Wd_1)}"]
  \arrow[dr,shift right=1.2pt,no head]
& \\
H^n\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK
  \arrow[ur,shift left=1.2pt,"{\scriptstyle(F,{}_Wd_1)}"]
  \arrow[ur,shift right=1.2pt,no head]
  \arrow[dr,shift left=1.2pt,"{\scriptstyle(W,{}_Fd_1)}"']
  \arrow[dr,shift right=1.2pt,no head]
&& H^nK \\
& H^n\Gr_F^pK
  \arrow[ur,shift left=1.2pt,"{\scriptstyle({}_Fd_1)}"']
  \arrow[ur,shift right=1.2pt,no head]
&
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\end{enumerate}
These constructions are symmetric in $F$ and $W$, \emph{via} the isomorphism
\[
\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^q\simeq\Gr_W^q\Gr_F^p.
\]

\paragraph{(1.4.10)} One may also interpret the ${}_{W,F}d_1$ as the initial morphisms of a morphism of spectral sequences (1.4.9.2), abutting to ${}_Wd_1$. Indeed, let $C^q$ be the cone of the morphism
\[
W^q(K)/W^{q+2}(K)\longrightarrow\Gr_W^q(K).
\]
In the diagram
\[
\Sigma:\Gr_W^{q+1}(K)[1]\xrightarrow{u} C^q\xleftarrow{i}\Gr_W^q(K),
\]
$u$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and one has
\[
{}_Wd_1=H(u)^{-1}\circ H(i).
\]
In fact, $u$ is even a filtered quasi-isomorphism (for $F$), and the preceding construction defines a morphism from the spectral sequence defined by $(\Gr_W^q(K),F)$ to the one defined by $(\Gr_W^{q+1}(K)[1],F)$, a morphism which abuts to ${}_Wd_1$. The initial term of this morphism, deduced from $\Gr_F(\Sigma)$, is precisely ${}_{W,F}d_1$.

\paragraph{(1.4.11)} These constructions pass unchanged to hypercohomology. Let $K$ be a complex endowed with two biregular filtrations $F$ and $W$.

A \emph{bifiltered $T$-acyclic resolution} of $K$ is a bifiltered quasi-isomorphism $i:K\to K'$ such that the $\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^n(K'^m)$ are $T$-acyclic. Such resolutions always exist. In the special case where $\calA$ is the category of sheaves of $A$-modules on a topological space $X$, and where $T$ is the functor $\Gamma$ from $\calA$ to $A$-modules, one example of a bifiltered $T$-acyclic resolution of $K$ is the simple complex associated with the Godement double-resolution complex $\mathcal C^*(K)$ of $K$, filtered by the $\mathcal C^*(F^p(K))$ and the $\mathcal C^*(W^n(K))$. Since $\mathcal C^*$ is exact, one indeed has
\[
\Gr_F\Gr_W(\mathcal C^*(K))\simeq \mathcal C^*(\Gr_F\Gr_W(K)).
\]
No other case will be needed here.

If $K'$ is a bifiltered $T$-acyclic resolution of $K$, the complex $TK'$ is filtered by the $TF^pK'$ and the $TW^qK'$ (1.4.3). Moreover, $\Gr_W^n(K')$ is a filtered $T$-acyclic resolution (for $F$) of $\Gr_W^n(K)$, $\Gr_F^n(K')$ is a filtered $T$-acyclic resolution (for $W$) of $\Gr_F^n(K)$, $\Gr_F^n\Gr_W^m(K')$ is a $T$-acyclic resolution of $\Gr_F^n\Gr_W^m(K)$, and
\[
\begin{gathered}
T\Gr_FK'\approx\Gr_FTK'\qquad\text{(as a $W$-filtered complex)}\\
T\Gr_WK'\approx\Gr_WTK'\qquad\text{(as an $F$-filtered complex)}\\
T\Gr_F\Gr_WK'\approx\Gr_F\Gr_WTK'.
\end{gathered}
\]

\paragraph{Lemma (1.4.12). ---} Under the hypotheses of (1.4.11):
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The initial terms of the hypercohomology spectral sequences
\[
\tag{1}
{}_WE_1^{q,n-q}=R^nT(\Gr_W^qK)\Rightarrow R^nT(K)
\]
\[
\tag{2}
{}_FE_1^{p,n-p}=R^nT(\Gr_F^pK)\Rightarrow R^nT(K)
\]
are the abutments of the hypercohomology spectral sequences of the filtered complexes $\Gr_W^qK$ and $\Gr_F^pK$, with $E_1$ term given by
\[
\tag{3}
E_1^{p,q,n-p-q}\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=}R^nT(\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK)\Rightarrow {}_WE_1^{q,n-q}\qquad(q\ \text{fixed})
\]
\[
\tag{4}
E_1^{p,q,n-p-q}\underset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=}R^nT(\Gr_F^p\Gr_W^qK)\Rightarrow {}_FE_1^{p,n-p}\qquad(p\ \text{fixed}).
\]
\item The filtration of ${}_WE_1^{p,n-p}$, the abutment of the spectral sequence (3), is the filtration of ${}_WE_1^{p,n-p}(TK')$ induced by the filtration $F$ of $TK'$.
\item The differentials of the complexes $\Gr_W^n(T(K))$ are strictly compatible with the filtration $F$ if and only if the hypercohomology spectral sequences (3) degenerate at $E_1$.
\item The morphisms $d_1$ of the spectral sequence (4) are the initial terms of degree-one morphisms of spectral sequences (3) abutting to the morphisms $d_1$ of the spectral sequence (1).
\end{enumerate}
Assertions (i) and (iv) follow from (1.4.9) and (1.4.10) applied to $TK'$, \emph{via} the isomorphisms (1.4.11). Assertion (ii) is then immediate from the definition of the recurrent filtration $F$ (identical with the direct filtrations by (1.3.10) and (1.3.13) (iii)), and assertion (iii) follows from (1.3.2).

\section*{2. Hodge structures}
\subsection*{2.1. Pure structures.}

\paragraph{(2.1.1)} In what follows, $\C$ will denote an algebraic closure of $\R$: we do not assume that a root $i$ of the equation $x^2+1=0$ has been chosen. The theory will be invariant under complex conjugation (cf. (2.1.14)).

\paragraph{(2.1.2)} Let $S$ denote the real algebraic group $\C^*$, obtained by Weil restriction of scalars from $\C$ to $\R$ of the group $\Gm$:
\[
\begin{gathered}
S=\prod_{\C/\R}\Gm.\\
S(\R)=\C^*.
\end{gathered}
\]
The group $S$ is a torus, i.e. it is connected and of multiplicative type. It is therefore described by the finitely generated free abelian group
\[
X(S)=\Hom(S_{\C},\Gm)=\Hom(S,\Gm)(\C)
\]
of its complex characters, endowed with the action of $\Gal(\C/\R)=\Z/(2)$.

The group $X(S)$ has generators $z$ and $\bar z$, inducing respectively the identity and complex conjugation:
\[
\C^*=S(\R)\longrightarrow S(\C)\longrightarrow \Gm(\C)=\C^*.
\]
Complex conjugation exchanges $z$ and $\bar z$.

\paragraph{(2.1.3)} There is a canonical map
\[
\tag{2.1.3.1}
w:\Gm\longrightarrow S
\]




which, on real points, induces the inclusion of $\R^*$ into $\C^*$. One has
\[
\tag{2.1.3.2}
z w=\bar z w=\operatorname{Id}.
\]
There is also a map
\[
\tag{2.1.3.3}
N:S\longrightarrow\Gm
\]
which, on real points, is identified with the norm $N_{\C/\R}:\C^*\to\R^*$. One has
\[
\tag{2.1.3.4}
N=z\bar z
\]
and
\[
\tag{2.1.3.5}
N\circ w=(x\mapsto x^2).
\]
