\paragraph{Definition (2.1.4).} --- \emph{A real Hodge structure is a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ endowed with an action of the real algebraic group $S$.}

\paragraph{(2.1.5)} By the general theory of groups of multiplicative type, giving a real Hodge structure on $V$ is equivalent to giving a bigrading $V^{pq}$ of $V_{\C}=\C\otimes_{\R} V$ such that $\overline{V^{pq}}=V^{qp}$. The action of $S$ and the bigrading determine one another \emph{via} the condition:
\[
\tag{2.1.5.1}
\text{On }V^{pq},\quad S\text{ acts by multiplication by }z^p\bar z^q.
\]

\paragraph{(2.1.6)} Let $(\C,\times)$ be the multiplicative monoid, and put
\[
\overline S=\prod_{\C/\R}(\C,\times).
\]
If $V$ is a real vector space, giving an action of $\overline S$ on $V$ is equivalent to giving on $V$ a bigrading such that $\overline{V^{pq}}=V^{qp}$ and $V^{pq}=0$ for $p<0$ or $q<0$.

\paragraph{(2.1.7)} Let $V$ be a real Hodge structure, defined by a representation $\sigma$ of $S$ and by a bigrading $V^{pq}$. The grading of $V_{\C}$ by the $V_{\C}^n=\sum_{p+q=n}V^{pq}$ is then defined over $\R$. It is called the \emph{weight grading}. On $V^n=V\cap V_{\C}^n$, the representation $\sigma w$ of $\Gm$ is multiplication by $x^n$.

We shall say that $V$ is \emph{of weight $n$} if $V^{pq}=0$ for $p+q\ne n$, i.e. if $\sigma w$ is multiplication by $x^n$.

\paragraph{(2.1.8)} Let $V$ be a real Hodge structure. The \emph{Hodge filtration} on $V_{\C}$ is defined by
\[
F^p(V_{\C})=\sum_{p'\ge p}V^{p'q'}.
\]
By (1.2.6), one has

\paragraph{Proposition (2.1.9).} --- {\itshape Let $n$ be an integer. The construction (2.1.8) establishes an equivalence of categories between:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item the category of real Hodge structures of weight $n$;
\item the category of pairs consisting of a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a filtration $F$ on $V_{\C}=\C\otimes_{\R} V$ which is $n$-opposed to its complex conjugate $\overline F$.
\end{enumerate}}

\paragraph{Definition (2.1.10).} --- {\itshape A Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ consists of
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item a finitely generated $\Z$-module $H_{\Z}$ (the ``integral lattice'');
\item a real Hodge structure of weight $n$ on $H_{\R}=\R\otimes_{\Z} H_{\Z}$.
\end{enumerate}}

\paragraph{(2.1.11)} A morphism $f:H\to H'$ is a homomorphism $f:H_{\Z}\to H'_{\Z}$ such that $f_{\R}:H_{\R}\to H'_{\R}$ is compatible with the action of $S$ (i.e. such that $f_{\C}$ is compatible with the bigrading, or with the Hodge filtration).

Hodge structures of weight $n$ form an abelian category. If $H$ has weight $n$ and $H'$ has weight $n'$, one defines a Hodge structure $H\otimes H'$ of weight $n+n'$ by the formulas:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item $(H\otimes H')_{\Z}=H_{\Z}\otimes H'_{\Z}$;
\item the action of $S$ on $(H\otimes H')_{\R}=H_{\R}\otimes H'_{\R}$ is the tensor product of the actions of $S$ on $H_{\R}$ and $H'_{\R}$.
\end{enumerate}
The bigrading (respectively, the Hodge filtration) of $(H\otimes H')_{\C}=H_{\C}\otimes H'_{\C}$ is the tensor product of the bigradings (respectively, of the Hodge filtrations (cf. (1.1.12))) of $H_{\C}$ and $H'_{\C}$.

Similarly one defines the Hodge structure $\Hom(H,H')$ (of weight $n'-n$), the Hodge structures $\bigwedge^pH$ (of weight $pn$), and the dual Hodge structure $H^*$.

The preceding internal \emph{Hom}, and the group of homomorphisms, are related by the \emph{Remark} \textbf{(2.1.11.1).} --- $\Hom(H,H')$ is the subgroup of
\[
\Hom(H,H')_{\Z}=\Hom_{\Z}(H_{\Z},H'_{\Z})
\]
formed by the elements of type $(0,0)$.

The actions of $S$ on $H_{\R}$, $H'_{\R}$, and $\Hom(H,H')_{\R}=\Hom(H_{\R},H'_{\R})$ are indeed related by
\[
s(f(x))=s(f)(s(x)).
\]
For $f$ to be of type $(0,0)$, i.e. invariant under $S$, therefore means that it commutes with the action of $S$.

\paragraph{(2.1.12)} For $A$ a noetherian subring of $\R$, an \emph{$A$-Hodge structure of weight $n$} is defined as consisting of a finite-type $A$-module $H_A$ and of a real Hodge structure of weight $n$ on $H_{\R}=\R\otimes_AH_A$. These definitions are used mainly for $A=\Q$. An $A$-Hodge structure consists of a finite-type $A$-module $H_A$ and of a real Hodge structure on $H_{\R}=H_A\otimes_A\R$, such that the weight grading is defined over the field of fractions of $A$.

\paragraph{Definition (2.1.13).} --- \emph{The Tate Hodge structure $\Z(1)$ is the Hodge structure of weight $-2$, of rank $1$, purely of bidegree $(-1,-1)$, with integral lattice $2\pi i\Z\subset\C$.}

The action of $S$ is therefore multiplication by the inverse of the norm (2.1.3.3). For $n\in\Z$, define $\Z(n)$ to be the $n$-th tensor power of $\Z(1)$: $\Z(n)$ is the Hodge structure of weight $-2n$, rank $1$, purely of bidegree $(-n,-n)$, with integral lattice $(2\pi i)^n\Z\subset\C$. The action of $S$ is multiplication by $N(x)^{-n}$.

\paragraph{(2.1.14)} The choice in $\C$ of a solution $i$ of the equation $x^2+1=0$ determines on every complex variety $X$ purely of dimension $n$ an orientation $\ornt_i(X)$. When $i$ is changed to $-i$, one has
\[
\ornt_{-i}(X)=(-1)^n\ornt_i(X).
\]
The choice of $i$ also defines an element $C$ of order $4$ in $S(\R)$: the image of $i$ under the isomorphism $S(\R)\simeq\C^*$.

Finally it defines an isomorphism between $\Z$ and the integral lattice of $\Z(n)$: multiplication by $(2\pi i)^n$.

Whenever $i$, an orientation of $X$, $C$, or an identification $\Z\simeq\Z(n)_{\Z}$ occurs in a formula, it will in principle be understood that they are subordinated to the same choice of $i$, and that changing $i$ to $-i$ would give an equivalent definition or formula.

\paragraph{Definition (2.1.15).} --- {\itshape A polarization of a Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is a homomorphism
\[
(x,y):H\otimes H\longrightarrow\Z(-n)
\]
such that the real bilinear form $(2\pi i)^n(x,Cy)$ on $H_{\R}$ is symmetric and positive definite.}

\paragraph{(2.1.16)} The \emph{real Tate Hodge structure} is the real Hodge structure $\R(1)$ underlying $\Z(1)$. Similarly one defines $\R(n)$ underlying $\Z(n)$. A polarization of a \emph{real} Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is a homomorphism
\[
(x,y):H\otimes H\longrightarrow\R(-n)
\]
such that the real bilinear form $(2\pi i)^n(x,Cy)$ on $H_{\R}$ is symmetric and positive definite. A polarization is entirely determined by the positive-definite quadratic form $(2\pi i)^n(x,Cy)$ on $H_{\R}$, subject only to the condition that it be invariant under the compact subtorus of $S$, the kernel of $N$.

One has
\[
(x,y)=(Cx,Cy)=(y,C^2x)=(-1)^n(y,x).
\]
The form $(x,y)$ is therefore symmetric or alternating according to the parity of $n$.

\paragraph{(2.1.17)} The reader will generalize these definitions to $A$-Hodge structures of weight $n$ (2.1.12).

\subsection*{2.2. Hodge theory.}

\paragraph{(2.2.1)} Let $X$ be a compact Kähler variety, for example smooth projective. By the holomorphic Poincaré lemma, the De Rham complex $\Omega_X^*$ is a resolution of the constant sheaf $\C$. Thus one has an isomorphism
\[
H^*(X,\C)\sim\mathbb H^*(X,\Omega_X^*),
\]
and the bête filtration of $\Omega_X^*$ (1.4.5) defines the hypercohomology spectral sequence
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(2.2.1.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle E_1^{pq}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,\C),$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(2.2.1.1)}}}
\]
whose abutment is the \emph{Hodge filtration} of $H^*(X,\C)$.

By Hodge theory [9], [12], one has:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Alph*)]
\item The spectral sequence (2.2.1.1) degenerates: $E_1=E_{\infty}$.
\item The Hodge filtration of $H^n(X,\C)$ is $n$-opposed to the complex conjugate filtration.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{(2.2.2)} Let $V$ be a local system of real vector spaces on $X$, i.e. a sheaf of $\R$-vector spaces locally isomorphic to a constant sheaf $\R^n$. Suppose that on $V$ there exists a bilinear form
\[
Q:V\otimes V\longrightarrow\R
\]
which is locally constant and \emph{definite}. For $X$ connected, this is the case if $V$ is defined by a representation of a finite quotient of the fundamental group of $X$.

The assertions (A) and (B) above remain valid exactly as stated, without any change in the proofs, for cohomology with coefficients in $V_{\C}=V\otimes_{\R}\C$: the spectral sequence
\[
E_1^{pq}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p(V))\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,V_{\C})
\]
deduced from the De Rham resolution of $V_{\C}$ by $\Omega_X^*(V_{\C})$ degenerates and abuts to a filtration on $H^n(X,V_{\C})$ which is $n$-opposed to the complex conjugate filtration.

The vector space $H^n(X,V)$ is therefore endowed with a canonical real Hodge structure of weight $n$.

\paragraph{(2.2.3)} It is shown in [2] that the statements (2.2.1) remain valid for $X$ a complete nonsingular algebraic variety, not necessarily Kähler. The proof in \emph{loc. cit.}, based on a reduction to the projective case \emph{via} Chow's lemma and resolution of singularities, extends to the setting (2.2.2).

\paragraph{(2.2.4)} Let $\cL$ be an invertible sheaf. Here are two ways to define the class $c_1(\cL)$.

\paragraph{(2.2.4.1)} The sheaf $\cL$ defines an element $c$ in $H^1(X,\cO^*)$. Its image under $df/f:\cO^*\to\Omega_X^1$ lies in $H^1(X,\Omega_X^1)$. More precisely, $df/f$ defines a morphism of complexes
\[
\dlog:\cO^*[-1]\longrightarrow [\,0\to\Omega_X^1\to\Omega_X^2\to\cdots\,]=\sigma_{\ge1}(\Omega_X^*).
\]
This complex maps to $\Omega_X^*$, whence
\[
\dlog:\cO^*[-1]\longrightarrow\Omega_X^*,
\]
and the image of $c$ under $\dlog$ lies in $H^2(\Omega_X^*)$. This construction would still make sense for an algebraic variety over an arbitrary field $k$. For $k=\C$, one also has
\[
H^2(X,\C)\sim H^2(X,\Omega_X^*)
\]
\noindent\makebox[\textwidth][s]{and hence a class\hfill$c_1'(\cL)\in H^2(X,\C).$\hfill\phantom{and hence a class}}

\paragraph{(2.2.4.2)} The exponential exact sequence
\[
0\to\Z(1)\to\cO\to\cO^*\to0
\]
defines a homomorphism
\[
\partial:H^1(X,\cO^*)\longrightarrow H^2(X,\Z(1)),
\]
\noindent\makebox[\textwidth][s]{hence a class\hfill$\partial c=c_1''(\cL)\in H^2(X,\Z(1)).$\hfill\phantom{hence a class}}
If $i$ is chosen, this class is identified with
\[
c_1'''(\cL)\in H^2(X,\Z),
\]
and for $\cL=\cO(D)$, $c_1'''(\cL)$ is just the integral cohomology class defined by $D$ (the orientations being defined by $i$).

\paragraph{(2.2.5)} We prove that:
\paragraph{(2.2.5.1)} For $\alpha$ the natural injection of $\Z(1)$ into $\C$, one has
\[
-\alpha c_1''(\cL)=c_1'(\cL).
\]
\paragraph{(2.2.5.2)} For $\beta$ the natural injection of $\Z$ into $\C$, one has
\[
-\beta c_1'''(\cL)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}c_1'(\cL).
\]

This is verified by contemplating the following diagram of complexes, in which $\simeq$ denotes a quasi-isomorphism, and whose upper rectangle is anticommutative up to homotopy
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.2em,row sep=1.5em]
\C \arrow[r,"\simeq"] \arrow[d,equal] & \Omega_X^* & \sigma_{\ge1}\Omega^* \arrow[l] \arrow[d,equal]\\
\C & {[\C\to\cO]} \arrow[l] \arrow[r,"\simeq","d"'] & \sigma_{\ge1}\Omega^*\\
\Z(1) \arrow[u] & {[\Z(1)\to\cO]} \arrow[l] \arrow[r,"\simeq","{\exp}"'] \arrow[u] & \cO^*[-1] \arrow[u,"\dlog"']
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\paragraph{(2.2.6)} Let $X$ be a nonsingular projective variety purely of dimension $n$. A choice of $i$ defines an orientation of $X$ and an isomorphism $\Z(1)\simeq\Z$. The corresponding trace morphism:
\[
H^{2n}(X,\Z(n))\longrightarrow\Z
\]
which follows from it does not depend on the choice of $i$.

According to Hodge, for $i\le n$ the morphism
\[
L^{\,n-i}=\wedge c_1''(\cO(1))^{\,n-i}:H^i(X,\Z)\longrightarrow H^{2n-i}(X,\Z(n-i)),
\]
is an isomorphism and, combined with Poincaré duality
\[
H^i(X,\Z)\otimes H^{2n-i}(X,\Z(n-i))\longrightarrow
H^{2n}(X,\Z(n-i))\longrightarrow \Z(-i),
\]
it furnishes a polarization on the \emph{primitive part} $\Ker(L^{\,n-i+1})$ of $H^i(X,\Z)$. It follows that the rational Hodge structures $H^i(X,\Q)$ are polarizable.

\subsection*{2.3. Mixed structures.}

\paragraph{Definition (2.3.1).} --- {\itshape A mixed Hodge structure $H$ consists of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item a finitely generated $\Z$-module $H_{\Z}$ (the ``integral lattice'').
\item a finite increasing filtration $W_n$ of $H_{\Q}=\Q\otimes_{\Z} H_{\Z}$, called the weight filtration.
\item a finite filtration $F^p$ of $H_{\C}=\C\otimes_{\Z} H_{\Z}$, called the Hodge filtration.
\end{enumerate}
It is required that on $H_{\C}$, the filtration $W_{\C}$ deduced from $W$ by extension of scalars, the filtration $F$, and its complex conjugate $\overline F$ form a system $(W_{\C},F,\overline F)$ of three opposed filtrations ((1.2.7) and (1.2.13)).}

\paragraph{(2.3.2)} Let $W$ again denote the filtration of $H_{\Z}$ which is the inverse image of the filtration $W$ of $H_{\Q}$. The axiom of mixed Hodge structures means that, for every $n$, the filtration $F$ induces on $\C\otimes_{\Z}\Gr_n^W(H_{\Z})$ a filtration $n$-opposed to its complex conjugate. By (2.1.9), $\Gr_n^W(H_{\Z})$ is endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $n$, with Hodge filtration induced by $F$.

\paragraph{Example (2.3.3).} --- If $H$ is a Hodge structure of weight $n$, one defines a mixed Hodge structure with the same integral lattice and the same Hodge filtration by putting
\[
W_i(H_{\Q})=0\quad\text{for }i<n\qquad\text{and}\qquad
W_i(H_{\Q})=H_{\Q}\quad\text{for }i\ge n.
\]

\paragraph{(2.3.4)} A \emph{morphism} $f:H\to H'$ of Hodge structures is a homomorphism $f:H_{\Z}\to H'_{\Z}$ compatible with the filtrations $W$ and $F$ (and therefore compatible with $\overline F$). One immediately deduces from (1.2.10) the following theorem.

\paragraph{Theorem (2.3.5).} --- {\itshape
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The category of mixed Hodge structures is abelian.
\item The kernel (respectively, cokernel) of a morphism $f:H\to H'$ has as integral lattice the kernel (respectively, cokernel) $K$ of $f:H_{\Z}\to H'_{\Z}$, with $K\otimes\Q$ and $K\otimes\C$ endowed with the induced (respectively, quotient) filtrations from the filtrations $W$ and $F$ of $H_{\Q}$ and $H_{\C}$ (respectively, of $H'_{\Q}$ and $H'_{\C}$).
\item Every morphism $f:H\to H'$ is strictly compatible with the filtration $W$ of $H_{\Q}$ and $H'_{\Q}$, and with the filtration $F$ of $H_{\C}$ and $H'_{\C}$. It induces morphisms of $\Q$-Hodge structures:
\[
\Gr_n^W(f):\Gr_n^W(H_{\Q})\longrightarrow\Gr_n^W(H'_{\Q})
\]
and morphisms strictly compatible with the filtration induced by $W_{\C}$:
\[
\Gr_F^p(f):\Gr_F^p(H_{\C})\longrightarrow\Gr_F^p(H'_{\C}).
\]
\item The functor $\Gr_n^W$ is an exact functor from the category of mixed Hodge structures to the category of $\Q$-Hodge structures of weight $n$.
\item The functor $\Gr_F^p$ is exact.
\end{enumerate}}

\paragraph{(2.3.6)} Let $H$ be a mixed Hodge structure. The $W_n(H_{\Z})$, endowed with the filtrations induced by $W$ and $F$, then form mixed Hodge substructures $W_n(H)$ of $H$. The quotient $W_n(H)/W_{n-1}(H)$ is identified with $\Gr_n^W(H_{\Z})$ endowed with its Hodge structure (2.3.2), (2.3.3). This Hodge structure will be denoted by $\Gr_n^W(H)$.

\paragraph{(2.3.7)} Put $H^{pq}=\Gr_F^p\Gr_{\overline F}^q\Gr_{p+q}^W(H_{\C})=\bigl(\Gr_{p+q}^W(H)\bigr)^{p,q}$. The \emph{Hodge numbers} of $H$ are the integers
\[
h^{pq}=\dim_{\C} H^{pq}.
\]
Thus the Hodge number $h^{pq}$ of $H$ is the Hodge number $h^{pq}$ of the Hodge structure $\Gr_{p+q}^W(H)$.

\paragraph{(2.3.8)} A \emph{$\Q$-mixed Hodge structure} $H$ is defined as consisting of a finite-dimensional vector space $H_{\Q}$ over $\Q$, a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H_{\Q}$, and a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of $H_{\C}$, the filtrations $W_{\C}$, $F$, and $\overline F$ being opposed. Theorem (2.3.5) generalizes trivially to this variant.

\section*{3. Hodge theory of nonsingular algebraic varieties}

\subsection*{3.1. Logarithmic poles and residues.}

\paragraph{(3.1.1)} We recall some classical properties of ``logarithmic poles'' of holomorphic differential forms. The reader will find proofs in [3], II, (3.1) to (3.7), for example.

\paragraph{(3.1.2)} A divisor $Y$ in a smooth complex analytic variety $X$ will be said \emph{to have normal crossings} if the inclusion of $Y$ into $X$ is locally isomorphic to the inclusion of a union of coordinate hyperplanes in $\C^n$; this does not imply that $Y$ is a union of smooth divisors. Let $Y$ be a normal-crossings divisor in $X$, and let $j$ be the inclusion of $X^*=X-Y$ in $X$. Let $\Omega_X^1\langle Y\rangle$ denote the locally free $\cO$-submodule of $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^1$ generated by $\Omega_X^1$ and by the $\frac{dz_i}{z_i}$, where $z_i$ is a local equation of a local irreducible component of $Y$. The \emph{sheaf $\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle$ of differential $p$-forms on $X$ with logarithmic pole along $Y$} is, by definition, the locally free subsheaf $\bigwedge^p\Omega_X^1\langle Y\rangle$ of $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^p$.

\paragraph{Proposition (3.1.3).} --- {\itshape
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item A section $\alpha$ of $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^p$ belongs to $\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle$ if and only if $\alpha$ and $d\alpha$ have at worst simple poles along the divisor $Y$.
\item The $\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle$ form the smallest subcomplex of $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*$, stable under exterior product, containing $\Omega_X^*$, and containing the logarithmic differential $df/f$ of every local section, meromorphic along $Y$, of $j_*\cO_{X^*}^*$.
\end{enumerate}}
The complex $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$ is called the \emph{logarithmic De Rham complex} of $X$ along $Y$. By (3.1.3), (ii), this complex is contravariant in the pair $(X,X^*)$.

\paragraph{(3.1.4)} Locally on $X$, $Y$ is a union of smooth divisors $Y_i$, and $Y^n$ (resp. $\widetilde Y^n$) denotes the union (resp. the disjoint sum) of the intersections $n$ at a time of the $Y_i$. The $Y^n$ glue to a subspace $Y^n$ of $X$, and the $\widetilde Y^n$ glue to the normalization of $Y^n$. One has $\widetilde Y^0=Y^0=X$ and puts $\widetilde Y=\widetilde Y^1$.

The two-element set of \emph{orientations} of a finite set $E$ with $n$ elements is defined to be the set of generators of $\bigwedge^n\Z^E$. For $n\ge2$, this set is the set of conjugacy classes, under the alternating group, of total orderings of $E$.

If to each point $y$ of $\widetilde Y^n$ one associates the set of the $n$ local components of $Y$ which contain the image in $X$ of a neighborhood of $y$ in $\widetilde Y^n$, then one defines on $\widetilde Y^n$ a local system $E_n$ of $n$-element sets. The local system of orientations of these sets is a torsor under $\Z/(2)$. This torsor defines, \emph{via} the inclusion of $\Z/(2)$ into $\C^*$, a rank-one complex local system $\varepsilon^n$ on $\widetilde Y^n$, endowed with an isomorphism
\[
(\varepsilon^n)^{\otimes2}\simeq\C.
\]
One has
\[
\varepsilon^n\simeq\bigwedge^n\C^{E_n}.
\]
Locally on $\widetilde Y^n$, $\varepsilon^n$ is endowed with two opposite isomorphisms $\pm\alpha:\varepsilon^n\iso\C$. Put
\[
\varepsilon_{\Z}^n=\alpha^{-1}\bigl((2\pi i)^{-n}\Z\bigr).
\]
The local system $\varepsilon^n$, endowed with $\varepsilon_{\Z}^n$, should be regarded as a twisted form of $\Z(-n)$ on $\widetilde Y^n$.

Let $\varepsilon_X^n$ (resp. $(\varepsilon_X^n)_{\Z}$) denote the direct image of $\varepsilon^n$ (resp. $\varepsilon_{\Z}^n$) under the map from $\widetilde Y^n$ to $X$. One has
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.4.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle \varepsilon_X^n\simeq\bigwedge^n\varepsilon_X^1\qquad(n\ge0).$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.4.1)}}}
\]
If $Y$ is a union of distinct smooth divisors $(Y_i)_{i\in I}$, the choice of a total order on $I$ trivializes the $\varepsilon^n$.

\paragraph{(3.1.5)} Let $W_n(\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle)$ denote the submodule of $\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle$ formed by linear combinations of products
\[
\alpha\wedge\frac{dt_{i(1)}}{t_{i(1)}}\wedge\cdots\wedge
\frac{dt_{i(m)}}{t_{i(m)}}\qquad(m\le n),
\]
with $\alpha$ holomorphic and with the $t_{i(j)}$ local equations of distinct local components $Y_j$ of $Y$. The \emph{weight filtration} of $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$ is the \emph{increasing} filtration by the subcomplexes $W_n(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle)$. One has
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.5.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle W_n(\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle)\wedge W_m(\Omega_X^q\langle Y\rangle)\subset W_{n+m}(\Omega_X^{p+q}\langle Y\rangle).$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.5.1)}}}
\]

Letting $i_n$ denote the map from $\widetilde Y^n$ to $X$, one checks that the correspondence
\[
\alpha\wedge\frac{dt_{i(1)}}{t_{i(1)}}\wedge\cdots\wedge
\frac{dt_{i(n)}}{t_{i(n)}}
\longmapsto
(\alpha\mid Y_{i(1)}\cap\cdots\cap Y_{i(n)})\otimes
(\text{orientation }i(1)\ldots i(n))
\]
defines isomorphisms of complexes
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.5.2)}\hfill$\displaystyle \Res:\Gr_n^W(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle)\simeq i_{n*}\Omega_{\widetilde Y^n}^*(\varepsilon^n)[-n]$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.5.2)}}}
\]
(the \emph{``Poincaré residue''}).

\paragraph{(3.1.6)} The following interpretation, in terms of (3.1.5.2), of the Leray spectral sequence for the inclusion of $X^*$ in $X$ was pointed out to me by N. Katz. It will make it possible to verify a point which I had initially considered evident ((3.2.5), (ii), first part).

\paragraph{(3.1.7)} Every point of $X$ admits a fundamental system of Stein open neighborhoods whose trace on $X^*$ is Stein. For $\mathcal F$ a coherent analytic sheaf on $X^*$, one therefore has $R^ij_*\mathcal F=0$ for $i>0$. The De Rham complex $\Omega_{X^*}^*$ is therefore a resolution of the constant sheaf $\C$ by sheaves acyclic for the functor $j_*$. Hence
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.7.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle H^*(X^*,\C)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb H^*(X^*,\Omega_{X^*}^*)\xleftarrow{\sim}\mathbb H^*(X,j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*)$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.7.1)}}}
\]
and the Leray spectral sequence for the morphism $j$ is identified with the hypercohomology spectral sequence for $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*$, corresponding to the filtration $\tau$ by the subcomplexes $\tau_{\le -n}(j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*)$ (1.4.6).

\paragraph{Proposition (3.1.8).} --- {\itshape The morphisms of filtered complexes
\[
(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle,W)
\xleftarrow{\ \alpha\ }
(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle,\tau)
\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }
(j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*,\tau)
\]
are filtered quasi-isomorphisms. They define an isomorphism between the Leray spectral sequence for $j$ in complex cohomology and the hypercohomology spectral sequence of the filtered complex $(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle,W)$ on $X$.}

By (1.4.5) and (3.1.7), it suffices to prove the first assertion. In [3], II, (6.9), or in [1], one finds the proof that $\beta$ is a quasi-isomorphism, hence a filtered quasi-isomorphism. One can also compute directly the cohomology sheaves of the two sides: those of $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$ are determined by (3.1.5.2), whereas those of $j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*$ are the $R^ij_*\C$, which can be computed topologically.

For $n\ge p$ one has
\[
W_n(\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle)=\Omega_X^p\langle Y\rangle,
\]
so that $\alpha$ is a morphism from $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$, endowed with $\tau$, to $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$, endowed with the decreasing filtration associated with $W$ (1.1.3). By (3.1.5.2), one has
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.8.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle \mathcal H^i(\Gr_n^W(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle))=\begin{cases}0&\text{for }i\ne n\\ \varepsilon_X^n&\text{for }i=n,\end{cases}$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.8.1)}}}
\]
from the first line of this formula one deduces that $\alpha$ is a filtered quasi-isomorphism. This proves (3.1.8).

By (3.1.7), the isomorphism (3.1.8.1) defines an isomorphism
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.8.2)}\hfill$\displaystyle R^nj_*\C\simeq \mathcal H^n(j_*\Omega_{X^*}^*)\simeq \mathcal H^n(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle)\simeq \varepsilon_X^n.$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.8.2)}}}
\]
The isomorphisms (3.1.4.1) correspond, \emph{via} (3.1.8.2), to the cup product.

\paragraph{Proposition (3.1.9).} --- {\itshape The canonical morphism from $R^nj_*\Z$ to $R^nj_*\C$ identifies, via (3.1.8.2), the sheaf $R^nj_*\Z$ with $(\varepsilon_X^n)_{\Z}$ (3.1.4).}

The question is local on $X$. One can therefore suppose that $X$ is an open polydisc $D^m$, with $D=\{z\in\C\mid |z|<1\}$, and that $Y=\bigcup_{k=1}^{\ell}Y_k$, $Y_k=\operatorname{pr}_k^{-1}(0)$. The fiber at $0$ of $R^nj_*\Z$ is then the integral cohomology of $X^*=D^{*\ell}\times D^{(m-\ell)}$, with $D^*=\{z\in\C\mid 0<|z|<1\}$.
The space $X^*$ has the homotopy type of a torus; its cohomology is therefore torsion-free, and the cup product defines isomorphisms
\[
\bigwedge^n(R^1j_*\Z)_0\xrightarrow{\sim}(R^nj_*\Z)_0.
\]
It is therefore enough to prove (3.1.9) for $n=1$.

The integral homology $H_1(X^*)$ is generated by the loops $\gamma_k$ winding around the various $Y_k$. One has
\[
\oint_{\gamma_k}\frac{dz_k}{z_k}=\pm2\pi i;
\]
the integral cohomology is therefore generated by the $\frac1{2\pi i}\frac{dz_k}{z_k}$, and this proves (3.1.9).

\paragraph{(3.1.10)} Let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic sheaf on $X^*$, given as the restriction to $X^*$ of a coherent analytic sheaf $\mathcal F'$ on $X$. The meromorphic direct image $j_*^m\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal F$ is the inductive limit
\[
j_*^m\mathcal F=\varinjlim_n \mathcal F'(nY).
\]
Locally on $X$, $Y$ is the sum of a finite family $(Y_i)_{i\in I}$ of smooth divisors, and the \emph{filtration by order of pole} $P$ on $j_*^m\cO_{X^*}$ is defined by the formula
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.10.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle P^p(j_*^m\cO_{X^*})=\sum_{\mathbf n\in A_p}\cO_X\Bigl(\sum_i(n_i+1)Y_i\Bigr)$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.10.1)}}}
\]
where
\[
A_p=\{(n_i)_{i\in I}\mid \sum_i n_i\le -p\ \text{ and }\ \forall i,\ n_i\ge0\}.
\]
This construction globalizes and provides on $j_*^m\cO_{X^*}$ an exhaustive filtration such that $P^p=0$ for $p>0$.

The \emph{filtration by order of pole} of the complex $j_*^m\Omega_{X^*}^*=j_*^m\cO_{X^*}\otimes\Omega_X^*$ is the filtration
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.1.10.2)}\hfill$\displaystyle P^p(j_*^m\Omega_{X^*}^k)=P^{p-k}(j_*^m\cO_{X^*})\otimes\Omega_X^k.$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.1.10.2)}}}
\]
The filtration $P$ induces on the subcomplex $\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle$ of $j_*^m\Omega_{X^*}^*$ the bête filtration by the $\sigma_{\ge p}(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle)$, a filtration also called the \emph{Hodge filtration} $F$.

\paragraph{Proposition (3.1.11).} --- {\itshape The inclusion morphism
\[
(\Omega_X^*\langle Y\rangle,F)\longrightarrow(j_*^m\Omega_{X^*}^*,P)
\]
is a filtered quasi-isomorphism.}

This statement was suggested to me by [4]. A proof appears in [3], II, (3.13).

\subsection*{3.2. Mixed Hodge theory.}

\emph{Recall that from now on, by a scheme we mean a scheme of finite type over $\C$, and by a sheaf on $S$ a sheaf on $S^{an}$.}

\paragraph{(3.2.1)} Let $X$ be a smooth separated scheme. By Nagata [11], $X$ is a Zariski open subset of a complete scheme $\overline X$. By Hironaka [8], one can take $\overline X$ smooth, and such that $Y=\overline X-X$ is a normal-crossings divisor.

The reader who would like to avoid the reference to Nagata may suppose $X$ quasi-



projective. The smooth completion $\overline X$ can then be chosen projective and such that $Y$ is a union of smooth divisors. When one restricts oneself to such compactifications, Hodge theory is needed only in its standard form (2.2.1).

\paragraph{(3.2.2)} By (3.1.7) and (3.1.8), one has
\[
H^*(X,\C)\simeq \mathbb H^*(\overline X,\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle).
\]
The \emph{Hodge filtration} $F$ on the complex $\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle$ is defined to be the filtration $F^p=\sigma_{\ge p}$ by bête truncations (1.4.5). Thus $\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle$ carries two filtrations: $F$ and $W$ (3.1.5).

\paragraph{(3.2.3)} We shall use the existence of bifiltered resolutions $i:\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle\longrightarrow K^*$ such that the $\Gr_F^p\Gr_n^W(K^j)$ are sheaves acyclic for the functor $\Gamma$:
\[
H^i(\overline X,\Gr_F^p\Gr_n^W(K^j))=0\qquad \text{for }i>0.
\]
Here are two ways to construct them:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textit{\alph*)}]
\item One may take for $K^*$ the canonical Godement resolution $\mathcal C^*(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle)$, filtered by the $\mathcal C^*(W_n(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle))$ and the $\mathcal C^*(F^p(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle))$. This is a bifiltered resolution because $\mathcal C^*$ is an exact functor.
\item One may take for $K^*$ the $d''$-resolution of $\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle$. Let $\Omega_{\overline X}^{pq}$ be the sheaf of $C^{\infty}$ forms of type $(p,q)$; then $K^*$ is the simple complex associated with the double complex of the $\Omega_{\overline X}^{p}\langle Y\rangle\otimes_{\mathcal O}\Omega_{\overline X}^{0,q}$ (a subcomplex of the $j_*\Omega_X^{**}$). This complex is filtered by the $F^p(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle)\otimes\Omega_{\overline X}^{0,*}$ and by the $W_n(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle)\otimes\Omega_{\overline X}^{0,*}$; to prove that this is a bifiltered resolution, one uses the fact that the sheaf $\mathcal O_{\infty}$ of complex-valued $C^{\infty}$ functions on $\overline X$ is flat over $\mathcal O$ (a corollary of Malgrange's $C^{\infty}$ preparation theorem). The sheaves $\Gr_F\Gr_W(K^*)$ are fine, because they are sheaves of modules over the soft sheaf $\mathcal O_{\infty}$.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{(3.2.4)} With the notation of (3.2.3), the complex cohomology of $X$ appears as the cohomology of the bifiltered complex $\Gamma(\overline X,K^*)$. Thus there are two spectral sequences abutting to $H^*(X,\C)$. With the notation of (3.1.4), they are
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.2.4.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle {}_W E_1^{pq}=H^{p+q}(\overline X,\varepsilon_{\overline X}^{-p}[p])=H^{2p+q}(\widetilde Y^p,\varepsilon^{-p})\Rightarrow H^n(X,\C)$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.2.4.1)}}}
\]
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.2.4.2)}\hfill$\displaystyle {}_F E_1^{pq}=H^q(\overline X,\Omega_{\overline X}^p\langle Y\rangle)\Rightarrow H^n(X,\C).$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.2.4.2)}}}
\]
The first of these, up to the renumbering ${}_W E_1^{pq}\mapsto E_2^{2p+q,-p}$, is just the Leray spectral sequence of the inclusion $j$.

\paragraph{Theorem (3.2.5).} --- {\itshape
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),font=\itshape]
\item On the terms ${}_WE_r^{pq}$ of the spectral sequence (3.2.4.1), the first direct filtration, the second direct filtration, and the recurrent filtration defined by $F$ coincide.
\item The filtration on $H^n(X,\C)$ which is the abutment of the spectral sequence ${}_WE$ is deduced from a filtration $W$ of $H^n(X,\Q)$. Neither it, nor the filtration $F$ which is the abutment of the spectral sequence ${}_FE$, depends on the chosen compactification $\overline X$ of $X$ or on the choice of $K^*$.
\item The filtrations $W[n]$ (1.1.2) and $F$ define on $H^n(X,\Z)$ a mixed Hodge structure, functorial in $X$.
\end{enumerate}}

By (3.1.7), the spectral sequence ${}_WE$ is the Leray spectral sequence for $j_*$ (up to renumbering). It is therefore obtained by tensoring with $\C$ a spectral sequence of $\Q$-vector spaces, and the first assertion of (ii) is true. Complex conjugation acts on the ${}_WE_r$; it can be computed via (3.1.10).

\paragraph{Lemma (3.2.6).} --- {\itshape The hypercohomology spectral sequences of the filtered complexes $\Gr_n^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle)$, endowed with the filtration induced by the Hodge filtration, degenerate at $E_1$.}

Define $Y^n$ and $\widetilde Y^n$ as in (3.1.4), and let $i_n:\widetilde Y^n\to\overline X$. By (3.1.5.2), one has
\[
\Gr_n^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle)
\simeq i_{n*}\Omega_{\widetilde Y^n}^{*}(\varepsilon^n)[-n].
\]
Moreover, the Hodge filtration induces the bête filtration (1.4.5), so that the spectral sequence (3.2.6) is obtained, by translations in the degrees, from the classical spectral sequence
\[
E_1^{pq}=H^q(\widetilde Y^n,\Omega_{\widetilde Y^n}^p(\varepsilon^n))
\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(\widetilde Y^n,\varepsilon^n).
\]
If $\overline X$ is projective and $Y$ is a union of smooth divisors, then $\widetilde Y^n$ is projective, $\varepsilon^n$ is a trivial local system, and classical Hodge theory (2.2.1) gives the degeneration (3.2.6). For the general case, one must refer to [2] (see (2.2.2), (2.2.3)).

Hodge theory further gives that the Hodge filtration on $H^k(\widetilde Y^n,\varepsilon^n)$ is $k$-opposed to its complex conjugate (complex conjugation being defined in terms of $\varepsilon_{\Z}^n$ (3.1.4)). Taking account here of the translations in the degrees, one has:

\paragraph{Lemma (3.2.7).} --- {\itshape The filtration on
\[
{}_W E_1^{-n,k+n}
=H^k(\overline X,\Gr_n^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle))
\approx H^{k-n}(\widetilde Y^n,\varepsilon^n),
\]
which is the abutment of the spectral sequence (3.2.6), is $(k+n)$-opposed to its complex conjugate.}

\paragraph{Lemma (3.2.8).} --- {\itshape The differentials $d_1$ of the spectral sequence ${}_WE$ are strictly compatible with the filtration $F$.}

On the terms $E_1$, there is only one filtration induced by $F$ to consider ((1.3.10) and (1.3.13), (iii)), and $d_1$ is compatible with this filtration ((1.3.13), (i)). This filtration is the abutment of the spectral sequence (3.2.6) ((1.4.8), (iii)). By (3.2.7), the arrow $d_1$
\[
d_1:H^k(\overline X,\Gr_n^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle))
\longrightarrow
H^{k+1}(\overline X,\Gr_{n-1}^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle))
\]
that is,
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.2.8.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle d_1:H^{k-n}(\widetilde Y^n,\varepsilon^n)\longrightarrow H^{k-n+2}(\widetilde Y^{n-1},\varepsilon^{n-1})$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.2.8.1)}}}
\]
is compatible with filtrations that are $(k+n)$-opposed to their complex conjugates. Since $d_1$ commutes with complex conjugation, it respects the bigrading, and hence the filtration defined by $F$ and $\overline F$; this proves (3.2.8). Moreover, the cohomology of the complex $E_1$ will still be bigraded.

\paragraph{Lemma (3.2.9).} --- {\itshape On ${}_WE_2^{pq}$, the recurrent filtration $F$ is $q$-opposed to its complex conjugate.}

We prove by induction on $r$ that:

\paragraph{Lemma (3.2.10).} --- {\itshape For $r\ge0$, the differentials $d_r$ of the spectral sequence ${}_WE$ are strictly compatible with the recurrent filtration $F$. For $r\ge2$, they are zero.}

For $r=0$ (resp. $r=1$), one applies (3.2.6) and (1.4.8), (iii) (resp. (3.2.8)). For $r\ge2$, it suffices to prove that $d_r=0$. By induction and by (1.3.16), one may suppose that on the terms ${}_WE_s$ $(s\ge r+1)$ one has $F_d=F_r=F_{d*}$, and that ${}_WE_r={}_WE_2$. By (1.3.13), (i), $d_r$ is therefore compatible with the filtration $F_r$.

On ${}_WE_r^{pq}={}_WE_2^{pq}$, the filtration $F_r$ is $q$-opposed to its complex conjugate. The morphism
\[
d_r:{}_W E_r^{pq}\longrightarrow {}_W E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}
\]
therefore satisfies, for $r-1>0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_r({}_W E_r^{pq})
&=d_r\!\left(\sum_{a+b=q}\bigl(F^a({}_W E_r^{pq})\cap
\overline F^{\,b}({}_W E_r^{pq})\bigr)\right)\\
&\subset
\sum_{a+b=q}\bigl(F^a({}_WE_r^{p+r,q-r+1})\cap
\overline F^{\,b}({}_WE_r^{p+r,q-r+1})\bigr)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (3.2.10), which by (1.3.16) implies (3.2.5) (i).

By (1.3.17), the filtration of ${}_WE_{\infty}^{pq}$ induced by the filtration $F$ of $H^{p+q}(X,\C)$ is $q$-opposed to its complex conjugate. Since $q=-p+(p+q)$, this proves the first part of (3.2.5) (iii).

\paragraph{(3.2.11)} We prove (ii) and (iii), which will complete the proof.

\paragraph{A.} \textit{Independence of the choice of $K^{*}$.} The filtrations $F$ and $W$ of $H^*(X,\C)$ are the abutments of the hypercohomology spectral sequences of $\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle$ for the filtrations $F$ and $W$. These entire spectral sequences do not depend on the choice of $K^{*}$.

\paragraph{B.} \textit{Functoriality.} Let $f:X_1\to X_2$ be a morphism of schemes. Suppose given a morphism of smooth compactifications
\[
\makebox[0pt][r]{\textbf{(3.2.11.1)}\hspace{0.28\textwidth}}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em,row sep=2.1em]
X_1 \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[hook,d,"j_1"'] & X_2 \arrow[hook,d,"j_2"']\\
\overline X_1 \arrow[r,"\overline f"'] & \overline X_2 ,
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $Y_i=\overline X_i-X_i$ are normal-crossings divisors. The canonical morphism (see (3.1.3)) from $\overline f^{\,*}\Omega_{\overline X_2}^{*}\langle Y_2\rangle$ to $\Omega_{\overline X_1}^{*}\langle Y_1\rangle$ is then a morphism of bifiltered complexes; on hypercohomology it induces a morphism compatible with $F$ and $W$, and therefore $f^*:H^n(X_2,\Z)\longrightarrow H^n(X_1,\Z)$ is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures, for the structures defined by the compactifications $\overline X_i$.

\paragraph{C.} \textit{Independence of the compactification.} With the notation of B, if $f$ is an isomorphism, then $f^*$ is a bijective morphism of mixed Hodge structures, hence an isomorphism (2.3.5).

If $\overline X_1$ and $\overline X_2$ are two smooth compactifications of $X$, with $Y_i=\overline X_i-X_i$ a normal-crossings divisor, there exists a third smooth compactification $\overline X$, with $Y=\overline X-X$ a normal-crossings divisor, fitting into a commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.2em,column sep=2.4em]
& X \arrow[hook,dl] \arrow[hook,d] \arrow[hook,dr] & \\
\overline X_1 & \overline X \arrow[l] \arrow[r] & \overline X_2
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Namely, one takes for $\overline X$ a resolution of the singularities of the closure of the diagonal image of $X$ in $\overline X_1\times\overline X_2$. The identity map from $H^n(X,\Z)$, endowed with the mixed Hodge structure defined by $\overline X_1$, to $H^n(X,\Z)$, endowed with that defined by $\overline X_2$, is therefore a composition of two isomorphisms.

To finish the proof of (ii) and (iii), one observes that every morphism $f$ fits into a diagram (3.2.11.1): choose compactifications $\overline X'_1$ and $\overline X_2$ of $X_1$ and $X_2$, and then take for $\overline X_1$ a resolution of the singularities of the closure of the image of $X_1$ in $\overline X'_1\times\overline X_2$.

\paragraph{Definition (3.2.12).} --- {\itshape The mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of a smooth separated algebraic variety is the mixed Hodge structure (3.2.5), (iii).}

\paragraph{Corollary (3.2.13).} --- {\itshape With the preceding notation:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The spectral sequence (3.2.4.1) degenerates at $E_2$, i.e. the Leray spectral sequence for the inclusion $j:X^*\hookrightarrow\overline X$ degenerates at $E_3$ $(E_3=E_{\infty})$.
\item The spectral sequence (3.2.4.2)
\[
{}_F E_1^{pq}=H^q(\overline X,\Omega_{\overline X}^p\langle Y\rangle)
\Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(X,\C)
\]
degenerates at $E_1$.
\item The spectral sequence defined by the sheaf $\Omega_{\overline X}^{p}\langle Y\rangle$, endowed with the filtration $W$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_1^{-n,k+n}
&=H^k(\overline X,\Gr_n^W(\Omega_{\overline X}^{p}\langle Y\rangle))\\
&\approx H^k(\widetilde Y^n,\Omega_{\widetilde Y^n}^{p-n}(\varepsilon^n))
\Longrightarrow H^k(\overline X,\Omega_{\overline X}^{p}\langle Y\rangle)
\end{aligned}
\]
degenerates at $E_2$.
\end{enumerate}}

Assertion (i) was proved in (3.2.10).

Consider the four spectral sequences of (1.4.12), relative to the bifiltered complex $\Omega_{\overline X}^{*}\langle Y\rangle$. By (i), one has
\[
\sum_n\dim H^n(X,\C)=\sum_{p,q}\dim {}_WE_2^{p,q}.
\]
The terms ${}_WE_1^{n,k-n}$ are, for fixed $n$, the abutment of a spectral sequence \emph{degenerate at $E_1$} (3.2.6), with initial terms $E_1^{p,n,k-p-n}$ (notation of (1.4.12)), the initial terms of spectral sequence (iii). Since ${}_Wd_1$ is strictly compatible with the filtration $F$ that is the abutment
of this spectral sequence (3.2.7), and is (1.4.12) the abutment of a morphism between these spectral sequences, beginning with the differentials of (iii), one has
\[
\Gr_F^p({}_WE_2^{n,k-n})\approx
H^*(E_1^{p,n-1,k-n-p}\to E_1^{p,n,k-n-p}\to E_1^{p,n+1,k-n-p})
\]
and $\Gr_F^*({}_WE_2^{**})$ is the sum of the terms $E_2^{***}$ of the spectral sequences (iii). Therefore
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(3.2.13.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle \sum_n \dim H^n(X,\C)=\sum\dim E_2^{***}.$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(3.2.13.1)}}}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\sum_n \dim H^n(X,\C)\le \sum \dim {}_F E_1^{**},
\]
with equality if and only if the spectral sequence (ii) degenerates at $E_1$, and
\[
\sum\dim {}_F E_1^{**}\le \sum\dim E_2^{***},
\]
with equality if and only if the spectral sequences (iii) degenerate at $E_2$. Comparing with (3.2.13.1), one obtains (3.2.13).

\paragraph{Corollary (3.2.14).} --- {\itshape Let $\omega$ be a meromorphic differential $p$-form on $\overline X$, holomorphic on $X$ and having at worst logarithmic poles along $Y$. Then the restriction $\omega|X$ of $\omega$ to $X$ is closed, and if the cohomology class in $H^p(X,\C)$ defined by $\omega$ is zero, then $\omega=0$.}

This is the special case ${}_FE_1^{p0}={}_FE_{\infty}^{p0}$ of (3.2.13), (ii).

\paragraph{Corollary (3.2.15).} --- {\itshape
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),font=\itshape]
\item If $X$ is a complete smooth algebraic variety, the mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(X,\Z)$ is the classical Hodge structure of weight $n$.
\item The Hodge numbers $h^{pq}$ of the mixed Hodge structure of $H^n(X,\Z)$ ($X$ smooth algebraic) can be nonzero only for $p\le n$, $q\le n$, and $p+q\ge n$.
\end{enumerate}}
Assertion (i) is clear. To prove (ii), one observes that, for $Y$ a union of smooth divisors, the rational Hodge structure $\Gr_k^W(H^n(X,\Q))$ is a quotient of a subobject of a Hodge structure of weight $n+k$, namely
\[
H^{n-k}(\widetilde Y^n,\Q)\otimes\Q(-k).
\]

\paragraph{(3.2.16)} Let $X$ be a smooth separated scheme. It is known that $X$ admits smooth compactifications $\overline X$, and that the subgroup of $H^n(X,\Z)$ which is the image of $H^n(\overline X,\Z)$ is independent of the choice of $\overline X$ (cf. [6], (9.1) to (9.4)).

\paragraph{Corollary (3.2.17).} --- {\itshape Under the hypotheses (3.2.16), the image of $H^n(\overline X,\Q)$ in $H^n(X,\Q)$ is} $W_n(H^n(X,\Q))$ ($W$ denoting the weight filtration (3.2.12)).

One may suppose that $\overline X-X$ is a normal-crossings divisor. The assertion then follows from the fact that $W[-n]$ is the abutment of the Leray spectral sequence for the inclusion $j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$.

\paragraph{Corollary (3.2.18).} --- {\itshape Let $f$ be a morphism from a proper smooth scheme $Y$ to a smooth scheme $X$ admitting a smooth compactification $\overline X$:
\[
Y\xrightarrow{f}X\xhookrightarrow{j}\overline X.
\]
Then the groups $H^n(X,\Q)$ and $H^n(\overline X,\Q)$ have the same image in $H^n(Y,\Q)$.}

Since $f^*$ and $(jf)^*$ are strictly compatible with the weight filtration ((3.2.5), (iii)), it is enough to prove that $\Gr^W(f^*)$ and $\Gr^W(f^*j^*)$ have the same image in $\Gr^W(H^n(Y,\Q))$. By (3.2.17) and (3.2.15), $\Gr_n^W(j^*)$ is an isomorphism, while $\Gr_m^W(f^*)=0$ for $m\ne n$ because $\Gr_m^W(H^n(Y,\Q))=0$ for $m\ne n$.

\paragraph{\emph{Remark} (3.2.19).} --- By (3.1.11) and (1.4.5), under the hypotheses of (3.2.5), the Hodge filtration on $H^n(X,\C)$ is the abutment of the hypercohomology spectral sequence of the complex $j_*^m\Omega_{X^*}^{*}$, endowed with the filtration by order of pole (3.1.10): this spectral sequence coincides with (3.2.4.2).

\section*{4. Applications and complements}

\subsection*{4.1. The fixed-part theorem.}

\paragraph{\emph{Theorem} (4.1.1).} --- {\itshape Let $S$ be a smooth separated scheme, and let $f:X\to S$ be a proper smooth morphism.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),font=\itshape]
\item In rational cohomology, the Leray spectral sequence
\[
E_2^{pq}=H^p(S,R^qf_*\Q)\Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(X,\Q)
\]
degenerates $(E_2=E_{\infty})$.
\item If $\overline X$ is a nonsingular compactification of $X$, the canonical morphism
\[
H^n(\overline X,\Q)\longrightarrow H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)
\]
is surjective.
\end{enumerate}}

For $f$ projective and smooth, assertion (i) is proved in [2]. The proof of [2] is rewritten more readably in [5]; it does not use the smoothness of $S$.

Fix $f$, and prove that (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii). We reduce to the case where $S$ is connected and nonempty. If $s\in S$ is a point of $S$, the local system $R^nf_*\Q$ is entirely described by its fiber $(R^nf_*\Q)_s$ at $s$, and by the action of the fundamental group $\pi=\pi_1(S,s)$ on this fiber. One has
\[
H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)\xrightarrow{\sim}[(R^nf_*\Q)_s]^{\pi}.
\]
If $X_s=f^{-1}(s)$, the composite arrow
\[
H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)\longrightarrow (R^nf_*\Q)_s\simeq H^n(X_s,\Q)
\]
is therefore injective. Consider the arrows
\[
H^n(\overline X,\Q)\xrightarrow{a}H^n(X,\Q)\xrightarrow{b}
H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)\xhookrightarrow{c}H^n(X_s,\Q).
\]
The arrows $cb$ and $cba$ have the same image by (3.2.18). The arrow $b$ is an edge homomorphism of the Leray spectral sequence, hence is surjective by hypothesis. Since $c$ is injective, $b$ and $ba$ have the same image and $ba$ is surjective. This proves (ii) for $f$ projective. We now deduce the general case. Again reduce to the case where $S$ is connected and nonempty.

By Chow's lemma and resolution of singularities, there exists a scheme
$X'$ which is quasi-projective and smooth, and a projective birational morphism
\[
p:X'\longrightarrow X.
\]
There then exists (by Bertini, or Sard) a nonempty Zariski open subset $S_1$ of $S$ such that $X'_1=(fp)^{-1}(S_1)$ is smooth over $S_1$. Finally, let $X_1=f^{-1}(S_1)$, let $\overline X$ be a smooth compactification of $X$, and let $\overline X'_1$ be a smooth compactification of $X'_1$ which dominates $\overline X$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.35em,column sep=2.8em]
\overline X && \overline X'_1 \arrow[ll,"\overline p"']\\
X \arrow[u,hook] \arrow[d,"f"'] & X_1 \arrow[l,hook] \arrow[d,"f_1"'] & X'_1 \arrow[l,"p"'] \arrow[u,hook] \arrow[d,"f'_1"']\\
S & S_1 \arrow[l,hook,"i"] & S_1 \arrow[l,equal]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
If $s\in S_1$, the morphism $i_*:\pi_1(S_1,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is surjective because the topological codimension of $S-S_1$ is $\ge2$. Therefore
\[
H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)\xrightarrow{\sim} H^0(S_1,R^nf_{1*}\Q),
\]
and it suffices to prove that
\[
H^n(\overline X,\Q)\longrightarrow H^0(S_1,R^nf_{1*}\Q)
\]
is surjective.

The vertical arrows of the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.2em,row sep=2.2em]
H^n(\overline X,\Q) \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\overline p^*"] &
H^n(X_1,\Q) \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"p^*"] &
H^0(S_1,R^nf_{1*}\Q) \arrow[d,"p^*"]\\
H^n(\overline X'_1,\Q) \arrow[r] &
H^n(X'_1,\Q) \arrow[r] &
H^0(S_1,R^nf'_{1*}\Q)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
admit as left inverses the \emph{Gysin morphisms} $\overline p_!$, $p_!$, and $p_!$, defined by Poincaré duality as transposes of the arrows analogous to the preceding ones in cohomology with proper support. Moreover, the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4em,row sep=2.2em]
H^n(\overline X,\Q) \arrow[r,"u"] &
H^0(S_1,R^nf_{1*}\Q)\\
H^n(\overline X'_1,\Q) \arrow[u,"\overline p_!"'] \arrow[r,"v"'] &
H^0(S_1,R^nf'_{1*}\Q) \arrow[u,"p_!"']
\end{tikzcd}
\]
is commutative. Thus $u$ is a direct factor of $v$. The latter being surjective (since $f'_1$ is projective), the same is true of $u$.

We now prove (i) in the general case. We reduce to the case where $f$ is purely of relative dimension $n$. Let $f\times f$ be the projection of $X\times_SX$ onto $S$.

Let $\delta$ be the image of the cohomology class of the diagonal of $X\times_SX$ in $H^0(S,R^n(f\times f)_*\Q)$. By Künneth,
\[
R^n(f\times f)_*\Q=
\sum_{p+q=n}(R^pf_*\Q\otimes R^qf_*\Q).
\]
Let $\delta'_{pq}$ ($p+q=n$) denote the components of $\delta$ in this decomposition, and let $\delta_{pq}$ be classes in $H^n(X\times_SX)$ whose images are the $\delta'_{pq}$.

The $\delta_{pq}$ define in the derived category $D^+(S)$ homomorphisms
\[
\delta_p:Rf_*\Q\longrightarrow Rf_*\Q
\]
such that $\mathcal H^q(\delta_p)$ is zero for $p\ne q$, and is the identity for $p=q$. By [2], one therefore has in $D^+(S)$
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(4.1.1.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle Rf_*\Q\approx\sum_p R^pf_*\Q[-p],$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(4.1.1.1)}}}
\]
and the Leray spectral sequence degenerates.

\paragraph{\emph{Corollary} (4.1.2).} --- {\itshape Let $f:X\to S$ be a proper smooth morphism whose target is a reduced connected separated scheme $S$. Let $(R^nf_*\Q)^0$ be the largest constant local subsystem of $R^nf_*\Q$, with fiber $H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)$. Then, for each $s\in S$, $(R^nf_*\Q)^0_s$ is a Hodge substructure of $(R^nf_*\Q)_s\simeq H^n(X_s,\Q)$, and the Hodge structure induced on $H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)$ is independent of $s$.}

Let $s\in S$ and $X_s=f^{-1}(s)$. If $S$ is smooth, and if $\overline X$ is a smooth compactification of $X$, then by (4.1.1) the subspace $(R^nf_*\Q)^0_s$ of $(R^nf_*\Q)_s$ is the image of $H^n(\overline X,\Q)$. Since the restriction map
\[
H^n(\overline X,\Q)\longrightarrow H^n(X_s,\Q)
\]
is a morphism of Hodge structures, its image is a Hodge substructure, and the Hodge structure induced on $H^0(S,R^nf_*\Q)$, a quotient of that of $H^n(\overline X,\Q)$, is independent of $s$.

In the general case, (4.1.2) also means that if $a$ is a global section of $R^nf_*\C$, then its components $a^{p,q}$ of type $(p,q)$, \emph{a priori} only continuous sections of the complex vector bundle defined by $R^nf_*\C$, are in fact locally constant, i.e. are sections of $R^nf_*\C$. This is so because $a^{p,q}$ is continuous and locally constant on the smooth locus (which is dense) of $S$, by what precedes.

\paragraph{(4.1.3)} In the case where $S$ is compact, a generalization of (4.1.2) is proved analytically in Griffiths [5].

As corollaries of (4.1.2), let us cite:

\paragraph{(4.1.3.1)} (Griffiths [5]) Let $f:X\to S$ be a proper smooth morphism as in (4.1.2). If a global section $a$ of $R^nf_*\C$ is of Hodge type $(p,q)$ at one point, then $a$ is of type $(p,q)$ everywhere. In particular, if $n=2$ and if, at one point $s$, $a$ is the cohomology class
of a divisor of $X_s$, then $a$ is at every point the cohomology class of a divisor and, for $S$ smooth, is even defined by a divisor $D$ on $X$.

\paragraph{(4.1.3.2)} (Grothendieck [7]) Let $S$ be a reduced connected scheme of finite type over $\C$, and let $f_1:X_1\to S$ and $f_2:X_2\to S$ be two abelian schemes over $S$. If a morphism
\[
u:R^1f_{2*}\Z\longrightarrow R^1f_{1*}\Z
\]
comes at one point $s$ of $S$ from a morphism of abelian varieties
\[
\widetilde u_s:(X_1)_s\longrightarrow (X_2)_s,
\]
then $u$ comes from one (and only one) morphism of abelian schemes
\[
\widetilde u:X_1\longrightarrow X_2.
\]

\paragraph{(4.1.3.3)} (Cf. Katz [10]) Let $S$ be a smooth connected scheme, let $s$ be a point of $S$, let $f:X\to S$ be a proper smooth morphism, and let $P$ be a direct factor of the local system $R^if_*\Q$ which is pointwise a Hodge substructure. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item The Hodge structure of $P$ is locally constant.
\item The representation $P_s$ of $\pi_1(S,s)$ factors through a finite quotient of $\pi_1(S,s)$.
\item There exists a nonempty finite étale covering $u:S'\to S$ such that $u^*P$ is a constant family of Hodge structures.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{4.2. The semisimplicity theorem.}

\paragraph{(4.2.1)} Let $S$ be a topological space. A \emph{continuous family of Hodge structures} on $S$ consists of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item A local system $H_{\Z}$ of finitely generated $\Z$-modules on $S$.
\item For every point $s\in S$, a Hodge structure on the fiber $(H_{\Z})_s$, this structure varying continuously with $s$.
\end{enumerate}
A continuous family $H$ of Hodge structures on $S$ is said to be \emph{of weight $n$} if the fibers $H_s$ $(s\in S)$ have weight $n$.

Similarly, a \emph{continuous family of $\Q$-Hodge structures} is defined as a local system of $\Q$-vector spaces endowed at each point with a continuously varying $\Q$-Hodge structure.

A \emph{polarization} of a continuous family $H$ of $\Q$-Hodge structures of weight $n$ is a morphism of local systems from $H_{\Q}\otimes H_{\Q}$ into the constant local system $\Q(-n)_{\Q}$, which at every point $s\in S$ defines a polarization of $H_s$.

\paragraph{(4.2.2)} Suppose $S$ is connected, and let $\mathcal C$ be a strictly full subcategory of the category of continuous families of $\Q$-Hodge structures on $S$. We shall consider the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(4.2.2.\arabic*)]
\item $\mathcal C$ is stable under direct factors, direct sums, and tensor products; the constant Tate families $\Q(n)$ $(n\in\Z)$ belong to $\mathcal C$.
\item Every homogeneous Hodge structure ($={}$ of some weight $n$) in $\mathcal C$ is polarizable.
\item For every $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$, there exists a local system $H'_{\Z}$ of free $\Z$-modules on $S$ such that $H'_{\Z}\otimes\Q\approx H_{\Q}$.
\item For every $H$ in $\mathcal C$, the largest constant local subsystem $H'$ of $H$ is a constant family of Hodge substructures of $H$.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{\emph{Lemma} (4.2.3).} --- {\itshape If $\mathcal C$ satisfies conditions (4.2.2.1) and (4.2.2.2), then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\mathcal C$ is a semisimple abelian subcategory of the abelian category of continuous families of $\Q$-Hodge structures on $S$.
\item If $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$, then its dual $H^*$ and the $\bigwedge^pH$ belong to $\mathcal C$; if $H_1,H_2\in\Ob\mathcal C$, then $\Hom(H_1,H_2)\in\Ob\mathcal C$.
\end{enumerate}}

If $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$ and $H_1$ is a subobject of $H$, in the category of continuous families of $\Q$-Hodge structures, we prove that $H_1$ is a direct factor of $H$ in that category. We may suppose $H$ homogeneous. If $\psi$ is a polarization form for $H$, the orthogonal complement of $H_1$ for $\psi$ is indeed a subobject of $H$ complementary to $H_1$. This proves (i).

If $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$ has weight $n$, a polarization of $H$ defines an isomorphism between $H^*$ and $H\otimes\Q(n)$. By (4.2.2.1), one therefore has $H^*\in\Ob\mathcal C$. For arbitrary $H$ in $\mathcal C$, decomposing $H$ into its homogeneous components, one has
\[
H^*=\bigoplus_n (H^n)^*,
\]
whence again $H^*\in\Ob\mathcal C$. Finally, $\bigwedge^pH$ is a direct factor in $\bigotimes^pH$, and $\Hom(H_1,H_2)\simeq H_1^*\otimes H_2$.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a proper smooth morphism of reduced schemes. The sheaf $R^if_*\Q$ is then a local system, and for $s\in S$,
\[
(R^if_*\Q)_s\simeq H^i(X_s,\Q)
\]
is endowed with a $\Q$-Hodge structure. This varies continuously with $s$.

\paragraph{\emph{Definition} (4.2.4).} --- {\itshape Let $S$ be a smooth connected scheme. A continuous family $H$ of $\Q$-Hodge structures on $S^{an}$ will be called algebraic if there exist a nonempty Zariski open subset $U$ of $S$, an integer $k$, and a projective smooth morphism $f:X\to U$ such that $H|U$ is a direct factor of $Rf_*\Q\otimes\Q(k)$.}

\paragraph{\emph{Proposition} (4.2.5).} --- {\itshape
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The category of algebraic continuous families of $\Q$-Hodge structures on $S$ satisfies the conditions of (4.2.2).
\item If a continuous family $H$ of Hodge structures on $S$ is such that its restriction to a dense Zariski open subset $U$ of $S$ is algebraic, then $H$ is algebraic.
\item If $f:X\to S$ is proper and smooth, then $Rf_*\Q$ is algebraic.
\end{enumerate}}

Assertion (ii) is evident. We prove (i). Let $\mathcal C_0$ be the set of continuous families of Hodge structures on $S$ that are of the form $Rf_*\Q$ ($f$ projective and smooth). Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item By the Künneth formula,
\[
R(f\times g)_*\Q\simeq Rf_*\Q\otimes Rg_*\Q,
\]
$\mathcal C_0$ is stable under tensor product.
\item $\mathcal C_0$ is stable under direct sum:
\[
R(f\amalg g)_*\Q\simeq Rf_*\Q\oplus Rg_*\Q.
\]
\end{enumerate}



\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item The homogeneous components of every $H\in\mathcal C_0$ are polarizable (cf. (2.2.6)).
\item The objects $H\in\mathcal C_0$ satisfy (4.2.2.3), since
\[
Rf_*\Q\simeq Rf_*\Z\otimes\Q.
\]
\item The objects $H\in\mathcal C_0$ satisfy (4.2.2.4), by (4.1.2).
\end{enumerate}
Let $\mathcal C_1$ be the set of direct factors of objects of $\mathcal C_0$. Then $\mathcal C_1$ is stable under tensor product, direct sum, and direct factor, and satisfies (4.2.2.2) to (4.2.2.4). Moreover $\Q(-1)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_1$, since it is of the form $R^2f_*\Q$ for the projective bundle $f:\bbP^1_S\to S$. The category $\mathcal C_2$ of the $H\otimes\Q(k)$ ($k\in\N$) therefore satisfies (4.2.2.1) to (4.2.2.4).

To deduce (i), it suffices to note that if $H$ is a continuous family of Hodge structures, and $U$ is a dense Zariski open subset of $S$, then a subobject, a polarization, or an integral lattice of $H|U$ extends uniquely to $H$.

We prove (iii). If $f:X\to S$ is projective and smooth, then there exist a dense Zariski open subset $U$ of $S$ and a commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em,row sep=2em]
X' \arrow[rr,"p"] \arrow[dr,"f'"'] && X|U \arrow[dl,"f|U"]\\
& U &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
with $f'$ projective and smooth and $p$ birational and surjective (apply Chow's lemma and resolution of singularities to the generic fiber of $f$). The restriction map
\[
p^*:(Rf_*\Q)|U\longrightarrow Rf'_*\Q
\]
is then a split injection of continuous families of Hodge structures, with left inverse the Gysin morphism $p_*$; hence $Rf_*\Q$ is algebraic.

\begingroup
\renewcommand{\thefootnote}{(\arabic{footnote})}
\paragraph{Theorem (4.2.6)\textsuperscript{(1)}.} --- {\itshape Let $S$ be a connected, locally connected and locally simply connected topological space, endowed with a base point $s$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a category of continuous families of Hodge structures on $S$ satisfying the conditions (4.2.2). Then, if $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$, the representation of $\pi_1(S,s)$ on the fiber $(H_{\Q})_s$ is semisimple.}
\footnotetext[1]{\emph{(Added in proof.)} Let $S$ be a smooth connected scheme. A \emph{family of Hodge structures on $S$} is a continuous family $H$ of Hodge structures on $S$ satisfying the following conditions:

\emph{a)} The Hodge filtration of $(H_{\C})_s$ varies holomorphically with $s$, i.e. corresponds to a filtration $F$ of $H_{\cO}=H_{\Z}\otimes\cO$.

\emph{b)} The covariant derivative $\nabla$ satisfies $\nabla F^p\subset\Omega_S^1\otimes F^{p-1}$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the category of those continuous families of $\Q$-Hodge structures on $S$ which underlie a family of Hodge structures, and whose homogeneous direct factors are polarizable. It is clear that $\mathcal C$ satisfies (4.2.2.1) to (4.2.2.3). From results of W. Schmid (August 1970, unpublished) and P. A. Griffiths [5] one can deduce that $\mathcal C$ satisfies (4.2.2.4). This theorem, of which (4.1.2) is a corollary, makes it possible to apply (4.2.6) and its corollaries to objects of $\mathcal C$.}
\endgroup

Let $H\in\Ob\mathcal C$. The local system $H_{\Q}$ defines a complex local system $H_{\C}=H_{\Q}\otimes\C$. For every complex local system $V$ on $S$, denote by $V^c$ the complex vector bundle which it defines, identified with the sheaf of its continuous sections.

By definition, the group $S$ (2.1.2) acts on $H_{\C}^c$. A subbundle of $H_{\C}^c$ will be called \emph{horizontal}, or \emph{locally constant}, if it is defined by a local subsystem of $H_{\C}$.

\paragraph{Lemma (4.2.7).} --- {\itshape Let $V$ be a rank-one local subsystem of $H_{\C}$. Suppose that a tensor power $V^{\otimes n}$ ($n\ge1$) of $V$ is a trivial local system, i.e. that $\pi_1(S,s)$ acts on $V_s$ through a finite group (necessarily cyclic). Then, for $t\in S$, $tV^c$ is again locally constant.}

For $tV^c$ to be locally constant, it suffices that
\[
(tV^c)^{\otimes n}=tV^{c\otimes n}\subset\bigotimes^n H_{\C}
\]
be locally constant. But $V^{\otimes n}$ is generated by a global horizontal section $v$, and by hypothesis $tv$ is again horizontal (4.2.2.4).

We proceed by induction on $\dim(H_{\Q})_s$. We may suppose $H$ homogeneous and nonzero. Let $d$ be the minimal dimension of the nonzero complex local subsystems of $H_{\C}$. The sum $W$ of all local subsystems of $H_{\C}$ of dimension $d$ (which are automatically simple) is ``defined over $\Q$'', i.e. is of the form $W_{\Q}\otimes\C$ for $W_{\Q}$ a local subsystem of $H_{\Q}$. By construction, $W_s$ is a semisimple complex $\pi_1(S,s)$-module, hence $(W_{\Q})_s$ is a semisimple $\pi_1(S,s)$-module over $\Q$.

Let $H_{\Z}$ be a local system of free $\Z$-modules such that $H_{\Z}\otimes\Q\simeq H_{\Q}$, and let $W_{\Z}=H_{\Z}\cap W_{\Q}$. If $W$ has dimension $e$, the local system $(\bigwedge^eW)^{\otimes2}$ is trivial. Indeed:
\[
\bigwedge^eW\simeq \bigwedge^eW_{\Z}\otimes\C,
\]
and $\pi_1(S,s)$ can act on $(\bigwedge^eW_{\Z})_s$ only by $\pm1$.

Let $V$ be a complex local subsystem of dimension $d$ of $H_{\C}$, and let $V'$ be a complement of $V$ in $W$ (semisimplicity of $W$). One has
\[
\bigwedge^eW\simeq \bigwedge^dV\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}V'.
\]
Apply (4.2.7) to the local subsystem $\bigwedge^dV\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}V'$ of $\bigwedge^dH_{\C}\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}H_{\C}$. We find that, for $t\in S$,
\[
t(\bigwedge^dV\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}V')^c=
\bigwedge^d tV^c\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}tV'^c
\subset \bigwedge^dH_{\C}\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}H_{\C}
\]
is locally constant. Hence $\bigwedge^d tV^c\subset\bigwedge^dH_{\C}$ and $tV^c\subset H_{\C}$ are locally constant.

By definition of $W$, one has $tV^c\subset W^c$: $W^c$ is stable under $S$, and $W_{\Q}$ is a Hodge substructure of $H$. If $\psi$ is a polarization of $H$, $H$ is therefore the direct sum of $W$ and of its orthogonal complement, both in $\mathcal C$, and the induction concludes.

\paragraph{Corollary (4.2.8).} --- {\itshape Under the hypotheses of (4.2.6):}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item {\itshape The algebra $A$ of endomorphisms of the local system $H_{\Q}$ is semisimple. It admits one (and only one) $\Q$-Hodge structure such that, at each point $s$, $A\otimes H_s\to H_s$ is a morphism of Hodge structures.}
\item {\itshape The center of $A$ is of type $(0,0)$ and the composition law $\cdot : A\otimes A\to A$ is a morphism of Hodge structures.}
\item {\itshape Let $W$ be a complex local subsystem of dimension $d$ of $H_{\C}$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item For $t\in S$, $tW^c\subset H_{\C}$ is locally constant and defines a local subsystem $tW$ isomorphic to $W$.
\item A power $(\bigwedge^dW)^{\otimes n}$ ($n\ge1$) of the local system $\bigwedge^dW$ is a trivial local system.
\end{enumerate}}
\end{enumerate}

The algebra $A$ is the commutant of $\pi_1(S,s)$ in $(H_{\Q})_s$. Its semisimplicity therefore follows from (4.2.6) and Bourb., \textit{Alg.}, chap. 8, § 5, no. 2, prop. 4. Moreover, $A$ is the fiber of the largest constant local subsystem of $\Hom(H,H)$. Since $\Hom(H,H)\in\mathcal C$ ((4.2.3), (ii)), the existence of the Hodge structure in (i) follows from hypothesis (4.2.2.4). It is clear that the composition law is a morphism of Hodge structures. It follows that the center $Z$ of $A$ is a Hodge substructure: $Z_{\C}$ is bigraded, as the intersection of the kernels of the bihomogeneous morphisms $[x,\,]$ for $x$ bihomogeneous. Finally $Z$, and hence $Z_{\C}$, is semisimple, and for $(p,q)\ne(0,0)$, $Z^{pq}$ is zero because it is nilpotent.

A complex local subsystem $W$ of $H_{\C}$ is defined by a projector $e$ of $A_{\C}$. For $t\in S$, $tW^c$ is defined by the projector $t.e$, and is therefore locally constant. Since the group $S$ is connected, to verify that $tW$ is isomorphic to $W$, it suffices to verify that for $t$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $1$, the $\C[\pi_1(S,s)]$-module $tW_s$ is isomorphic to $W_s$. Let $H_i$ be the isotypic components of the $\C[\pi_1(S,s)]$-module $(H_{\C})_s$. One has
\[
W_s=\bigoplus_i(W_s\cap H_i)
\]
and
\[
tW_s=\bigoplus_i(tW_s\cap H_i).
\]
Moreover, for $t$ sufficiently close to $1$, $tW_s$ is close to $W_s$ in the Grassmannian, and hence
\[
\makebox[\textwidth][s]{\textbf{(4.2.8.1)}\hfill$\displaystyle \dim(tW_s\cap H_i)\le \dim(W_s\cap H_i).$\hfill\phantom{\textbf{(4.2.8.1)}}}
\]
In fact, since $\dim(tW_s)=\dim(W_s)$, equality holds in (4.2.8.1). The respective isotypic components of $W_s$ and $tW_s$ therefore have the same length, and $W_s$ is isomorphic to $tW_s$.

We prove (iii), \textit{b}). It suffices to treat the case where $H$ is homogeneous and $W_s$ is a simple $\C[\pi_1(S,s)]$-module. Let $H_1$ be the isotypic component of $(H_{\C})_s$ which contains $W_s$. By \textit{a}), $H_1$ is stable under $S$. If $W_s$ has dimension $d$ and $H_1$ has length $k$, one has
\[
\bigwedge^{kd}H_1\simeq(\bigwedge^dW_s)^{\otimes k}
\]
as a $\C[\pi_1(S,s)]$-module. If $\chi$ is the character of $\pi_1(S,s)$ defined by $\bigwedge^dW$, the character $\chi_1$ defined by $\bigwedge^{kd}H_1$ is therefore $\chi^k$. Put $H_2=H_1+\overline{H_1}$. Since $H_1$ is stable under $S$, $H_2$ is defined by a real Hodge substructure of $(H_{\R})_s$. Every polarization form on $H$ therefore induces on $H_2$ a nondegenerate bilinear form invariant under $\pi_1(S,s)$.

If $\dim(H_2)=e$, the representation $(\bigwedge^eH_2)^{\otimes2}$ of $\pi_1(S,s)$ is therefore trivial. Thus:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item For $H_1$ real: $\chi^{2k}$ is trivial;
\item For $H_1$ nonreal $(H_1\ne\overline{H_1})$: $\chi^{2k}\cdot\bar{\chi}^{2k}$ is trivial.
\end{enumerate}
In both cases one has $|\chi|=1$.

The representation of $\pi_1(S,s)$ on $(H_{\C})_s$ is obtained by extension of scalars from a representation defined over $\Q$ (namely $(H_{\Q})_s$). The conjugate representations of $W$ therefore occur in $(H_{\C})_s$; there are at most $N=\dim(H)$ of them, and for every automorphism $\sigma$ of $\C$ one has
\[
|\sigma(\chi)|=1.
\]
For $\gamma\in\pi_1(S,s)$, $\chi(\gamma)$ is an algebraic integer with at most $N$ complex conjugates, all of absolute value $1$; $\chi(\gamma)$ is therefore a $k$-th root of unity, with $k\le N$. Hence $\chi^{N!}=1$, which proves b).

\paragraph{Corollary (4.2.9).} --- {\itshape Let $S$ be a smooth connected separated scheme, endowed with a base point $s\in S$. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes such that $R^nf_*\Q$ is a local system on $S$, let $G$ be the Zariski closure of the image of $\pi_1(S,s)$ in $\Aut_{\C}((R^nf_*\C)_s)$, and let $G^0$ be the identity component of $G$. Then:}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item {\itshape If $f$ is proper and smooth, $G^0$ is semisimple.}
\item {\itshape In general, $G^0$ has no quotient of multiplicative type (i.e., the radical of $G^0$ is unipotent).}
\end{enumerate}

We prove \textit{a}). After replacing $S$ by a finite étale covering, we reduce to the case $G=G^0$. By ((4.2.5), (iii)), the local system $R^nf_*\Q$ underlies an algebraic family $H$ of Hodge structures, so (4.2.8) applies to it ((4.2.5), (i)). The group $G$ is reductive, since it has a faithful semisimple representation, namely $(R^nf_*\C)_s$. If $G$ (assumed connected) were not semisimple, it would admit a nontrivial complex representation $\rho$ of rank one; since $H_s$ is faithful, $\rho$ would be a direct summand of $((H_{\C}+H_{\C}^*)^{\otimes m})_s$ for some $m$. This contradicts (4.2.8), (iii), \textit{b}), because $(H+H^*)^{\otimes m}$ is algebraic and no tensor power of $\rho$ is trivial.

Let $\pi$ be a group, and consider the following property of a representation $\rho$ of $\pi$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$:
\begin{quote}
\noindent $(*)\quad$ The identity component $G^0$ of the Zariski closure $G$ of $\rho(\pi)$ in $\Aut(V)$ has no quotient of multiplicative type.
\end{quote}

\paragraph{Lemma (4.2.10).} --- {\itshape Let $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ be an exact sequence of representations of the preceding kind. Then $V$ satisfies $(*)$ if (and only if) $V'$ and $V''$ satisfy $(*)$.}

Let $G$, $G'$, and $G''$ be the groups defined by $V$, $V'$, and $V''$. Since, like $\pi$, $G$ leaves $V'$ invariant, there is a morphism
\[
u=(u',u''):G\longrightarrow G'\times G'',
\]
with unipotent kernel, and such that $u'$ and $u''$ are surjective. Let $N$ be the identity component of the kernel of $u''$. Since $u'$ is surjective, $u'(N)$ is normal in $G'$, and therefore has no
quotient of multiplicative type. If $\chi$ is a character of $G^0$, then $\chi$ factors through $u(G^0)$, is trivial on $N$, a power of $\chi$ factors through $G''^0$, and $\chi$ is trivial.

We prove (4.2.9), \textit{b)}, by dévissage and induction on the relative dimension of $f$. We may suppose $X$ reduced.

First suppose that $X$ is quasi-projective. Then there exist a nonempty open subset $U$ of $S$, a dense open subset $X'$ of $X_U=f^{-1}(U)$ smooth over $U$, and a compactification $\overline X'$ of $X'$ over $U$, proper and smooth over $U$. One can choose $\overline X'$ so that an open $X''$ of $\overline X'$ contains $X'$ and is proper over $X_U$
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.8em,row sep=2.8em]
X_U \arrow[ddrr,"f_U"'] &&&&
X'' \arrow[llll,"p"] \arrow[rr,hook,"k"'] \arrow[ddll,"f''"] &&
\overline X' \arrow[ddllll,"\bar f'"] \\
&& X' \arrow[ull,hook,"i"] \arrow[urr,hook,"j"] \arrow[d,"f'"] &&&& \\
&& U &&&&
\end{tikzcd}
\]
We have long exact sequences of sheaves
\[
\begin{gathered}
\to R^if_{U*}(i_!\Q)\to R^if_{U*}\Q\to R^if_{U*}(\Q/i_!\Q)\to\\
\to R^if''_*(j_!\Q)\to R^if''_*\Q\to Rf''_*(\Q/j_!\Q)\to\\
\to R^if''_!\Q\to R^i\bar f'_*\Q\to R^i\bar f'_*(\Q/k_!\Q)\to
\end{gathered}
\]
For $U$ sufficiently small, these sheaves are local systems and the induction hypothesis applies to $R^*f_{U*}(\Q/i_!\Q)$, to $R^*f''_*(\Q/j_!\Q)$, and to $R^*\bar f'_*(\Q/k_!\Q)$. By \textit{a)}, condition $(*)$ is satisfied by $R^*\bar f'_*\Q$. By (4.2.10), it is therefore satisfied by $R^*f''_!\Q$, and by the dual local system $R^*f''_*\Q$ (Poincaré duality). By (4.2.10), condition $(*)$ is satisfied by $R^*f''_*(j_!\Q)$, which is isomorphic to $R^*f_{U*}(i_!\Q)$ because $p$ is proper, and also by $R^*f_{U*}\Q$. Since the morphism $\pi_1(U)\to\pi_1(S)$ is surjective, $R^if_*\Q$ satisfies (4.2.9), \textit{b)}.

To pass from the quasi-projective case to the general case, it suffices to use the Leray spectral sequence for a covering $(U_i)$ of $X$ by quasi-projective open subsets:
\[
R^*f_*(\bigcap_i U_i,\Q)\Rightarrow R^*f_*\Q,
\]
and (4.2.10).

\subsection*{4.3. Complement to [2].}

In [2], (5.4) (footnote), I assert without proof that

\paragraph{Proposition (4.3.1).} --- {\itshape Let $X$ be a proper smooth scheme over $\C$. If a $C^{\infty}$ form on $X$ satisfies $d'\alpha=d''\alpha=0$ and is cohomologous to zero, then there exists $\beta$ such that $\alpha=d'd''\beta$.}

Here is the proof. As in \textit{loc. cit.}, we reduce to the case where $\alpha$ is bihomogeneous, of bidegree $(p,q)$. Since the spectral sequence of the double complex $H^0(X,\mathcal A^{pq})$ degenerates, the exterior differential $d$ is strictly compatible with the filtration by first degree $p$ (1.3.2). If $\alpha\sim0$, there is therefore a form $\beta_1$ such that $d\beta_1=\alpha$ and such that the components $\beta_1^{p'q'}$ of $\beta_1$ are zero for $p'<p$.

By complex conjugation, there similarly exists $\beta_2$ such that $d\beta_2=\alpha$ and $\beta_2^{p'q'}=0$ for $q'<q$. One has $d(\beta_1-\beta_2)=0$.

Let $\gamma$ be a form satisfying $d'\gamma=d''\gamma=0$ in the cohomology class of $\beta_1-\beta_2$ (\textit{loc. cit.}). Let $\gamma_1$ (resp. $\gamma_2$) be the sum of the components of $\gamma$ of type $(p',q')$ with $p'\ge p$ (resp. $q'\ge q$). Setting $\beta'_1=\beta_1-\gamma_1$ and $\beta'_2=\beta_2+\gamma_2$, one still has $d\beta'_1=d\beta'_2=\alpha$; moreover, $\beta'_1-\beta'_2=\beta_1-\beta_2-\gamma$ is cohomologous to zero: there exists $\delta$ such that
\[
d\delta=\beta'_1-\beta'_2.
\]
Let $\delta_1$ be the sum of the components of type $(p',q')$ of $\delta$ with $p'<p-1$, let $\delta_2$ be the sum of the components for which $q'>q-1$, and let $\beta$ be the component of type $(p-1,q-1)$.
\[
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=.68cm,y=.68cm,baseline=(current bounding box.center),line cap=round,line join=round]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(3.25,0) node[below right] {$p$};
\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,3.35) node[above left] {$q$};
\fill (2.45,2.72) circle (1.3pt) node[below left=2pt] {$\beta$};
\fill (5.15,4.35) circle (1.3pt) node[right=5pt] {$(p,q)$};
\draw (-1.15,5.15)--(1.18,3.55)
  .. controls (1.48,3.34) and (1.68,3.55) .. (1.42,3.87)--(-.55,5.70);
\fill (.92,3.82) circle (1.2pt);
\node[rotate=-39] at (.45,4.35) {$\delta_2$};
\draw (-.48,5.95)--(2.42,3.86)
  .. controls (2.76,3.61) and (3.02,3.86) .. (2.70,4.22)--(.02,6.42);
\fill (-.08,6.12) circle (1.2pt);
\fill (2.40,4.12) circle (1.2pt);
\node[rotate=-39] at (1.20,4.94) {$\beta_2,\gamma_2,\beta'_2$};
\draw (5.62,-1.00)--(3.20,1.34)
  .. controls (2.91,1.62) and (3.14,1.88) .. (3.48,1.63)--(6.03,-.62);
\fill (3.28,1.55) circle (1.2pt);
\node[rotate=-43] at (4.08,.62) {$\delta_1$};
\draw (6.48,-.28)--(4.20,2.04)
  .. controls (3.90,2.35) and (4.17,2.62) .. (4.53,2.34)--(6.93,.12);
\fill (4.31,2.27) circle (1.2pt);
\fill (6.54,-.03) circle (1.2pt);
\node[rotate=-42] at (5.38,1.17) {$\beta_1,\gamma_1,\beta'_1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\]
One has $\beta'_2=d\delta_2+d''\beta$ and $\alpha=d\beta'_2=dd\delta_2+dd''\beta=d'd''\beta$.

\subsection*{4.4. Homomorphisms of abelian schemes.}

We propose to show how, in some cases, one can remove from (4.1.3.2) the hypothesis of algebraicity at one point.

\paragraph{(4.4.1)} For $f:X\to S$ a proper smooth morphism, we shall denote by $R_if_*\Z$ the local system on $S^{an}$ of the homology of the fibers of $f$. At each point $s\in S$, $(R_if_*\Z)_s\simeq H_i(X_s,\Z)$ is endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $-i$, dual to the Hodge structure of $H^i(X_s,\Z)$. This structure varies continuously with $s\in S$.

\paragraph{(4.4.2)} If $f:X\to S$ is an abelian scheme, the exponential defines an exact sequence of sheaves on $S^{an}$
\[
0\to R_1f_*\Z\to\Lie(X)\to X\to0,
\]
and the Hodge filtration is the short exact sequence
\[
0\to\Ker(\alpha)\to R_1f_*\Z\otimes\cO\xrightarrow{\alpha}\Lie(X)\to0.
\]
It is known that

\paragraph{Reminder (4.4.3). ---} {\itshape Let $S$ be a smooth scheme of finite type over $\C$. The construction (4.4.2) establishes an equivalence of categories between:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item the category of abelian schemes over $S$;
\item the category of polarizable continuous families of Hodge structures $H$ of type $(-1,0)+(0,-1)$ on $S$, such that $H_{\Z}$ is torsion-free and the Hodge filtration varies holomorphically on $S$.
\end{enumerate}}
Essential surjectivity of the functor a)$\mapsto$b) follows from Borel [13]; full faithfulness follows from the fact that, for $X_1$ and $X_2$ two abelian schemes over $S$, the $S$-scheme $\Hom_S(X_1,X_2)$ is unramified over $S$, and therefore has the same algebraic and holomorphic sections.

\paragraph{(4.4.4)} Let $Z$ be a commutative field, $H$ a central simple algebra over $Z$, and $*$ a $Z$-linear anti-automorphism of $H$. After extension of scalars, one has $H\simeq\End(V)$ for a vector space $V$ over $Z$, and $*$ is then transposition with respect to a bilinear form $\Phi$ on $V$, unique up to scalar. Suppose that $*$ is involutive; the forms $\Phi(X,Y)$ and $\Phi(Y,X)$ are then proportional: $\Phi(X,Y)=\lambda\Phi(Y,X)$, with $\lambda^2=1$. \emph{Put} $\varepsilon_*=\lambda$. If $[H:Z]=d^2$, then
\[
\Tr(*:H\to H)=\varepsilon_*\cdot d.
\]
Every $Z$-linear automorphism $C$ of $H$ is inner: $Cx=cxc^{-1}$. If $C$ is involutive and commutes with $*$, the elements $c^2$ and $cc^*$ are central, so that $c^*=\lambda c$ with $\lambda$ central. Since $c^{**}=c$, one has $\lambda^2=1$. \emph{Put} $\varepsilon_C=\lambda$.

One checks easily that the involution $C\circ *$ satisfies
\[
\varepsilon_{C\circ *}=\varepsilon_C\cdot\varepsilon_*.
\]

\paragraph{Reminder (4.4.5). ---} {\itshape Let $X$ be a simple abelian variety over a field $K$ and let $H$ be the division algebra $\End_K(X)\otimes\Q$. Every polarization of $X$ defines a positive involution $*$ of $H$:
\[
\Tr(hh^*)>0\qquad\text{if }h\ne0.
\]
If $Z_0$ is the subfield invariant under $*$ in the center $Z$ of $H$, then $Z_0$ is totally real and one is in one of the following cases:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item $Z=Z_0$; for every real place $\rho$ of $Z$, $H\otimes_{\rho}\R$ is a matrix algebra over $\R$, and $\varepsilon_*=1$.
\item $Z=Z_0$; for every real place $\rho$ of $Z$, $H\otimes_{\rho}\R$ is a matrix algebra over $\mathbb H$, and $\varepsilon_*=-1$.
\item $Z$ is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of $Z_0$.
\end{enumerate}}

\paragraph{(4.4.6)} Let $f_i:X_i\to S$ ($i=1,2$) be two abelian schemes over a smooth scheme $S$. The free abelian group
\[
\Hom(R_1f_{1*}\Z,R_1f_{2*}\Z)
\simeq\Gamma\bigl(S,\Hom(R_1f_{1*}\Z,R_1f_{2*}\Z)\bigr)
\]
is then endowed with a Hodge structure of weight $0$ (4.2.8). Moreover, by (2.1.11.1) and (4.4.3), the group $\Hom_S(X_1,X_2)$ is the component of type $(0,0)$ of this group.

\paragraph{(4.4.7)} Let $S$ be a nonempty smooth connected scheme with generic point $\eta$, and let $f:X\to S$ be an abelian scheme over $S$. The center $Z$ of $H=\End(R_1f_*\Z)$ is then of type $(0,0)$ (4.2.8), and is therefore contained in $\End_S(X)\simeq \End_{k(\eta)}(X_{\eta})$.

A polarization of $X$ defines an involution $*$ of $H$. Its restriction to $\End_S(X)$ is positive, so that $Z$ is a product of totally real fields or totally imaginary quadratic extensions of totally real fields.

Let $C$ denote the actions of $i\in S(\R)$ on $H_{\R}=H\otimes\R$ and on the $(R_1f_*\R)_s$, for $s\in S$. On $H_{\R}$, $C^2=1$, and $C$ commutes with $*$; on $(R_1f_*\R)_s$, $C^2=-1$. If $\psi$ is the alternating form on $R_1f_*\Z$, with integral values, deduced from the polarization of $X$, then
\[
\psi(hx,Cy)=\psi(x,h^*Cy)=\psi(x,C\cdot C(h^*)\cdot y).
\]
It follows that
\[
\tag{4.4.7.1}
\Tr(h\cdot C(h^*))>0\qquad\text{for }h\ne0.
\]

\paragraph{(4.4.8)} Now suppose that $X_{\eta}$ is simple, so that $Z$ is a field. Let $\rho:Z\to\C$ be a complex embedding. The algebra
\[
H_{\rho}=H\otimes_{Z,\rho}\C
\]
is then a matrix algebra and a bigraded direct factor in $H_{\C}=H\otimes_{\Q}\C$. Choose an isomorphism
\[
\tag{4.4.8.1}
H_{\rho}\simeq\End(V_{\rho}).
\]
Since the infinitesimal generators of $S$ act on $H_{\rho}$ by derivations, necessarily inner, it follows that $V_{\rho}$ admits a bigrading, unique up to translation, such that (4.4.8.1) is a bigraded isomorphism. Let $(R_1f_*\C)_{\rho}$ be the bigraded local system
\[
(R_1f_*\C)\otimes_{Z\otimes\C,\rho}\C,
\]
a direct factor of $R_1f_*\C$. Denote by $T_{\rho}$ the local system
\[
T_{\rho}=\Hom_{H_{\rho}}(V_{\rho},(R_1f_*\C)_{\rho}).
\]
One has
\[
\tag{4.4.8.2}
V_{\rho}\otimes_{\C} T_{\rho}\iso (R_1f_*\C)_{\rho}
\]
(a bigraded isomorphism). Since $(R_1f_*\C)_{\rho}$ has type $(-1,0)+(0,-1)$, one of the following conditions is satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item $V_{\rho}$ is bihomogeneous;
\item $T_{\rho}$ is bihomogeneous.
\end{enumerate}
It is clear that condition a) (respectively b)) is simultaneously satisfied for $\rho$ and for $\bar{\rho}$. If condition a) is satisfied at every place, then $H$ is of type $(0,0)$. If condition b) is satisfied at every place, then the Hodge structure on $R_1f_*\Q$ is locally constant.

% Authority physical page 49 / printed page 52 ends here.

\paragraph{(4.4.9)} Now suppose that $Z$ is totally real. For every real embedding $\varphi$ of $Z$, put $\varepsilon_{H,\varphi}=+1$ if $H\otimes_{Z,\varphi}\R$ is a matrix algebra and $\varepsilon_{H,\varphi}=-1$ otherwise. If a complex embedding $\rho$ induces a real embedding $\varphi$, put $\varepsilon_{H,\rho}=\varepsilon_{H,\varphi}$.

Let $\rho:Z\to\C$ factor through $\varphi:Z\to\R$. Complex conjugation on $H_{\rho}$ is induced by an antilinear automorphism $\sigma_1$ of $V_{\rho}$, unique up to a real scalar factor, with scalar square.
