\ReaderFont

\SourcePage{79}{1}
\noindent{\sffamily\fontsize{7.4}{8.2}\selectfont Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians\\Vancouver, 1974}

\vspace*{15mm}
\begin{center}
{\sffamily\bfseries\fontsize{15}{17}\selectfont Weights in the Cohomology of Algebraic Varieties\par}
\vspace{5mm}
{\sffamily\bfseries\fontsize{10}{11}\selectfont Pierre Deligne\par}
\end{center}
\vspace{5mm}

\NumPara{1.} Let \(X\) be a complex algebraic variety (i.e., a separated scheme of finite type over \(\C\)). We also write \(X\) for the usual topological space \(X(\C)\) underlying \(X\). In this lecture, we describe a remarkable filtration on the rational cohomology groups of \(X\), the \emph{weight filtration}, and we give a collection of results concerning its properties. Its definition will be given in §12. For proofs, we refer to the works cited in the bibliography, where the theorems are often proved in more general settings; working over \(\C\) allows us to use simultaneously Hodge theory, actions of Galois groups, and resolution of singularities.

The weight filtration is a finite increasing filtration. We denote it by \(W\). It is also defined in relative situations (or in cohomology with proper support). It depends not only on the topological space \(X\), but also on the way in which \(X\) is realized as an algebraic variety. It is compatible with the Künneth isomorphisms (i.e., under the isomorphism \(H^*(X\times Y)=H^*(X)\otimes H^*(Y)\), one has
\[
W_j\bigl(H^*(X\times Y)\bigr)=\sum_{j'+j''=j}W_{j'}\bigl(H^*(X)\bigr)\otimes W_{j''}\bigl(H^*(Y)\bigr)
\]
and is functorial for algebraic morphisms. More precisely, if \(f:X\to Y\) is algebraic, then \(f^*:H^*(Y)\to H^*(X)\) is strictly compatible with the weight filtrations on \(H^*(Y)\) and \(H^*(X)\): if the class \(x\in H^i(X)\) lies in the image of \(f^*\), it has filtration \(\le i\) if and only if it is the image of a class of filtration \(\le i\). More generally, every natural map is strictly compatible with the weight filtrations.

The weight filtration is a discrete invariant; it is invariant under de-

\vfill
\noindent{\sffamily\fontsize{6.7}{7.3}\selectfont \textcopyright\ 1975, Canadian Mathematical Congress}
\EndSourcePage

\SourcePage{80}{2}
\ReaderFont
formation of the algebraic structure of \(X\). More precisely, one has the following theorem.

\TheoremPara{2. THEOREM.} Let \(f:X\to S\) be a morphism. For \(t\in S\), let \(X_t=f^{-1}(t)\). If the sheaf \(R^if_*\Q\) is locally constant (a local system), then there exists a weight filtration \(W\) on \(R^if_*\Q\) by local subsystems, such that the maps \(r_t:(R^if_*\Q)_t\to H^i(X_t)\) are strictly compatible with the weight filtrations and, in particular, wherever \(r_t\) is an isomorphism, \(W\) induces the weight filtration on \(H^i(X_t)\).\EndTheorem

\NumPara{3.} Roughly speaking, the weight filtration expresses how the cohomology of \(X\) can be built in terms of the cohomology of nonsingular projective varieties. Here are some examples.

\NamedPara{Example 3.1.} If \(X\) is proper (= compact, for example projective) and smooth (= nonsingular), then \(H^i(X)=_{\mathrm{def}}H^i(X,\Q)\) is pure of weight \(i\): \(\Gr_j^W(H^i(X))=0\) for \(i\ne j\). In other words, \(W_{i-1}(H^i(X))=0\) and \(W_i(H^i(X))=H^i(X)\).

\NamedPara{Example 3.2.} Let \(X\) be proper, smooth, connected, of dimension \(d\), and let \(P\) be a point of \(X\). Among the cohomology groups with support \(H^i_{\{P\}}(X)=H^i(X\mathbin{\mathrm{mod}}(X-\{P\}))\), only the one in degree \(2d\) is nonzero, and
\begin{equation}\tag{3.2.1}
H^{2d}_{\{P\}}(X)\simeq H^{2d}(X)=\Q.
\end{equation}
By our principles, \(H^{2d}_{\{P\}}(X)\) is therefore pure of weight \(2d\). The inverse of the isomorphism (3.2.1) may be viewed as a Thom--Gysin isomorphism
\[
\Q=H^0(P)\simeq H^{2d}_{\{P\}}(X);
\]
one observes that it does not preserve weights. The general situation is as follows: for \(Y\) a smooth subvariety of pure codimension \(d\) in a smooth variety \(X\), the Thom--Gysin isomorphism \(H^i(Y)\simeq H_Y^{i+2d}(X)\) carries \(W^k\) to \(W^{k+2d}\). Writing \((n)\) for a shift of \(2n\) in \(W\) (\(W(n)_k=W_{k-2n}\)), this becomes a filtered isomorphism
\[
H^i(Y)(-d)\simeq H_Y^{i+2d}(X).
\]

\NamedPara{Example 3.3.} Let \(X\) be proper and smooth, and let \(Y\) be a smooth (closed) subvariety of pure codimension \(d\). There is an exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to H^i(X)\to H^i(X-Y)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_Y^{i+1}(X)\to\cdots
\]
By 3.1 and 3.2, \(\Gr_j^W(H^i(X-Y))=0\) for \(j\ne i,i+1\); \(W_i\) is the image of \(H^i(X)\).

\NamedPara{Example 3.4.} Let \(X\) be proper and smooth except at an isolated singular point \(P\). Suppose that the variety \(\widetilde X\) obtained from \(X\) by blowing up \(P\) is smooth, and that the exceptional divisor \(D\), the inverse image of \(P\), is smooth: \(X\) is obtained from \(\widetilde X\) (proper and smooth) by contracting \(D\) (proper and smooth) to a point. The space \(X\) has the homotopy type of \([\widetilde X\cup(\text{a cone with base }D)]\), whose cohomology is computed by Mayer--Vietoris; one obtains an exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to H^{i-1}(D)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^i(X)\to H^i(\widetilde X)\oplus H^i(P)\to\cdots
\]
which shows that \(\Gr_j^W(H^i(X))=0\) for \(j\ne i-1,i\); \(W_{i-1}\) is the image of \(\delta\). For
\EndSourcePage

\SourcePage{81}{3}
\ReaderFont
\(i\ne0\), it is also the kernel of \(H^i(X)\to H^i(\widetilde X)\), and \(\Gr_i^W(H^i(X))\) is the image of \(H^i(X)\) in \(H^i(\widetilde X)\).

\NamedPara{Example 3.5.} Flag varieties are proper and smooth. The weight filtration on their cohomology is therefore given by 3.1. If \(G\) is a connected reductive group, the same result holds for the cohomology of \(BG\) [1, III]. This makes it possible to calculate the weight filtration on the cohomology of \(G\), which is related by transgression to that of \(BG\). One finds that \(W_iH^i(G)=0\), and that \(W_{i+1}H^i(G)\), zero for even \(i\), is equal to the primitive part of the degree-\(i\) cohomology of \(G\) [1, III]. If \(f:G\to H\) is an algebraic map between varieties of reductive groups, the inverse image of a primitive rational cohomology class of \(H\) is therefore again primitive. For other corollaries, see [1, III].

\NumPara{4.} The weight filtration admits a grading in a very strong sense. There exist gradings \(\Wg\) of the \(H^i(X)\) that split \(W\):
\begin{equation}\tag{4.1}
W_n(H^i(X))=\bigoplus_{j\le n}\Wg_j(H^i(X))
\end{equation}
and that are compatible with the cup product and with higher operations derived from the cup product (Massey products, \ldots). Since the latter are not defined everywhere, the meaning of “compatible with a grading” must be made precise. The simplest approach is to regard a grading as an action of the group \(G_m\), i.e., an action of \(\Q^*\) given by algebraic formulas: to a grading \(\Wg\) one associates the action in which \(\lambda\in\Q^*\) acts on \(\Wg_j\) by multiplication by \(\lambda^j\). “Compatibility” means that \(\Q^*\) acts by automorphisms of \(H^*(X)\), together with its cohomological grading, cup product, and the higher operations derived from the cup product.

\NumPara{5.} For simplicity, suppose that \(X\) is connected, and let \(\Mmin\) be the minimal model of the rational homotopy type of \(X\) in the sense of Sullivan [7]. It is a differential graded algebra in degrees \(\ge0\), connected (\(\Mmin^0=\Q\)), free (anti)commutative as a graded algebra, and generated by its indecomposable elements (i.e., \(d\Mmin\subset(\Mmin^{>0})^2\)). One has \(H^*(\Mmin)=H^*(X)\), and if \(X\) is simply connected, \(\Mmin^{>0}/(\Mmin^{>0})^2=(\pi_*(X)\otimes\Q)^{\vee}\).

A more precise, and more convenient, statement than the one in §4 is that there exists a grading \(\Wg\) satisfying (4.1), induced by a grading \(\Wg\) of \(\Mmin\) (in degrees \(\ge0\), the sum of gradings of the \(\Mmin^i\)), such that \(d\) and the product are homogeneous of degree 0; in other words, \(\Q^*\) acts by automorphisms of \(\Mmin\)).

\NumPara{6.} The mere existence of \(W\) and \(\Wg\) imposes no restriction on the homotopy type of \(X\): one may always declare that all of \(\Mmin\) has weight 0. Moreover, every finite polyhedron has the same homotopy type as an algebraic variety. Indeed, let \(S\) be a finite set furnished with a collection \(\Simp\) of subsets (the simplices). Assume that every subset of an element of \(\Simp\) also belongs to \(\Simp\). Identify \(S\) with the set of basis vectors of \(\R^S\), and for \(\sigma\subset S\) let \(|\sigma|\) be the simplex spanned by the \(s\in\sigma\). We show that \(|S|=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\Simp}|\sigma|\) has the homotopy type of an algebraic variety \(X\). If \(|\sigma|_{\C}\) denotes the complex affine space spanned by \(\sigma\subset\C^S\), it is enough to take \(X=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\Simp}|\sigma|_{\C}\), of which \(|S|\) is a deformation retract. One can veri-
\EndSourcePage


% BEGIN included source: works/D022_PUBLIC_SAFE/build_source/D022_EN_P04_P07.tex
\SourcePage{82}{4}
\ReaderFont
fy that in this example \(H^*(X)\) is pure of weight-filtration degree 0.

Nevertheless, as soon as the weights are nonzero, constraints appear on the homotopy type of \(X\) (cf. §10). The following rules help locate the weights.

\NumPara{7.} For a cohomology group \(H\) of a given type, each rule will consist in describing a subset \(\region\) of \(\Z\times\Z\). The weights are controlled by \(\region\) in the following sense: if \(\Gr_n^W(H)\ne0\), then there exists \((p,q)\in\region\) with \(p+q=n\). This manner of speaking, which may seem artificial here, is not so: information other than the possible weights is controlled by the same region \(\region\); cf. §15.

\NumPara{(7.1)} \(H^n(X)\) is controlled by the square \([0,n]\times[0,n]\).

\NumPara{(7.2)} If \(X\) is proper, \(H^n(X)\) is controlled by the part of this square below the second diagonal, namely \(\{(p,q)\in[0,n]\times[0,n]\mid p+q\le n\}\). If \(X\) is smooth, \(H^n(X)\) is controlled by the part of this square above that diagonal, namely \(\{(p,q)\in[0,n]\times[0,n]\mid p+q\ge n\}\).

\NumPara{(7.3)} If \(N=\dim X\le n\), the square \([0,n]\times[0,n]\) may be replaced by the square \([n-N,N]\times[n-N,N]\).

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=.50\textwidth]{../assets/D022_P082_DIAGRAMS_PRESENTATION.png}
\end{center}

\NumPara{8. Variants.} \textbf{(8.1)} The compactly supported cohomology group \(H_c^n(X)\) is controlled by the part of the square \([0,n]\times[0,n]\) below the second diagonal. If \(N=\dim X\le n\), this square may again be replaced by \([n-N,N]\times[n-N,N]\). In particular, \(H_c^{2N}(X)\) is pure of weight \(2N\).

\NumPara{(8.2)} The “duality” between the proper and smooth cases follows from Poincaré duality: for \(X\) smooth and purely of dimension \(N\),
\[
H^n(X)=\Hom\bigl(H_c^{2N-n}(X),H_c^{2N}(X)\bigr)=\bigl(H_c^{2N-n}(X)^{\vee}\bigr)(-N).
\]
This argument extends the results given for smooth \(X\) to the case in which \(X\) is a “rational homology manifold.” For such an \(X\), the image of \(H_c^n(X)\) in \(H^n(X)\) is pure of weight \(n\).

\NumPara{(8.3)} If \(X\) is only assumed normal, it remains true that \(H^1(X)\) is controlled by \(\{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}\).

\NumPara{9.} Let \(X\) be a connected variety, \(x\in X\), and let \(\Pi^{(n)}\) be the largest torsion-free nilpotent quotient of length \(n\) of \(\pi_1(X,x)\). It is known that finite-index subgroups \(H\) of \(\Pi^{(n)}\) that are sufficiently small have the following property.

\NumPara{(*)} There exists a nilpotent Lie algebra of length \(n\), \((\LieH,[\ ,\ ])\), with \(\LieH\) a free
\EndSourcePage

\SourcePage{83}{5}
\ReaderFont
\(\Z\)-module, such that the Campbell--Hausdorff formula
\[
x\circ y=x+y+[x,y]/2+[x,[x,y]]/12+[y,[y,x]]/12+\cdots
\]
makes \(\LieH\) into a group isomorphic to \(H\).

Moreover, the Lie algebra \(\LieL^{(n)}=\LieH\otimes\Q\) depends only on \(\Pi^{(n)}\), not on \(H\).

\TheoremPara{10. THEOREM (MORGAN).} If \(X\) is normal, \(\LieL^{(n)}\) admits a grading \(\Wg\) in degrees \(<0\), such that \(\LieL^{(n)}\) is generated by elements of degrees \(-1\) and \(-2\), subject only to relations of degrees \(-2\), \(-3\), and \(-4\), together with the vanishing of \(n\)-fold iterated commutators.\EndTheorem

It is more convenient to work with the inverse system \(\LieL^{(\infty)}\) of the \(\LieL^{(n)}\). Defining \(H^i(\LieL^{(\infty)})=\varinjlim H^i(\LieL^{(n)})\), one has
\[
H^1(\LieL^{(\infty)})=H^1(X),\qquad H^2(\LieL^{(\infty)})\subset H^2(X).
\]
Moreover, a grading \(\Wg\) of \(\Mmin\) as in §5 defines compatible gradings of \(\LieL^{(\infty)}\), its cohomology, and that of \(X\). By (8.3) (respectively, (7.1)), \(H^1(X)\) has weights 1 and 2 and \(H^2(X)\) has weights \(\le4\). Consequently, \(H^1(\LieL^{(\infty)})\) (the dual of the group \(\LieL^{(\infty)}/[\LieL^{(\infty)},\LieL^{(\infty)}]\) of generators of \(\LieL^{(\infty)}\)) has weights 1 and 2, and \(H^2(\LieL^{(\infty)})\), the dual of the group of relations among generators, has weights \(\le4\). This proves the theorem.

\NumPara{11.} For a proper smooth variety, the weight filtration reduces to very little (3.1). Its gradability in the sense of §4 implies the vanishing of all Massey products. Its gradability in the sense of §5 even implies that the rational homotopy type of \(X\) can be read off from its cohomology algebra---see [3].

\NumPara{12. Hodge theory.} The cohomology group \(H^i(X)\) of every complex algebraic variety is endowed with a mixed Hodge structure \((W,F)\) (\(W\) is a filtration on \(H^i(X)\), and \(F\) is a filtration on \(H^i(X)\otimes\C=H^i(X,\C)\), with \(W\) and \(F\) satisfying suitable axioms---see [1]). The weight filtration is, by definition, the filtration \(W\).

\NumPara{13. \(l\)-adic theory.} An algebraic variety \(X\) is defined by finitely many polynomial equations. The coefficients of these equations generate a finitely generated subring \(R\) of \(\C\), with fraction field \(K\), and \(X\) is obtained by extension of scalars to \(\C\) from a scheme over \(K\), or even over \(R\). The following statements become true after replacing \(R\) by \(R[1/f]\), with \(f\in R\) sufficiently divisible.

\NumPara{(13.1)} Let \(l\) be a prime number. The group \(H^i(X)\otimes\Q_l\) is identified with the \(l\)-adic cohomology group \(H^i(X,\Q_l)\). The latter is defined in a purely algebraic manner and therefore carries, by transport of structure, an action of \(\Aut(\C/K)\).

\NumPara{(13.2)} Let \(\overline K\) be the algebraic closure of \(K\) in \(\C\). The action factors through \(\Gal(\overline K/K)\). It is unramified over \(R[1/l]\), i.e., it factors through the Galois group of the largest extension \(K_{\mathrm{nr}}^{(l)}\subset\overline K\) of \(K\) unramified over \(R[1/l]\).

\NumPara{(13.3)} Let \(\mathfrak m\) be a maximal ideal of \(R[1/l]\), and let \(N(\mathfrak m)=\#R/\mathfrak m\) (\(R/\mathfrak m\) is a finite field). To \(\mathfrak m\) there corresponds a conjugacy class of Frobenius substitutions \(\varphi_{\mathfrak m}\in\Gal(K_{\mathrm{nr}}/K)\), whose inverses are the geometric Frobenius substitutions \(F_{\mathfrak m}=\varphi_{\mathfrak m}^{-1}\).

\TheoremPara{14. THEOREM.} For \(f\) sufficiently divisible, one has\EndTheorem
\EndSourcePage

\SourcePage{84}{6}
\ReaderFont
\TheoremPara{(i)} For every \(l\) and \(\mathfrak m\), the eigenvalues \(\alpha\) of \(F_{\mathfrak m}\) (in a suitable finite extension of \(\Q_l\)) are algebraic integers. For each \(\alpha\), there is an integer \(w(\alpha)\) such that all complex conjugates of \(\alpha\) have absolute value \(N(\mathfrak m)^{w(\alpha)/2}\).

\NumPara{(ii)} Choose a geometric Frobenius \(F_{\mathfrak m}\), and let \({}_{\mathfrak m}W_j\) be the sum of the generalized eigenspaces corresponding to eigenvalues \(\alpha\) of \(F_{\mathfrak m}\) such that \(w(\alpha)=j\). The filtration by the \(\bigoplus_{j\le i}{}_{\mathfrak m}W_j\) is independent of \(\mathfrak m\) and of the choice of \(F_{\mathfrak m}\); it is rational, and its trace on \(H^i(X)\) is independent of \(l\); it is the weight filtration.\EndTheorem

\ProofHeadEN One expresses the cohomology of \(X\), by means of a spectral sequence, in terms of the cohomology of proper smooth varieties, as in [1]. The spectral sequence abuts to a filtration \(W\) on \(H^*(X)\), which is by definition the weight filtration of Hodge theory. This spectral sequence has an \(l\)-adic analogue; the \(l\)-adification \(W_l\) of \(W\) is therefore stable under a Galois group. The Weil conjecture implies that the eigenvalues of \(F_{\mathfrak m}\) on \(\Gr_j^{W_l}\) are algebraic integers whose complex absolute values are \(N(\mathfrak m)^{j/2}\), and the theorem follows.

\NumPara{15.} In the cases considered in (7.1), (7.2), and (7.3), the region \(\region\) described there controls not only the weights, but also the Hodge numbers and the divisibility of the eigenvalues of the \(F_{\mathfrak m}\): in (7.1), (7.2), and (7.3), a region \(\region\) has been assigned to a group \(H\), and

\NumPara{(a)} The nonzero Hodge numbers \(h^{pq}\) of the Hodge structures \(\Gr_j^W(H)\) satisfy \((p,q)\in\region\).

\NumPara{(b)} (Useful only in case (7.3).) If the \((p,q)\in\region\) with \(p+q=j\) satisfy \(p,q\ge k\), then (still for \(f\) sufficiently divisible) the eigenvalues of \(F_{\mathfrak m}\) with complex absolute value \(N(\mathfrak m)^{j/2}\) are divisible by \(N(\mathfrak m)^k\).

One hopes that this is a special case of a general principle; cf. [4].

\NumPara{16.} The following result is clear from the viewpoint of Hodge theory.

\NumPara{(16.1)} For odd \(j\), \(\dim\Gr_j^W H^i(X)\) is even.

On the other hand, up to now I know how to prove §§ 2 and 5 only by \(l\)-adic methods. For §5, the method of §14 yields an \(l\)-adic grading; a device of Sullivan then gives the existence of rational gradings of the desired kind.

The functoriality properties of the weight filtration are evident from the \(l\)-adic viewpoint (because Galois commutes with everything that can be defined). It is nevertheless useful to prove them from the viewpoint of Hodge theory in order to obtain analogous properties for the filtration \(F\). Morgan has obtained numerous results in this direction---enough to prove by Hodge theory a result slightly weaker than §10.

\NumPara{17.} As §5 suggests, a weight filtration also exists on homotopy groups (tensored with \(\Q\)) under simple-connectivity hypotheses.

It also exists on groups of vanishing cycles (cf. [6]), and I hope that these filtrations will help us to understand the latter better.

\section{Real Homotopy Theory of Kähler
Manifolds}\label{D023-real-homotopy-theory-of-kuxe4hler-manifolds}

Pierre Deligne (Bures-sur-Yvette), Phillip Griffiths* (Cambridge,
Mass.), John Morgan (New York) and Dennis Sullivan (Bures-sur-Yvette)

\subsection{Table of Contents}\label{D023-table-of-contents}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Homotopy Theory of Differential Algebras \ldots\ldots\ldots. 248
\item
  De Rham Homotopy Theory \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots{} 254
\item
  Relation between De Rham Homotopy Theory and Classical Homotopy Theory
  \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots{} 256
\item
  Formality of Differential Algebras \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots.. 260
\item
  The De Rham Complex of a Compact Kähler Manifold \ldots.. 262
\item
  The Main Theorem and Two Proofs \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots. 270
\item
  An Application \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots. 272
\end{enumerate}

This paper brings together the strengthened de Rham theory of the last
author {[}12, 13{]} and {[}14{]} concerning the homotopy information of
a manifold contained in the algebra of its differential forms, and the
classical results {[}15{]} about the forms on a compact Kähler manifold
to prove statements about the algebraic topology of compact Kähler
manifolds, and consequently about smooth, complex, projective algebraic
varieties.

The nature of the results is that the \emph{homotopy type of a compact
Kähler manifold, over the real numbers, is a formal consequence of the
real cohomology ring.} For any manifold there is a differential graded
algebra with rational structure constants whose isomorphism type is an
invariant of the homotopy type of the space. The cohomology ring of this
differential algebra is the rational cohomology ring of the space, but
the algebra itself contains, for example, the higher order cohomology
products. The isomorphism type of the differential algebra is equivalent
to the ``rational form of the nilpotent structure in the space''. For a
simply connected manifold this differential algebra is equivalent to the
rational Postnikov tower of manifold. Our results here are that, for a
compact Kähler manifold, from the real cohomology ring one can produce
the real form of this differential algebra. These results complement the
known structure of the cohomology ring of such a manifold. We prove no
new results about it.

The initial motivation for these results was the relation in a Kähler
manifold between harmonic forms and holomorphic forms. In particular the
\((p,0)\) harmonic forms for any Kähler metric are exactly the
holomorphic forms. Consequently, products of \((p,0)\) and \((q,0)\)
harmonic forms are harmonic\textsuperscript{1}, and thus there are no

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  This research was partially supported by NSF grant GP-38886.
\end{itemize}

1 Chen in {[}2{]} was the first to exploit this idea to obtain higher
order information about Kähler manifolds.

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 246}{D023-d023-source_language-p0002}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 246}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

higher order products starting from \(H^{*,0}\). The possibility that
the full theorem would be true is related to the Weil conjectures. We
were led to prove such a complete result by ``using the Weil conjectures
in characteristic \(p\) to guess results in characteristic \(0\) which
can then be proved using Hodge theory''. The relevant remark here is
that the classical higher order cohomology products of Massey are
multilinear operations, but the dimension of the product is always less
than the sum of the dimensions of the various elements being multiplied.
Thus, if we were working in a situation in characteristic \(p\) on which
the Frobenius automorphism operated (for instance, the Čech cochains in
étale cohomology theory), and if the eigenvalues of the Frobenius action
are as predicted by the Weil conjectures\textsuperscript{2}, then the
multilinearity of the product over the action would imply that the
absolute value of the eigenvalues on the space of higher order products
in a certain dimension would be different from the possible values in
that dimension. The only way this can happen is for these spaces of
higher order products to be zero.

In proving these results for compact Kähler manifolds we use the
implications for the forms of the existence of a Kähler metric. If \(M\)
is a complex manifold, form the differential algebras and algebra maps

\[
\{H^*(M,\mathbb R),d=0\}\longleftarrow\{\operatorname{Ker}(d^c),d\}\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow\{\text{all }C^{\infty}\text{ forms},d\}.
\]

If \(M\) is a compact Kähler manifold, both maps above induce
isomorphisms of cohomology. All our results about the homotopy type of
compact Kähler manifolds can be deduced from this statement, which is
itself a consequence of the \(dd^c\) lemma.

\textbf{\(dd^c\) Lemma.} \emph{Let \(M\) be a compact Kähler manifold,
and \(d^c=J^{-1}dJ\), where \(J\) gives the complex structure in the
cotangent bundle. Evidently, \(d^c\) is a real operator. If \(x\) is a
form with}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(dx=0=d^c x\)
\end{enumerate}

\emph{and}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \(x=dy\) or \(x=d^c y'\)
\end{enumerate}

\emph{then \(x=dd^c z\) for some form \(z\).}

In Sections 1--4 we describe the machinery needed to deduce the
consequences in homotopy theory of these statements about forms.
Sections 1, 2, and 3 constitute a sketch of the theory in {[}12{]} and
{[}14{]}, (c.f. also {[}10{]}). Section 1 describes the construction of
the minimal model (real Postnikov tower) of any differential algebra and
proves a uniqueness result. To do this, some of the abstract homotopy
theory of differential algebras is developed. For instance, we define
the de Rham fundamental group of an algebra by using a minimal model for
the algebra. This ``group'' is an inverse system of nilpotent Lie
groups. We also define the higher homotopy groups of any simply
connected differential algebra. These are vector spaces with a graded
Lie algebra structure which should be thought of as the structure of
``Whitehead products''.

In Section 2 we assign to any simply connected\textsuperscript{3},
\(C^{\infty}\)-manifold, \(M\), the de Rham complex of \(C^{\infty}\)-forms
on \(M\), \(\mathscr E_M^*\), and its minimal model \(\mathcal M_M\);
and to any simply

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 247}{D023-d023-source_language-p0003}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 247}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

connected simplical complex, \(X\), the differential algebra
\(\mathscr E_X^*\), of \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on \(X\) and its
minimal model \(\mathcal M_X\). The former algebras are over
\(\mathbb R\); the latter are over \(\mathbb Q\). The minimal model
\(\mathcal M_M\) is defined to be the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy type
of \(M\), and \(\mathcal M_X\) is, similarly, the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham
homotopy type of \(X\). These constructions satisfy

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\item
  the cohomology of the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on \(X\) is the
  \(\mathbb Q\)-cohomology ring of \(X\), and
\item
  the inclusions of the \(C^{\infty}\) forms on \(M\) and the
  (\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on a \(C^1\)-triangulation \(K\) of
  \(M\))\(\otimes\mathbb R\) into the piecewise \(C^{\infty}\) forms on
  \(K\) induce isomorphisms of cohomology.
\end{enumerate}

The fact that the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms are a
\(\mathbb Q\)-differential algebra is useful when we make the connection
with homotopy theory in Section 3. There is an isomorphism between the
category of \(\mathbb Q\)-minimal differential algebras and the category
of towers of rational principal fibrations. The homotopy groups of
algebras correspond to the homotopy groups of the fibration under this
isomorphism. The main result is that, \emph{for a simply connected
space, the tower of rational principal fibrations built from the minimal
model of the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms is the rational form of the
Postnikov tower of the space. Thus the homotopy-theoretic information
available in the differential algebra of \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms
on a simply connected simplical complex is exactly the rational homotopy
type.} Consequently the differential algebra of \(C^{\infty}\) forms on a
simply connected manifold determines the real form of the rational
homotopy type of the manifold. There are analogous results concerning
the nilpotent completion of the fundamental group for general simplical
complexes and manifolds (see {[}14{]} Appendix N).

Section 4 discusses the question of when the minimal model of a
differential algebra is determined by the cohomology ring of the
algebra. We give examples of spaces where the higher order cohomology
products are non-zero, and then show that a minimal model is a formal
consequence of its cohomology ring if, and only if, all the higher order
products vanish in a uniform way.

Section 5 is a discussion of the forms on a compact, complex manifold
admitting a Kähler metric. From the identity (which is equivalent to the
metric being Kähler)

\[
\Delta_d=2\Delta_{\partial}=2\Delta_{\bar\partial}
\]

between the various Laplacians, we prove the \(dd^c\) lemma. We then
give a cohomological interpretation of this lemma, and show that it is
valid on more general complex manifolds (e.g., Moišezon spaces).

In Section 6 we prove the main theorem that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  For any complex manifold for which the \(dd^c\) lemma is true (for
  example Kähler manifolds), the minimal model of the \(C^{\infty}\)
  differential forms is a formal consequence of the real cohomology
  ring.
\item
  Given a holomorphic map between two such manifolds, the effect of the
  map on the minimal models is determined by the map on the cohomology
  level.
\end{enumerate}

The work of Sections 1, 2, and 3, allows us to translate this into the
assertion that the real homotopy type of a compact Kähler manifold is a
formal consequence of its real cohomology ring, and the real homotopy
type of a holomorphic map

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 248}{D023-d023-source_language-p0004}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 248}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

between compact Kähler manifolds is a formal consequence of the induced
map on cohomology. In particular, if a compact Kähler manifold \(M\) is
simply connected, then its real homotopy groups,
\(\pi_*(M)\otimes\mathbb R\), can be read off from the real cohomology
ring. Likewise in this case, the effect of a holomorphic map on the real
homotopy groups may be read off from the effect of the map on
cohomology. In the non-simply connected case, the real nilpotent tower
of the fundamental group can be read off from \(H^1\) and the cup
product \(H^1\otimes H^1\to H^2\). The effect of a holomorphic map on
the nilpotent tower of \(\pi_1\) can similarly be read off from the map
on \(H^1\).

In Section 7 we give an application of this theory to a union of
divisors with normal crossings. Using the fact that forms on a Kähler
manifold can be naturally replaced by the cohomology, we give a
different proof that a spectral sequence calculating the cohomology
degenerates at \(E_2\), i.e., \(E_2=E_{\infty}\). Here \(E_1\) is built
from the cohomologies of the various intersections, and \(d_1\) is built
from the various restriction maps.

The third author has studied the open complement of a divisor with
normal crossings in a Kähler manifold where related but much more
complicated results ensue {[}20{]}.

\subsection{Section 1. Homotopy Theory of Differential
Algebras}\label{D023-section-1.-homotopy-theory-of-differential-algebras}

This section, together with Sections 2 and 3, constitutes a sketch of
the theory of the last author relating differential algebras and
homotopy theory. For a more complete treatment of this theory see {[}6,
10, 12{]} and {[}13{]}. The discussion in this section is a completely
algebraic one in which the fundamental group of any differential algebra
and the higher homotopy groups (in fact the homotopy type) of an
one-connected differential algebra are defined. This theory is valid for
differential algebras over any field containing the rational numbers
\(\mathbb Q\), but the only fields arising in geometric applications
are, in addition to \(\mathbb Q\), the reals \(\mathbb R\) and the
complexes \(\mathbb C\).

As the terminology suggests, these constructions are motivated by the
theory of Postnikov towers and homotopy theory for spaces. The Hirsch
lemma of Section 3 shows that the connection is stronger than just an
analogy. In fact, the homotopy theory for differential algebras over
\(\mathbb Q\) and the theory of towers of principle fibrations with
fibers \(K(V,n)\), \(V\) a \(\mathbb Q\)-vector space, are equivalent.

A \emph{differential graded algebra} (= differential algebra) is a
graded algebra

\[
\mathscr A=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}\mathscr A^k
\]

with a differential \(d:\mathscr A\to\mathscr A\) of degree \(+1\), such
that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathscr A\) is graded commutative, i.e.,
\end{enumerate}

\[
x\cdot y=(-1)^{k\ell}y\cdot x\qquad(x\in\mathscr A^k\text{ and }y\in\mathscr A^{\ell})
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \(d\) is a derivation, i.e.,
\end{enumerate}

\[
d(x\cdot y)=dx\cdot y+(-1)^k x\cdot dy\qquad(x\in\mathscr A^k),
\]

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

and

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  \(d^2=0\).
\end{enumerate}

The cohomology \(H^*(\mathscr A)\) is an algebra. We shall always assume
that it is finite dimensional in each degree. \(\mathscr A\) is
connected if \(H^0(\mathscr A)\) is the ground field, and \(\mathscr A\)
is one-connected if, in addition, \(H^1(\mathscr A)=0\). A map between
two differential algebras \(\mathscr A\) and \(\mathscr B\) is an
algebra homomorphism preserving the grading and \(d\). Such a map,
\(f:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\), induces an algebra map
\(f^*:H^*(\mathscr A)\to H^*(\mathscr B)\).

\emph{Examples of Differential Algebras.} (i) the de Rham complex
\(\mathscr E_M^*\) of \(C^{\infty}\) forms on a manifold \(M\);

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  the cohomology ring of a \(CW\) complex \(X\),
\end{enumerate}

\[
\{H^*(X;k);d=0\}\qquad(k\text{ a field}).
\]

The cochains on a simplicial complex form only a non-commutative
differential algebra, even though they induce on cohomology a graded
commutative algebra structure.

If \(\mathscr A^0\) is the ground field, then we define the augmentation
ideal \(A(\mathscr A)=\bigoplus_{k>0}\mathscr A^k\), and the graded
space of indecomposables,
\(I(\mathscr A)=A(\mathscr A)/A(\mathscr A)\cdot A(\mathscr A)\). In
such an algebra the derivation \(d\) is decomposable if for every
\(x\in\mathscr A\), \(dx\in A\cdot A\). This is equivalent to saying
that \(d(x)\) is a sum of products of elements of positive degree. By
the free algebra on a vector space \(V_n\) whose elements are of degree
\(n\), \(\Lambda(V_n)\) or just \((\Lambda_n)\), we mean the polynomial
algebra generated by \(V_n\) if \(n\) is even, or the exterior algebra
generated by \(V_n\) if \(n\) is odd. A tensor product (in the graded
sense) of such algebras is again a free algebra. The algebraic analogue
of a principal fibration is an \emph{elementary extension}. An
elementary extension of \((\mathscr A,d_{\mathscr A})\) is any algebra
of the form
\((\mathscr B=\mathscr A\otimes\Lambda(V_k),d_{\mathscr B})\) where
\(d_{\mathscr B}|_{\mathscr A}=d_{\mathscr A}\),
\(d_{\mathscr B}(V_k)\subset\mathscr A\), and \(V_k\) is a finite
dimensional vector space.\textsuperscript{4} We denote such extensions
by \(\mathscr A\otimes_d\Lambda(V_k)\). Note that if \(\mathscr A\) is
free as an algebra, then so is \(\mathscr B\), and if \(d\) is
decomposable in \(\mathscr A\), then it is also decomposable in
\(\mathscr B\) if, and only if,
\(d(V_k)\subset A(\mathscr A)\cdot A(\mathscr A)\). Our first main
definition is that \(\mathcal M\) is a \emph{minimal differential
algebra} if \(\mathcal M\) may be written as an increasing union of
sub-differential algebras

\[
\text{ground field}\subset\mathcal M_1\subset\mathcal M_2\subset\cdots,\qquad \bigcup_{i\ge0}\mathcal M_i=\mathcal M
\]

with \(\mathcal M_i\subset\mathcal M_{i+1}\) an elementary extension,
and with \(d\) decomposable. Such a collection of sub-differential
algebras is a \emph{series for \(\mathcal M\)}. If \(\mathcal M\) is
minimal, then

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  \(d\) is decomposable, and
\item
  \(\mathcal M\) is free as an algebra.
\end{enumerate}

If we let \(\{\mathcal M^{(i)}\}\) denote the subalgebra of
\(\mathcal M\) generated by elements of degree \(\le i\), then \(d\)
being decomposable implies that these are sub-differential algebras. If
\(\mathcal M\) is any one-connected differential algebra satisfying 1)
and 2), then \(\mathcal M^1=0\), and the sequence
\(\mathcal M^{(2)}\subset\mathcal M^{(3)}\subset\cdots\) is a series for
\(\mathcal M\). Thus a one-connected algebra satisfying 1) and 2) has a
canonical series. For any minimal differential algebra \(\mathcal M\),

4 Always placed in a degree greater than zero.

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 250}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

\(\mathcal M^{(1)}\) also has a canonical series

\[
0\subset\mathcal M_1^{(1)}\subset\mathcal M_2^{(1)}\subset\cdots,\qquad \bigcup_{i\ge0}\mathcal M_i^{(1)}=\mathcal M^{(1)}
\]

defined by: \(\mathcal M_i^{(1)}\) = algebra generated by all
\(x\in\mathcal M^{(1)}\) such that \(dx\in\mathcal M_{i-1}^{(1)}\).

Given a finitely generated free differential algebra \(\mathcal K\) with
decomposable \(d\), we can form the dual space to the indecomposables

\[
\mathcal L_{\mathcal K}=\bigoplus\mathcal L_i,\qquad \mathcal L_i=[I(\mathcal K)^i]^*.
\]

Since \(d\) is decomposable, it induces a map
\(d:I(\mathcal K)\to I(\mathcal K)\otimes I(\mathcal K)\) whose dual is
a map \(\mathcal L_i\otimes\mathcal L_j\to\mathcal L_{i+j-1}\). This
makes \(\mathcal L\) into a graded Lie algebra. An elementary extension
\(\mathcal K\to\mathcal K\otimes_d\Lambda(V_n)\) with \(d\) decomposable
dualizes to a central extension of Lie algebras

\[
0\to V_n^*\to\mathcal L_{\mathcal K\otimes_d\Lambda(V_n)}\to\mathcal L_{\mathcal K}\to0
\]

with \([v,x]=0\) for \(v\in V_n^*\) and
\(x\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal K\otimes_d\Lambda(V_n)}\). If
\(0\subset\mathcal M_1\subset\mathcal M_2\subset\cdots\) is a series of
a minimal algebra \(\mathcal M\), then let
\(\mathcal L^i=[I(\mathcal M_i)]^*\). We have an inverse system of
central extensions of Lie algebras

\[
\cdots\to\mathcal L^3\to\mathcal L^2\to\mathcal L^1\to0.
\]

By induction, each \(\mathcal L^i\) is nilpotent. For a general
differential algebra, \(\mathcal M\), satisfying 1) and 2) above it is
this extra condition of nilpotence on the dual Lie algebra,
\(\mathcal L\), which is equivalent to minimality. This nilpotence is
automatic if \(\mathcal M^1=0\), as is easily verified by a degree
argument.

\emph{Example.} Let \(S=\Lambda_1(x,y,z)\), \(dx=y\wedge z\),
\(dy=z\wedge x\), \(dz=x\wedge y\). \(S\) is not minimal, and the dual
Lie algebra to \(S\) is \(\operatorname{so}(3)\) which is simple, not
nilpotent.

In the one-connected case our inverse system of Lie algebras is
eventually stable in each degree (at \(\mathcal L^n\) we are adding
generators in degree \(n\)), and thus coalesces into one Lie algebra
\(\mathcal L=\bigoplus_{n\ge2}\mathcal L_n\). Each \(\mathcal L_n\) is
finitely generated, and we have
\([\ ,\ ]:\mathcal L_n\otimes\mathcal L_k\to\mathcal L_{n+k-1}\). The
vector space \(\mathcal L_n\) is defined to be the \(n\)-th \emph{de
Rham homotopy group} of \(\mathcal M\), and the graded Lie algebra
bracket is called the Whitehead product. In the case of a non-simply
connected minimal differential algebra, \(\mathcal M\), we have
associated to \(\mathcal M^{(1)}\) a canonical series, and dually a
canonical inverse system of nilpotent Lie algebras
\(\cdots\to\mathcal L_1^2\to\mathcal L_1^1\to0\). \(\mathcal L_1^n\) is
nilpotent of order \(n\). The Campbell-Hausdorff formula

\[
X\cdot Y=X+Y+\tfrac12[X,Y]+\cdots,
\]

then defines nilpotent Lie group structures on each \(\mathcal L_1^n\).
This tower of nilpotent Lie groups is the \emph{de Rham fundamental
group} of \(\mathcal M\).

The above discussion can be applied to any differential algebra by the
following idea. If \(\mathscr A\) is a differential algebra, then
\(\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\xrightarrow{\rho}\mathscr A\) is a
\emph{\(k\)-stage minimal model for \(\mathcal M\)} if

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  \(\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\) is a minimal algebra generated in
  dimensions \(\le k\);
\item
  \(\rho\) induces an isomorphism on cohomology in dimensions \(\le k\)
  and an injection in dimension \(k+1\).
\end{enumerate}

We use the term minimal model for \(k=\infty\).

\clearpage

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

To make applications the following theorem is essential. Recall we are
assuming all Betti numbers are finite.

\textbf{(1.1) Theorem.} a) \emph{Every one-connected differential
algebra has a minimal model unique up to isomorphism.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Every connected differential algebra has a 1-stage minimal model
  unique up to isomorphism.}
\end{enumerate}

Thus we define the \emph{de Rham homotopy groups} of a one-connected
differential algebra \(\mathscr A\), denoted \(\pi_*(\mathscr A)\) (with
Whitehead product), to be those of any minimal model for \(\mathscr A\).
Likewise, we define the \emph{de Rham fundamental group} of a
differential algebra to be the de Rham fundamental group of any minimal
model for the algebra.

If \(f:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\) is an isomorphism on cohomology, then
the de Rham fundamental groups of \(\mathscr A\) and \(\mathscr B\) are
isomorphic. If \(\mathscr A\) is one connected, then the de Rham
homotopy groups of \(\mathscr A\) and \(\mathscr B\) are isomorphic. In
the simply connected case we define \(\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\) to be
the de Rham homotopy type of \(\mathscr A\).

\emph{Examples.} 1) Suppose \(\mathscr A=\mathscr E^*_{S_n}\) is the de
Rham complex on the \(n\)-sphere. Then \[
\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\cong
\begin{cases}
\Lambda_n(y),&n\text{ odd},\\
\Lambda_n(y)\otimes\Lambda_{2n-1}(z),\quad dz=y^2,&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\] In either case \(\rho:\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\to\mathscr E^*_{S_n}\)
sends \(y\) to a generator of \(H^n(S^n)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Suppose \(\mathscr A=\mathscr E^*_{\mathbb CP_n}\). Then \[
  \mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\cong\Lambda_2(x)\otimes_d\Lambda_{2n+1}(y),\qquad dy=x^{n+1}.
  \] \(\rho:\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\to\mathscr E^*_{\mathbb CP_n}\)
  sends \(x\) to a closed form whose cohomology class generates
  \(H^2(\mathbb CP^n)\). Thus in these cases the de Rham homotopy groups
  of \(\mathscr E^*_{M^n}\) are equal the usual homotopy groups tensored
  with \(\mathbb R\): \[
  \pi_*(\mathscr E^*_{M^n})\cong\pi_*(M^n)\otimes\mathbb R.
  \] (cf.~Serre {[}11{]}). It is a consequence of Sullivan's theory that
  a similar relation holds for all simply connected smooth manifolds.
\end{enumerate}

For one-connected algebras the existence of the minimal model is
straightforward. One inductively assumes the existence of
\(\mathcal M^{(k)}\xrightarrow{\rho}\mathscr A\) inducing an isomorphism
on cohomology through dimension \(k\) and an injection on \(H^{k+1}\).
Then \(\mathcal M^{(k)}\subset\mathcal M^{(k+1)}\) is an elementary
extension on \(V_{k+1}=C_{k+1}\oplus N_{k+1}\), where \(C_{k+1}\) is the
subspace of closed elements included to make \(\rho\) surjective on
\(H^{k+1}\), and \(N_{k+1}\) is a space of nonclosed generators whose
image under \(d\), \(d(N)\subset(\mathcal M^{(k)})^{k+2}\), makes exact
a space of closed forms representing kernel \(\rho^*\) in degree
\((k+2)\).

In the general case, the construction of \(\mathcal M^{(1)}\) is
similar: \(\mathcal M_1^{(1)}=\Lambda(H^1(\mathscr A))\) and
\(\mathcal M_i^{(1)}\subset\mathcal M_{i+1}^{(1)}\) is an elementary
extension by
\(\Lambda_1(\operatorname{Ker}H^2(\mathcal M_i^{(1)})\to H^2(\mathscr A))\).
It is necessary to keep killing the kernel in degree 2 repeatedly since
at each step one is creating more kernel in that degree.

The uniqueness statements in these two cases require the development of
the theory of homotopy for maps between differential algebras. Let
\((t,dt)\) denote the polynomials in the variable \(t\) of degree zero
tensor the exterior algebra on its

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 252}{D023-d023-source_language-p0008}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

differential, \(dt\), in degree one. This is a contractible algebra
which we think of as the real line. There are evaluations at \(t=0\) and
at \(t=1\), which we think of as two points on the line. A map
\(H:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\otimes(t,dt)\) is a homotopy from
\(f:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\) to \(g:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\) if
\(H|_{t=0}=f\) and \(H|_{t=1}=g\). (Note that a homotopy
\(H:X\times I\to Y\) induces a map \[
\mathscr E_Y^*\xrightarrow{H^*}\mathscr E_X^*\otimes\mathscr E_I^*.
\] Thus the contravariant nature of forms requires that \((t,dt)\) be in
the range rather than the domain.)

Given an elementary extension
\(\mathcal N=\mathcal M\otimes_d\Lambda(V_n)\), maps \(f\) and
\(g:\mathcal N\to\mathscr A\), and a homotopy
\(H:\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\otimes(t,dt)\) from \(f|\mathcal M\) to
\(g|\mathcal M\), then \(H\) extends to a homotopy
\(\bar H:\mathcal N\to\mathscr A\otimes(t,dt)\) from \(f\) to \(g\) if
and only if the homomorphism
\(V_n\xrightarrow{\sigma}H^{n+1}(\mathscr A)\) given by \[
\left\{\sigma(x)=\text{cohomology class of }\left(f(x)-g(x)+(-1)^{\deg x}\int_{t=0}^{t=1}H(dx)\right)\right\}
\] is 0. If \(\sigma=0\), then an extension of \(H\) to \(\bar H\) is
determined by choosing linearly, for each \(x\), \(\alpha(x)\) such that
\(d(\alpha(x))=\sigma(x)\). The formula for \(\bar H\) is then \[
\bar H(x)=f(x)+(-1)^{\deg x}\int_0^tH(dx)-d(\alpha(x)\otimes t).
\] Thus we find a sequence of cohomological obstructions for building a
homotopy whose algebraic structure is exactly analogous to the
topological situation.

\textbf{(1.2) Theorem (Lifting and lifting up to homotopy).} \emph{Given
a diagram of solid arrows} \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
&\mathscr A&\\[-2mm]
&\downarrow\scriptstyle\varphi&\\[-2mm]
\mathcal M&\xrightarrow{f}&\mathscr B
\end{array}
\] \emph{with \(\mathcal M\) minimal and \(\varphi^*\) an isomorphism on
cohomology, then there is a \(\tilde f:\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\) so that
\(\varphi\tilde f\) is homotopic to \(f\). If \(\varphi\) is also onto,
then we can choose \(\tilde f\) so that \(\varphi\tilde f\) is equal to
\(f\).}

\textbf{(1.3) Corollary.} \emph{Homotopy is an equivalence relation on
the set of maps \(\{f:\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\}\) for \(\mathcal M\)
minimal. We denote the set of equivalence classes by
\([\mathcal M,\mathscr A]\).}

\textbf{(1.4) Corollary.} \emph{If \(\psi:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\) is
an isomorphism on cohomology, then \(\psi\) induces a bijection of sets
\(\psi:[\mathcal M,\mathscr A]\to[\mathcal M,\mathscr B]\).}

\textbf{(1.5) Corollary.} \emph{If \(f:\mathscr A\to\mathscr B\) is any
map of differential algebras and
\(\rho_{\mathscr A}:\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\to\mathscr A\) and
\(\rho_{\mathscr B}:\mathcal M\to\mathscr B\) are minimal models for
\(\mathscr A\) and \(\mathscr B\), then \(f\) induces
\(\tilde f:\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}\to\mathcal M_{\mathscr B}\), unique
up to homotopy, subject to the condition that} \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathscr A&\xrightarrow{f}&\mathscr B\\
\uparrow\scriptstyle\rho_{\mathscr A}&&\uparrow\scriptstyle\rho_{\mathscr B}\\
\mathcal M_{\mathscr A}&\xrightarrow{\tilde f}&\mathcal M_{\mathscr B}
\end{array}
\]

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 253}{D023-d023-source_language-p0009}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 253}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

\textbf{(1.6) Corollary.} \emph{Any two \(k\)-stage minimal models of an
algebra are isomorphic by an isomorphism unique up to homotopy.}

Theorem (1.2) and its corollaries are sufficient for the proof of
Theorem (1.1).

The first part of Theorem (1.2) is proved by induction using the
cohomological form of the obstruction to extending a homotopy. The
second part is proved by a direct algebraic argument. To prove Corollary
(1.3) let \((s,t,ds,dt)\) represent the plane and
\((s,t,ds,dt)/\{s\cdot(t-1)=0,sdt=0\}\) represent the union of the lines
\(s=0\) and \(t=1\). Both are contractible algebras. \[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{the lines }s=0,\quad t=1,\quad\text{and the diagonal }s=t
\end{array}
\] Two homotopies \(H:\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\otimes(t,dt)\) and
\(H':\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\otimes(s,ds)\) with \(H|_{t=1}=H'|_{s=0}\)
define a map \[
H\mathrel{\widetilde{+}}H':\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\otimes(s,t,ds,dt/\{s\cdot(t-1)=0,sdt=0\}).
\] Use Theorem (1.2) to produce a
\(\bar H:\mathcal M\to\mathscr A\otimes(s,t,ds,dt)\) which extends
\(H\mathrel{\widetilde{+}}H'\). Restricting \(\bar H\) to the line
\(\{s=t\}\) gives the required homotopy from \(H|_{t=0}\) to
\(H'|_{s=1}\).

The lifting up to homotopy theorem proves that the map
\(\psi:[\mathcal M,\mathscr A]\to[\mathcal M,\mathscr B]\) of Corollary
(1.4) is onto if \(\psi^*:H^*(\mathscr A)\to H^*(\mathscr B)\) is an
isomorphism. That \(\psi\) is one-to-one is proved using a relative
version of lifting up to homotopy.

Corollary (1.5) is an immediate consequence of (1.2).

To prove Corollary (1.6) we need to know that any map of minimal
differential algebras inducing an isomorphism on cohomology induces an
isomorphism on the subalgebras generated by elements in degree \(k\).
This is proved inductively over the canonical series.

\emph{Example.} Let \(f:S^{4n-1}\to S^{2n}\) be a \(C^{\infty}\) map. It
induces
\(\tilde f:\Lambda_{2n}(y)\otimes\Lambda_{4n-1}(z)\to\Lambda_{4n-1}(x)\)
unique up to homotopy. There are no homotopies here; thus \(\tilde f\)
is unique. It is completely determined by \(\tilde f(z)=H(f)\cdot x\)
for some real number \(H(f)\). By explicit computation
\(H(f)=\int_{S^{4n-1}}\bar u\wedge f^*(\bar y)\), where
\(\bar y=\rho(y_{2n})\) and \(\bar u\in\mathscr E^{2n-1}(S^{4n-1})\)
satisfies \(d\bar u=f^*\bar y\). This is exactly Whitehead's formulation
of the Hopf invariant of \(f\) as given in {[}17{]}. Thus, \(H(f)\) is
an integer. Also we see that the homotopy theoretic nature of \(f\)
modulo torsion is determined by maps on forms, even though \(f^*\) is
zero in cohomology.

As a general comment, to understand cohomology and maps on cohomology
one need deal only with closed forms, but to detect the finer homotopy
theoretic information one also needs to use non-closed forms.
Differential geometric aspects of this philosophy have been given by
Chern and Simons: ``The manner in which a closed form which is zero in
cohomology actually becomes exact contains geometric information''.

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

\subsection{Section 2. De Rham Homotopy
Theory}\label{D023-section-2.-de-rham-homotopy-theory}

There are two natural ``geometric'' differential algebras; one is the
\(C^{\infty}\) de Rham forms on a smooth manifold, and the other is the
\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on a simplical complex. Associated to
each type of algebra is a de Rham theorem. Also, given a \(C^1\)
triangulation of a \(C^{\infty}\) manifold, the two algebras of forms are
related through the piecewise \(C^{\infty}\) forms in that triangulation.

Let \(\mathscr E_M^*\) be the \(C^{\infty}\) forms on \(M\) and
\(\mathcal M_M\) a minimal model for it. If \(M\) is simply connected,
we call \(\mathcal M_M\) the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy type of \(M\)
and \(\pi_i(\mathcal M_M)=\pi_i(\mathscr E_M^*)\) the \(i\)-th
\(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy group of \(M\). These vector spaces are
given a graded Lie algebra structure called the de Rham-Whitehead
product. These groups and their products are invariants of \(M\). If
\(f:M\to N\) is an isomorphism on cohomology, then it induces an
isomorphism \(\tilde f:\mathcal M_N\cong\mathcal M_N\) and
\(f_\#:\pi_i(\mathcal M_M)\cong\pi_i(\mathcal M_N)\). More generally,
given any smooth map \(f:M\to N\), it induces
\(\tilde f:\mathcal M_N\to\mathcal M_M\) unique up to homotopy. The
various homotopic \(\tilde f\)'s induce the same map
\(f_\#:\pi_i(\mathcal M_M)\to\pi_i(\mathcal M_N)\). There are analogous
statements about the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham fundamental group of any
manifold.

In the next section we shall state how these homotopy invariants of
manifolds are related to the more classical ones, thus justifying the
terminology.

In particular we shall find that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  \(\pi_1(\mathcal M_M)\) is the real form of the nilpotent completion
  of \(\pi_1(M)\).
\item
  If \(\pi_1(M)=\{e\}\), then
  \(\pi_n(\mathcal M_M)\cong\pi_n(M)\otimes\mathbb R\) by a natural
  isomorphism preserving the Whitehead product structures.
\item
  If \(\pi_1(M)=\{e\}\), then \(\mathcal M_M\) contains all the
  algebraic topology of \(M\) over real numbers. It is the real homotopy
  type of \(M\).
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Explanation.} 1) If \(\pi\) is any group, then \[
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
\cdots&\subset&[\pi,[\pi,\pi]]&\subset&[\pi,\pi]&\subset&\pi\\
&&\Vert&&\Vert&&\Vert\\
\cdots&\subset&\Gamma_2&\subset&\Gamma_1&\subset&\pi
\end{array}
\] is the lower central series. The quotients \[
\cdots\to\pi/\Gamma_3\to\pi/\Gamma_2\to\pi/\Gamma_1=\text{abelianization of }\pi
\] is a tower of nilpotent groups in the sense that \((n+1)\)-fold
commutators are 0 in \(\pi/\Gamma_n\). This tower is the \emph{nilpotent
completion} of \(\pi\). It is possible to ``tensor'' such nilpotent
groups with \(\mathbb R\) (or \(\mathbb Q\), or \(\mathbb C\)), and
produce real (rational or complex) nilpotent Lie groups, {[}1, 13{]}.
These are the real (rational or complex) form of the nilpotent
completion of \(\pi_1\).

To give meaning to statement 3), much less prove it, we must relate
\(\mathcal M_M\) to some Postnikov tower related to \(M\). As we will
see in the next section it is possible to homotopy-theoretically tensor
a Postnikov tower with \(\mathbb Q\). However, there is no such direct
process for tensoring with \(\mathbb R\).\textsuperscript{5} We must
therefore relate \(\mathcal M_M\) to a

5 Theorems (3.3) and (3.4) below provide a meaningful algebraic method
for ``tensoring'' a space with \(\mathbb R\). Finding a geometric
process for tensoring a space with \(\mathbb R\) presents interesting
problems.

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 255}{D023-d023-source_language-p0011}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 255}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

rational differential algebra which then may be related to a rational
Postnikov tower. This leads us to the other class of differential
algebras: the \(\mathbb Q\) polynomial forms on a simplicial complex.
The following discussion is motivated by Whitney's work {[}18{]},
especially Chapter IV, Sections 24-29 and Chapter VII, Sections 10-12.

Let \(\sigma_n\) be an \(n\)-simplex embedded in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\)
using barycentric coordinates. A \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial form on
\(\sigma_n\) is the restriction to the simplex of a differential form \[
\psi=\psi_{i_1\ldots i_{\ell}}(t)\,dt_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{i_{\ell}}
\] in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) where the \(\psi_{i_1\ldots i_{\ell}}(t)\) are
polynomials with \(\mathbb Q\)-coefficients. On a simplicial complex
\(X\), a \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial form \(\psi\) is given by a
\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial form \(\psi_{\sigma}\) in each simplex
\(\sigma\subset X\) such that the compatibility condition,
\(\omega_{\sigma}\) restricted to \(\tau\) equals \(\omega_{\tau}\) whenever
\(\sigma\) contains \(\tau\) as a face, is satisfied. The
\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms give a differential algebra
\(\mathscr E_X^*\) defined over \(\mathbb Q\). Moreover, Stokes' theorem
\[
\int_{\partial C}\psi=\int_Cd\psi
\] is valid for simplical chains, and thus integration gives a chain map
\(\mathscr E_X^*\xrightarrow{i}C^*(X,\mathbb Q)\). We obtains rational
cochains because integration of polynomials is a rational operation.

\textbf{(2.1) Theorem (p.~l. de Rham Theorem, see {[}18, 14, 6{]}).}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\item
  \emph{The induced mapping
  \(H^*(\mathscr E_X^*)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^*(X,\mathbb Q)\) is an
  isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q\)-algebras.}
\item
  \emph{If \(K\xrightarrow{\psi}M\) is a \(C^1\) triangulation of a
  \(C^{\infty}\) manifold, let \(\widetilde{\mathscr E}_M^*\) be the
  complex of piecewise \(C^{\infty}\) forms on \(M\) with respect to the
  triangulation \(K\) (i.e.~forms whose restrictions to each simplex of
  \(K\) is \(C^{\infty}\)). Then the inclusions} \[
  \begin{array}{ccc}
  &\widetilde{\mathscr E}_M^*&\\[-2mm]
  \nearrow&&\nwarrow\\[-2mm]
  \mathscr E_M^*&&\mathscr E_K^*\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R
  \end{array}
  \] \emph{induce isomorphisms on cohomology rings.}
\end{enumerate}

These two isomorphism theorems are proved similarly to the way Whitney
proves the de Rham theorem and the isomorphism theorem for flat
cochains, see {[}18{]}. For the fact that the isomorphism in a) is a
ring map see {[}19{]}.

To each simplicial complex \(X\), we assign \(\mathscr E_X^*\), the
differential algebra of \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms. From this we
obtain \(\mathcal M_{\mathscr E_X^*}^{(1)}\) and dually a natural tower
of nilpotent Lie groups
\(\cdots\to\mathcal L_1^2(X)\to\mathcal L_1^1(X)\to0\). This tower is
the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham fundamental group of \(X\). If \(X\) is simply
connected, then \(\mathcal M_{\mathscr E_X^*}=\mathcal M_X\) is an
invariant of \(X\). It is the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham homotopy type of
\(X\) and its homotopy groups \(\pi_*(\mathcal M_X)\), with their
Whitehead products, are the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham homotopy groups of
\(X\). A simplicial map \(F:X\to Y\) induces
\(\tilde f:\mathcal M_Y^{(1)}\to\mathcal M_X^{(1)}\) unique up to
homotopy. All the homotopic \(\tilde f\) induce the same map
\(\pi_1(\mathcal M_X)\xrightarrow{f_*}\pi_1(\mathcal M_Y)\), which is
the map induced by \(f\) on the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham fundamental group.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are simply connected, then the various
\(f:\mathcal M_Y\to\mathcal M_X\) induce the same map
\(f_\#:\pi_*(\mathcal M_X)\to\pi_*(\mathcal M_Y)\).

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 256}{D023-d023-source_language-p0012}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 256}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

If \(K\xrightarrow{\psi}M\) is a \(C^1\) triangulation of a \(C^{\infty}\)
manifold, applying theorem 2.1, b) gives:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  (\(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham fundamental group of
  \(K\))\(\otimes\mathbb R\cong C^{\infty}\) de Rham fundamental group of
  \(M\):
  \(\pi_1(\mathcal M_K)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\cong\pi_1(\mathcal M_M)\),
\item
  If \(M\) is simply connected, then (\(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham homotopy
  type of \(K\))\(\otimes\mathbb R\cong C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy type
  of \(M\):
  \(\mathcal M_K\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\cong\mathcal M_M\), also
  \(\pi_*(\mathcal M_K)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\cong\pi_*(\mathcal M_M)\)
  by an isomorphism preserving Whitehead products.
\end{enumerate}

In the next section we will relate all this to the classical homotopy
theory for \(X\) and for \(M\).

To do this it is necessary to be able to subdivide simplicial complexes
(e.g., for the simplicial approximation theorem). Since we wish to
preserve the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms, it is necessary to restrict
to \emph{rational barycentric subdivisions}, i.e., those where all new
vertices have rational coordinates in the old vertices. With this
restriction the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on \(X\) induce
\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on the subdivision. The category of
simplicial complexes with \(\mathbb Q\)-subdivision and
\(\mathbb Q\)-piecewise linear maps is equivalent to the usual homotopy
category.

\subsection{Section 3. Relation between De Rham Homotopy Theory and
Classical Homotopy
Theory}\label{D023-section-3.-relation-between-de-rham-homotopy-theory-and-classical-homotopy-theory}

To relate the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy type of a manifold \(M\) to
the classical homotopy theory of \(M\), we relate the \(\mathbb Q\)-de
Rham homotopy type of some \(C^1\) triangulation, \(K\), to the
classical homotopy type, and then use the relationship
\(\mathcal M_K\otimes\mathbb R\cong\mathcal M_M\). For another
connection between differential (co-) algebras and homotopy theory
compare {[}10{]}, which motivated the questions answered in this
section.

To each space \(X\) we can associate a tower of fibrations \(P_X\), the
Postnikov tower to \(X\), \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
&&\vdots\\
&&X_2\\
&\nearrow\scriptstyle f_2&\downarrow\scriptstyle p_2\\
&&X_1\\
&\nearrow\scriptstyle f_1&\downarrow\scriptstyle p_1\\
X&\xrightarrow{\ f_0\ }&X_0
\end{array}
\] such that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  the fiber of \(X_n\to X_{n-1}\) has only one non-zero homotopy group,
  that being in dimension \(n\):
\item
  \(f_n\) is an isomorphism on homotopy groups in dimension \(\le n\),
  and
\item
  \(X_0\) is a point.
\end{enumerate}

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 257}{D023-d023-source_language-p0013}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 257}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

Homotopy questions about \(X\) can be formulated in terms of this tower.
To study such a tower with ordinary forms (i.e., forms taking values in
a constant bundle), we need the fibrations \(\rho\) to be principal.
They are principal if, and only if, \(\pi_1(X_{n-1})\cong\pi_1(X)\) acts
trivially on \(\pi_n\) of the fiber (which is \(\pi_n(X)\)). Under
weaker assumptions on \(X\), namely that \(\pi_1(X)\) is nilpotent and
acts in a nilpotent manner in \(\pi_n(X)\), the Postnikov tower admits a
(finite) refinement into principal fibrations which can be treated
algebraically using ordinary forms.

More generally every space maps to its universal tower of principal
fibrations \(P_X\) (unique up to a pro-equivalence) which is convenient
for our algebraic manipulations, but does not contain all the homotopy
theoretic information in the space unless we are in the ``nilpotent
case'' above.

Towers of principle fibrations can be inductively ``tensored with
\(\mathbb Q\)'', see {[}13{]} for example, to produce a system of
rational principal fibrations, i.e., ones in which the homotopy group of
each fiber is a rational vector space. If \(X\) is simply connected (or
even nilpotent) then \(P_X\otimes\mathbb Q\) is the \emph{rational
Postnikov tower} of \(X\), or the \emph{rational homotopy type} of
\(X\). It contains the rational form of all the algebraic homotopy
information in the space. We will see one way to construct this tower,
\(P_X\otimes\mathbb Q\), using \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms on \(X\)
below. To treat twisted fibrations directly one would need to use
twisted forms (forms with coefficients in a flat vector bundle). The
connection between forms and principal fibrations is achieved by the
Hirsch lemma and its converse. Given a fibration
\(F\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}B\), an element \(\alpha\in H^k(F;\mathbb Q)\)
is transgressive if it is possible to take a \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial
form representing \(\alpha\) and extend it to a form
\(\widetilde{\alpha}\) on \(E\) such that
\(d\widetilde{\alpha}=\pi^*(\beta)\) for some closed form \(\beta\) in
\(B\). If \(H^*(F)\) is a free algebra, we say that it is transgressive
if it has an algebra basis consisting of transgressive elements.

\textbf{(3.1) Lemma (Hirsch Lemma).} Given a fibration
\(F\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}B\) with \(H^*(F)\) free and transgressive and
a differential algebra \(\mathcal A\to\mathcal E_B^*\) giving an
isomorphism on cohomology, then there is a map of differential algebras
\(\mathcal A\otimes_d H^*(F)\to\mathcal E_E^*\) also inducing an
isomorphism on cohomology.

\textbf{Proof.} Pick an algebra basis \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) for
\(H^*(F)\). Let \(\widetilde\alpha_i\in\mathcal E_E^*\) be a form which
when restricted to \(F\) gives a closed form representing \(x_i\). Let
\(\beta_i\) be such that \(d\widetilde\alpha_i=\pi^*(\beta_i)\). Since
\(\rho:\mathcal A\to\mathcal E_B^*\) is an isomorphism on cohomology, we
may pick \(\widetilde\alpha_i\) such that \(\beta_i=\rho(a_i)\) for some
closed form \(a_i\in\mathcal A\).

Define \(d:H^*(F)\to\mathcal A^{*+1}\) by \(d(x_i)=a_i\), and
\(\widetilde{\rho}:\mathcal A\otimes H^*(F)\to\mathcal E_E^*\) by
\(\widetilde{\rho}|_{\mathcal A}=\pi^*\circ\rho\) and
\(\widetilde{\rho}(x_i)=\widetilde\alpha_i\). \(\widetilde{\rho}\) is a map
of differential algebras. If one uses the \(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial forms
on the base \(\mathcal E_B^*\) for \(\mathcal A\) with \(\rho=id\), then
an easy induction argument over the cells of the base using the five
lemma shows that \(\widetilde{\rho}\) is an isomorphism on cohomology. An
easy algebraic induction shows that
\(\rho\otimes id:\mathcal A\otimes_d H^*(F)\to\mathcal E_B^*\otimes H^*(F)\)
is an isomorphism on cohomology if \(\rho\) is. Thus the Serre spectral
sequence is, in effect, replaced in our \(\mathbb Q\)-theory by the
algebraically simpler Hirsch lemma. The latter also contains more
information than the rational Serre spectral sequence.

\emph{Examples of Such Fibrations.} 1) \emph{The frame bundle of a
smooth manifold:} By the Chern-Weil theory, the fiber has free
cohomology which is transgressive.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Principal fibrations:} Using the Hirsch lemma, one proves
  inductively that
  \(H^*(K(\pi,n);\mathbb Q)\cong\Lambda(\operatorname{Hom}(\pi,\mathbb Q))\).
\end{enumerate}

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 258}{D023-d023-source_language-p0014}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 258}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

Thus the cohomology of the fiber is free and generated in dimension
\(n\). It is transgressive, since this is the case in the universal
principal fibration

\[K(\pi,n)\to P\to K(\pi,n+1).\]

We also need the converse of the Hirsch lemma. It is at this point that
it is necessary to work with \(\mathbb Q\)-algebras and
\(\mathbb Q\)-polynomial-forms rather than \(\mathbb R\)-algebras and
classical forms.

\textbf{(3.2) Lemma.} Given a \(\mathbb Q\)-differential algebra,
\(\mathcal A\) and a space \(B\) with
\(\rho:\mathcal A\to\mathcal E_B^*\) inducing an isomorphism on
\(\mathbb Q\)-cohomology, and an elementary extension
\(\mathcal A\otimes_d\Lambda_n\) of \(\mathcal A\), then there is a
principal fibration \(F\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}B\), and
\(\widetilde{\rho}:\mathcal A\otimes_d\Lambda_n\to\mathcal E_E^*\)
inducing an isomorphism on \(\mathbb Q\)-cohomology. Furthermore, this
fibration is unique if we require \(\pi_*(F)\) to be a
\(\mathbb Q\)-vector space.

\textbf{Proof.} Set \(\Lambda_n=\Lambda(V_n^*)\). Then

\[d:V_n^*\to\{\text{closed forms in }\mathcal A^{n+1}\}\to H^{n+1}(\mathcal A)\]

defines
\(k\in H^{n+1}(\mathcal A,V)\xrightarrow[\rho]{\cong}H^{n+1}(B;V)\).

Form the principal fibration over \(B\) with fiber \(K(V,n)\) and
characteristic class \(k\in H^{n+1}(B;V)\), i.e.,

\[\begin{CD}K(V,n)@>>>K(V,n)\\@VVV@VVV\\E@>>>P\\@VVV@VVV\\B@>{k}>>K(V,n+1).\end{CD}\]

To define \(\rho:\mathcal A\otimes_d\Lambda_n\to\mathcal E_E^*\)
inducing an isomorphism on \(\mathbb Q\)-cohomology, we need only know
that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  \(H^*(K(V,n);\mathbb Q)\cong\Lambda(V^*)=\Lambda_n\) (This is true
  since we are working over \(\mathbb Q\). The analogous statement over
  \(\mathbb R\) is false.), and
\item
  the transgression \(\tau:V^*\to H^{n+1}(B)\) equals \(k\).
\end{enumerate}

Thus given an algebra which is presented as a sequence of elementary
extensions,
\(0\subset\mathcal A_1\subset\mathcal A_2\subset\cdots\bigcup\mathcal A_i=\mathcal A\)
(e.g., a minimal differential algebra with a series), we can form a
tower of rational fibrations \(X_1\leftarrow X_2\leftarrow\cdots\) using
(3.2). Conversely given a tower of principal fibrations, we use (3.1) to
build a sequence of elementary extensions of differential algebras. A
main result, see {[}12{]} and {[}13{]}, is that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  the composition:
\end{enumerate}

\[\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{tower of}\\\text{principal}\\\text{fibrations}\end{array}\right\}\longrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{sequence of}\\\text{elementary}\\\text{extensions of}\\\mathbb Q\text{-differential}\\\text{algebras}\end{array}\right\}\longrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{tower of}\\\text{rational}\\\text{principal}\\\text{fibrations}\end{array}\right\}\]

tensors a tower with \(\mathbb Q\), and that

\clearpage

\pdfbookmark[1]{D023 folio 259}{D023-d023-source_language-p0015}

\noindent{\small\sffamily D023 · Source-language English edition · folio 259}

\par

\vspace{0.7mm}\hrule\vspace{1.6mm}

\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  the composition
\end{enumerate}

\[\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{sequence of}\\\text{elementary}\\\text{extensions of}\\\mathbb Q\text{-differential}\\\text{algebras}\end{array}\right\}\longrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{tower of}\\\text{rational}\\\text{principal}\\\text{fibrations}\end{array}\right\}\longrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{sequence of}\\\text{elementary}\\\text{extensions of}\\\mathbb Q\text{-differential}\\\text{algebras}\end{array}\right\}\]

is the identity.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  If a sequence of elementary extensions of differential algebras
  \(0\subset\mathcal A_1\subset\mathcal A_2\subset\cdots\) determines
  principal fibrations \(X_1\leftarrow X_2\leftarrow\cdots\), then each
  \(\mathcal A_i\) maps into \(\mathcal E_{X_i}^*\) inducing an
  isomorphism on cohomology. Thus, if each \(\mathcal A_i\) is minimal
  (i.e., \(d\) is decomposable), then \(\mathcal A_i\) is the minimal
  model for \(\mathcal E_{X_i}^*\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{(3.3) Theorem.} a) If \(X\) is simply connected (or nilpotent),
then the rational Postnikov tower of \(X\) and the rational de Rham
homotopy type of \(X\) determine each other,
\(\mathcal M_X\longleftrightarrow P_X\otimes\mathbb Q\). (This justifies
calling \(\mathcal M_X\) the rational homotopy type of \(X\).) In
particular if \(X\) is simply connected
\(\pi_*(\mathcal M_X)\cong\pi_*(X)\otimes\mathbb Q\) by an isomorphism
preserving Whitehead products.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\pi_1(\mathcal M_X)\cong\) rational form of the nilpotent completion
  of \(\pi_1(X)\), for any \(X\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{(3.4) Corollary.} a) If \(M^n\) is a simply connected
\(C^{\infty}\) manifold, then the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy type is
the real form of an algebra with rational structure constants.
Furthermore, this rational algebra can be taken to be that of the
rational Postnikov tower of \(M\). (This justifies calling
\(\mathcal M_M\) the real homotopy type of \(M\).) In particular
\(\pi_*(\mathcal M_M)\cong\pi_*(M)\otimes\mathbb R\) by an isomorphism
preserving Whitehead products, if \(M\) is simply connected.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  The \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham fundamental group of \(M\) is the real form
  of the nilpotent completion of \(\pi_1(M)\), for any \(M\).
\item
  If we use complex valued forms on \(M\), then a) and b) have complex
  analogues. Thus \(\pi_1(\mathcal E_M^*\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)\)
  is the nilpotent completion of \(\pi_1(M)\), and
  \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal E_M^*\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C}\) is the
  complex homotopy type of \(M\) and contains
  \(\pi_*(M)\otimes\mathbb C\), if \(M\) is simply connected.
\end{enumerate}

There are also versions of these theorems for maps.

If \(f:X\to Y\) is a simplical map, then

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  if \(X\) and \(Y\) are simply connected, the induced map on the
  \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham homotopy type determines the map induced by
  \(f\) between the rational Postnikov towers of \(X\) and \(Y\), and
  \(f_\#: \pi_*(\mathcal M_X)\to\pi_*(\mathcal M_Y)\) equals
  \(f_\#: \pi_*(X)\otimes\mathbb Q\to\pi_*(Y)\otimes\mathbb Q\),
\item
  if \(X\) and \(Y\) are not simply connected, then the map \(f_\#\) on
  the \(\mathbb Q\)-de Rham fundamental group equals the map \(f_\#\) on
  the \(\mathbb Q\) form of the nilpotent completion of \(\pi_1\).
\end{enumerate}

If \(f:M\to N\) is a \(C^{\infty}\) map between \(C^{\infty}\) manifolds,
then

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  if \(M\) and \(N\) are simply connected, the induced map on
  \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham homotopy groups equals the induced map on
  classical homotopy groups with \(\mathbb R\),
\item
  if \(M\) and \(N\) are non simply connected, the map induced by \(f\)
  on the \(C^{\infty}\) de Rham fundamental group equals the map induced
  by \(f\) on the real form of the nilpotent completion of \(\pi_1(M)\).
\end{enumerate}
