(2.6.2)    I^±: H_B^±(M) ⊗ ℂ → H_{D̅R̅}^±(M) ⊗ ℂ,
\end{D030Diagram}
are isomorphisms of E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-modules between complexifications of E-vector spaces. Set\par
c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M) \ensuremath{=} det(I\ensuremath{^{±}}) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*,    \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{=} det(I) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*,\par
where the determinant is computed in E-rational bases of H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{±}}(M) and H\ensuremath{_{\overline{D}\overline{R}}}\ensuremath{^{±}}(M), respectively H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) and H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M). The definition of \ensuremath{δ}(M) does not require the hypotheses imposed on M. Up to multiplication by an element of E*, these numbers depend only on M. Again by 1.6, c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M), i\ensuremath{^{d^−(M)}}c\ensuremath{^{−}}(M), and i\ensuremath{^{d^−(M)}}\ensuremath{δ}(M) lie in (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℝ})*.\par
Conjecture 2.7. Set \ensuremath{ℜ}(M) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}w/2. If M is critical, (i) L(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) never has a pole at s \ensuremath{=} 0 and can vanish there only when \ensuremath{ℜ}(M) \ensuremath{=} 1/2; (ii) the order of vanishing of L(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) at s \ensuremath{=} 0 is independent of \ensuremath{σ}.\par
For (i), see the discussion at the end of 1.3. B. Gross suggested that (ii) should be reasonable.\par
Conjecture 2.8. If M is critical and L(\ensuremath{σ}, M) \ensuremath{≠} 0, then L*(M) is the product of c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) and an element of E*.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{12}{324}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
REMARK 2.9. A motive M over a number field k with coefficients in E also defines an L-function L*(M, s). These functions are covered by the conjecture because L*(M, s) \ensuremath{=} L*(R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M, s), where R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}} denotes restriction of scalars from k to \ensuremath{ℚ}; apply (0.5.3).\par
The functions L(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) are Euler products indexed by the finite places of k. They must be completed by the infinite factors L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s), indexed by the infinite places and defined in 5.2. In general they depend on \ensuremath{σ}. Only L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M, s), the product over the infinite places v of the L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s), is independent of \ensuremath{σ}.\par
REMARK 2.10. Let F be an extension of E, let \ensuremath{ι}: E \ensuremath{→} F be the structural morphism, and let \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{_{C}}: E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{↪} F \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} be its complexification. Then L*(M \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F, s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{_{C}} L*(M, s) and c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{_{C}} c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M). Thus the conjecture is compatible with extension of the coefficient field. If F/E is Galois with group G, Hilbert’s Theorem 90, H\ensuremath{^{1}}(G, F*) \ensuremath{=} 0, gives ((F \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*/F*)\ensuremath{^{G}} \ensuremath{=} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*/E*, so the conjecture is invariant under extension of coefficients.\par
REMARK 2.11. If E is an extension of F, then L*(R\ensuremath{_{E/F}}M, s) \ensuremath{=} N\ensuremath{_{E/F}}L*(M, s). Since the periods c\ensuremath{^{±}} satisfy the same identity, the conjecture is compatible with restriction of coefficients.\par
REMARK 2.12. Let D be a division algebra of rank d\ensuremath{^{2}} over E. A motive M over \ensuremath{ℚ} with a D-module structure and rank n over D defines a Dirichlet series with coefficients in E whose Euler factors almost all have degree nd. For a finite place \ensuremath{λ} of E, H\ensuremath{_{λ}}(M) is a free module over D\ensuremath{_{λ}} \ensuremath{=} D \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} E\ensuremath{_{λ}}, and definition (2.2.1) is used with\par
Z\ensuremath{_{p}}(M, t) \ensuremath{=} det red(1 \ensuremath{−} F\ensuremath{_{p}} t, H\ensuremath{_{λ}}(M)\ensuremath{^{I_p}})\ensuremath{^{−1}}.\par
If D\ensuremath{_{λ}} is a matrix algebra over E\ensuremath{_{λ}} and e is an indecomposable idempotent, the reduced determinant of an endomorphism A of a D\ensuremath{_{λ}}-module H is the determinant, over E\ensuremath{_{λ}}, of the restriction of A to eH; the general case is obtained by descent.\par
The freedom afforded by 2.10 to extend the coefficient field also brings these L-functions under Conjecture 2.8. Choose an extension \ensuremath{ι}: E \ensuremath{↪} F that splits D and an indecomposable idempotent e of D \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F. Then \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{_{C}} L*(M, s) \ensuremath{=} L*(e(M \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F), s).\par
One may also define c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) directly in this setting, as explained in 2.13 below.\par
The remainder of this section is not used later.\par
2.13. Let D be a simple algebra over a field E, or even an Azumaya algebra over a ring. For the tensor formalism it is convenient to regard D-modules as “fictitious E-vector spaces”:\par
(a) To give an E-vector space V is equivalent to giving, for every étale extension F/E, an F-vector space V\ensuremath{_{F}} and compatible isomorphisms V\ensuremath{_{G}} \ensuremath{=} V\ensuremath{_{F}} \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{F}} G for extensions G/F. One takes V\ensuremath{_{F}} \ensuremath{=} V \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F. By descent it is enough to give V\ensuremath{_{F}} for sufficiently large F.\par
(b) Let W be a D-module. For every étale extension F/E and every F-isomorphism D \ensuremath{⊗} F \ensuremath{≅} End\ensuremath{_{F}}(L), with L free, set W\ensuremath{_{F,L}} \ensuremath{=} Hom\ensuremath{_{D⊗F}}(L, W \ensuremath{⊗} F), where all unlabelled tensor products are over E. There is an isomorphism of D \ensuremath{⊗} F-modules\par
W \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E}} F \ensuremath{=} L \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{F}} W\ensuremath{_{F,L}}.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{13}{325}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
If F is large enough to split D, L is unique up to a nonunique isomorphism; the nonuniqueness is due to scalar homotheties, which act trivially on End(L). This is why the data W\ensuremath{_{F,L}} are not of type (a); they form a “fictitious vector space over E.”\par
Let (W\ensuremath{^{α}}) be a family of D-modules, and let T be a tensor operation. If the scalar homotheties of L act trivially on T(W\ensuremath{_{F,L}}\ensuremath{^{α}}), the F-vector space T(W\ensuremath{_{F,L}}\ensuremath{^{α}}) is independent of the choice of L, and one obtains a system of type (a), hence an E-vector space T(W\ensuremath{^{α}}).\par
EXAMPLE. If W\ensuremath{′} and W\ensuremath{″} are two D-modules of rank n\ensuremath{·}[D:E]\ensuremath{^{1/2}} over E, one may take T \ensuremath{=} Hom(\ensuremath{∧}\ensuremath{^{n}}W\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{F,L}}, \ensuremath{∧}\ensuremath{^{n}}W\ensuremath{″}\ensuremath{_{F,L}}); one obtains a one-dimensional E-vector space \ensuremath{δ}(W\ensuremath{′}, W\ensuremath{″}), and every homomorphism f: W\ensuremath{′} \ensuremath{→} W\ensuremath{″} has a reduced determinant det red(f) \ensuremath{∈} \ensuremath{δ}(W\ensuremath{′}, W\ensuremath{″}).\par
To define c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M), apply this construction to the D-modules H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) and H\ensuremath{_{\overline{D}\overline{R}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M). Set \ensuremath{δ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ}(H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M), H\ensuremath{_{\overline{D}\overline{R}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)). The reduced determinant of the isomorphism of D \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-modules I\ensuremath{^{+}}: H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)\ensuremath{_{ℂ}} \ensuremath{→}\ensuremath{≃} H\ensuremath{_{\overline{D}\overline{R}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)\ensuremath{_{ℂ}} lies in the free rank-one E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-module \ensuremath{δ} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}. Set det red(I\ensuremath{^{+}}) \ensuremath{=} c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)\ensuremath{·}e for a basis e of \ensuremath{δ}.\par
\SectionLead{3. Example: the \ensuremath{ζ}-function.} 3.1. To understand the various realizations of the Tate motive \ensuremath{ℤ}(1), the simplest course is to write \ensuremath{ℤ}(1) \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{1}}(\ensuremath{𝔾}\ensuremath{_{m}}). Since the multiplicative group is not a projective variety, this does not fit Grothendieck’s framework, which instead requires \ensuremath{ℤ}(1) to be defined as the dual of the direct factor H\ensuremath{^{2}}(\ensuremath{ℙ}\ensuremath{^{1}}) of H*(\ensuremath{ℙ}\ensuremath{^{1}}).\par
The realization of \ensuremath{ℤ}(1) in \ensuremath{ℤ}\ensuremath{_{l}}-cohomology is the Tate module T\ensuremath{_{l}}(\ensuremath{𝔾}\ensuremath{_{m}}) of \ensuremath{𝔾}\ensuremath{_{m}}:\par
\ensuremath{ℤ}\ensuremath{_{l}}(1) \ensuremath{=} proj lim \ensuremath{μ}\ensuremath{_{lⁿ}}.\par
In the Hodge realization, H\ensuremath{_{B}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(1)) \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{1}}(\ensuremath{ℂ}*) is isomorphic to \ensuremath{ℤ}—or rather to \ensuremath{ℚ} in rational homology. This group is purely of type (\ensuremath{−}1, \ensuremath{−}1), and F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}1.\par
In the de Rham realization, H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(1)) is the dual of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{𝔾}\ensuremath{_{m}}), isomorphic to \ensuremath{ℚ} and generated by the class of dz/z. The unique period of H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{𝔾}\ensuremath{_{m}}) is\par
(3.1.1)    \ensuremath{∮} dz/z \ensuremath{=} 2\ensuremath{π}i.\par
On \ensuremath{ℤ}\ensuremath{_{l}}(1), arithmetic Frobenius \ensuremath{φ}\ensuremath{_{p}} (p \ensuremath{≠} l) acts by multiplication by p. Geometric Frobenius therefore acts by multiplication by p\ensuremath{^{-1}}; this justifies the identity cited in 1.3:\par
(3.1.2)    L(M(n), s) \ensuremath{=} L(M, n \ensuremath{+} s).\par
Since F\ensuremath{_{∞}} acts as (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}} on H\ensuremath{_{B}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)), H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{ε}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) vanishes for \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}(\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}}, and c\ensuremath{^{ε}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} 1. For \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}}, (3.1.1) gives c\ensuremath{^{ε}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{n}}:\par
(3.1.3)    c\ensuremath{^{ε}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{n}}                 for \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}}, c\ensuremath{^{ε}}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} 1,   \ensuremath{δ}(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{n}}  for \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}(\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}}.\par
3.2. The function \ensuremath{ζ}(s) is the L-function attached to the unit motive \ensuremath{ℤ}(0) \ensuremath{=} H*(Point). The critical integers for \ensuremath{ℤ}(0) are the even integers \ensuremath{>} 0 and the odd integers \ensuremath{≤} 0. Because \ensuremath{ζ}(s) has a pole at s \ensuremath{=} 1, 0 is not a trivial zero, and it would be reasonable to define the critical integers so as to include 0. Equation (3.1.3) and the known values\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{14}{326}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
of \ensuremath{ζ}(n) \ensuremath{=} L(\ensuremath{ℤ}(n)) for critical n verify 1.8: \ensuremath{ζ}(n) is rational for odd n \ensuremath{≤} 0, and is a rational multiple of (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{n}} for even n \ensuremath{≥} 0.\par
\SectionLead{4. Compatibility with the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.} 4.1. Let A be an abelian variety over \ensuremath{ℚ}, of dimension d. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture [15] asserts in particular: (a) L(H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A), 1) is nonzero if and only if A(\ensuremath{ℚ}) is finite. (b) Let \ensuremath{ω} be a generator of H\ensuremath{^{0}}(A, \ensuremath{Ω}\ensuremath{^{d}}). Then L(H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A), 1) is the product of \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{A(ℝ)}} \ensuremath{|}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{|} and a rational number.\par
The motive H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1) is isomorphic to the dual H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A) of H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A); this expresses the existence of a polarization, an autoduality of H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A) with values in \ensuremath{ℤ}(\ensuremath{−}1). By 1.7, c\ensuremath{^{+}}(H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1)) is therefore computed as follows: if \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{1}},\ensuremath{⋯},\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{d}} is a basis of H\ensuremath{^{0}}(A, \ensuremath{Ω}\ensuremath{^{1}}) \ensuremath{=} F\ensuremath{^{+}}H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(A), and c\ensuremath{_{1}},\ensuremath{⋯},c\ensuremath{_{d}} is a basis of H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A(\ensuremath{ℂ}), \ensuremath{ℚ})\ensuremath{^{+}}, then\par
(4.1.1)    c\ensuremath{^{+}}(H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1)) \ensuremath{=} det\ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{i}}, e\ensuremath{_{j}}\ensuremath{⟩}.\par
Again denoting by e\ensuremath{_{i}} a representative cycle, one has \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{i}}, e\ensuremath{_{j}}\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{e_j}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{i}}. Take as (e\ensuremath{_{i}}) a \ensuremath{ℤ}-basis of H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A(\ensuremath{ℝ})\ensuremath{^{\circ}}, \ensuremath{ℤ}) \ensuremath{⊂} H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A(\ensuremath{ℂ}), \ensuremath{ℤ}). The Pontryagin product of the e\ensuremath{_{i}} is represented by the d-cycle A(\ensuremath{ℝ})\ensuremath{^{\circ}} in A(\ensuremath{ℂ}), with a suitable orientation; if \ensuremath{ω} is the exterior product of the \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{i}}, the determinant (4.1.1) is \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{A(ℝ)°}} \ensuremath{ω}. Thus\par
\ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{A(ℝ)}} \ensuremath{|}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{=} [A(\ensuremath{ℝ}): A(\ensuremath{ℝ})\ensuremath{^{\circ}}] \ensuremath{|}\ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{A(ℝ)°}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{|},\par
and 1.8 for H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1) is therefore equivalent to 4.1(b) above.\par
4.2. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture gives the exact value of L(H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A), 1); the description of the rational factor in 4.1(b) in terms of the motive H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1) has the following form: (a) The datum M \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A)(1) is equivalent to that of A up to isogeny. One must begin by choosing A. This amounts to choosing an integral lattice in H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) whose l-adic completions are stable under Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ}). (b) One then chooses \ensuremath{ω}, for example as the exterior product of the elements of a basis of an integral lattice in H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M). This \ensuremath{ω} determines the period c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) and, for each prime p, a rational factor c\ensuremath{_{p}}(M). Almost all c\ensuremath{_{p}}(M) equal 1, and the product formula ensures that c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)\ensuremath{·}\ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{p}} c\ensuremath{_{p}}(M) is independent of \ensuremath{ω}. (c) Another rational number h(M) is defined in terms of cohomological invariants of A; the desired rational number is h(M)\ensuremath{·}\ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{p}} c\ensuremath{_{p}}(M)\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
The invariance of the conjecture under isogeny is, moreover, a nontrivial theorem.\par
4.3. To generalize 4.1(a) to an arbitrary motive M of weight \ensuremath{−}1, one would need an analogue of A(\ensuremath{ℚ}). The group A(\ensuremath{ℚ}) may be interpreted as the group of extensions of \ensuremath{ℤ}(0) by H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A) in the category of 1-motives [6, \S{}10] over \ensuremath{ℚ}. This suggests considering the group of extensions of \ensuremath{ℤ}(0) by M in a category of mixed motives parallel to mixed Hodge structures, but not even a conjectural definition of such a category is available.\par
I shall only observe that, in all the usual cohomology theories, a cycle Y of dimension d, homologous to zero, on a proper algebraic variety\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{15}{327}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
and smooth X determines a torsor under H\ensuremath{^{2d−1}}(X)(d): there is an exact cohomology sequence\par
0 \ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{^{2d−1}}(X)(d) \ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{^{2d−1}}(X \ensuremath{−} Y)(d) --\ensuremath{∂}\ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{_{Y}}\ensuremath{^{2d}}(X)(d) \ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{^{2d}}(X)(d).\par
The cycle Y defines a cohomology class cl(Y) \ensuremath{∈} H\ensuremath{_{Y}}\ensuremath{^{2d}}(X)(d) whose image in H\ensuremath{^{2d}}(X)(d) is zero, and one takes \ensuremath{∂}\ensuremath{^{-1}}cl(Y). This construction is the analogue of assigning a point of the Jacobian to a degree-zero divisor on a curve.\par
\SectionLead{5. Compatibility with the functional equation.} Let E be a number field. In (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*, write \ensuremath{∼} for the equivalence relation defined by the subgroup E*.\par
PROPOSITION 5.1. Let M be a motive over \ensuremath{ℚ} with coefficients in E. Assume the hypotheses of 1.7. Then\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{−d⁻(M)}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{·} c\ensuremath{^{+}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}}(1)).\par
For a free module L of rank n over a commutative ring A, where A is E or E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}, set det L \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∧}\ensuremath{^{n}}L. By localization this definition extends to L projective of finite type; that generalization is not needed for the proof of 5.1. There are canonical isomorphisms\par
(5.1.1)    det(L\ensuremath{^{∨}}) \ensuremath{=} det(L)\ensuremath{^{-1}},\par
and, for any direct factor P of L,\par
(5.1.2)    det(L) \ensuremath{=} det(P) \ensuremath{·} det(L/P).\par
Here \ensuremath{·} denotes a tensor product and \ensuremath{^{-1}} denotes a dual. Sign issues arise; they are best resolved by regarding det(L) as an invertible graded module placed in degree rank L. Since the final results are taken modulo \ensuremath{∼}, we shall not be concerned with them.\par
For X and Y of the same rank, set \ensuremath{δ}(X, Y) \ensuremath{=} Hom(det X, det Y) \ensuremath{=} det(X)\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{·} det(Y). The determinant of f: X \ensuremath{→} Y lies in \ensuremath{δ}(X, Y). Equations (5.1.1) and (5.1.2) give isomorphisms\par
(5.1.3)    \ensuremath{δ}(X, Y) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ}(Y\ensuremath{^{∨}}, X\ensuremath{^{∨}}),\par
and, for F \ensuremath{⊂} X and G \ensuremath{⊂} Y,\par
(5.1.4)    \ensuremath{δ}(X, Y) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ}(F, Y/G) \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{δ}(G, X/F)\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
LEMMA 5.1.5. Under the isomorphism (5.1.3), det(u) \ensuremath{=} det(\ensuremath{^{t}}u).\par
LEMMA 5.1.6. Let F and G be direct factors of X and Y. Suppose that the isomorphism f: X \ensuremath{→} Y induces isomorphisms f\ensuremath{_{F}}: F \ensuremath{→} Y/G and f\ensuremath{_{G}}\ensuremath{^{-1}}: G \ensuremath{→} X/F. Under the isomorphism (5.1.4), det(f) \ensuremath{=} det(f\ensuremath{_{F}}) det(f\ensuremath{_{G}}\ensuremath{^{-1}})\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
The verification of these lemmas is left to the reader. For 5.1.6, note only that, with G\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{=} f\ensuremath{^{-1}}(G) and F\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{=} f(F), one has X \ensuremath{=} F \ensuremath{⊕} G\ensuremath{^{1}} and Y \ensuremath{=} G \ensuremath{⊕} F\ensuremath{^{1}}, and f exchanges F with F\ensuremath{^{1}} and G with G\ensuremath{^{1}}.\par
Apply Lemma 5.1.6 to the complexifications of H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) \ensuremath{⊂} H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) and F\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{⊂} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M). Under the isomorphism (5.1.4), the determinant of I: H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} is the product of the determinant of I\ensuremath{^{+}}: H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{→}\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{16}{328}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
(H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M)/F\ensuremath{^{-}}) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} and the inverse of the determinant of the morphism induced by I\ensuremath{^{-1}}:\par
J\ensuremath{^{-}}: F\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{→} (H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M)/H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}.\par
The morphism J\ensuremath{^{-}} is the transpose of the morphism I\ensuremath{^{-}} for the dual motive \ensuremath{\check{M}}. Applying 5.1.5 and choosing E-bases of the spaces \ensuremath{δ}(X, Y) involved, one finally obtains\par
(5.1.7)    \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{∼} c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) \ensuremath{·} c\ensuremath{^{-}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}})\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
Proposition 5.1 follows by applying to \ensuremath{\check{M}} the following consequence of 3.1:\par
(5.1.8)    c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{−d^±(M)·n}} c\ensuremath{^{±(−1)ⁿ}}(M(n)).\par
For later use, also note the analogous formula\par
(5.1.9)    \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{−d(M)·n}} \ensuremath{δ}(M(n)).\par
5.2. We recall the exact form of the conjectural functional equation for motivic L-functions ([12], [4]). We work in the general case of a motive over a number field k with coefficients in a field E equipped with a complex embedding \ensuremath{σ} (cf. 2.9). First, the general form: (a) For each place v of k, define a local factor L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s). For finite v, the definition L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{σ}Z\ensuremath{_{v}}(M, Nv\ensuremath{^{−s}}), with Z\ensuremath{_{v}}(M, t) \ensuremath{∈} E(t), depends on a compatibility hypothesis analogous to (1.2.1). One has Z\ensuremath{_{v}}(M, t) \ensuremath{=} det(1 \ensuremath{−} F\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{vt}}}, H\ensuremath{_{λ}}(M)\ensuremath{^{I_v}})\ensuremath{^{-1}}. For an infinite place v induced by a complex embedding \ensuremath{τ}, L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) is obtained by decomposing H\ensuremath{_{τ}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E,σ}} \ensuremath{ℂ} as a direct sum of minimal subspaces stable under the projectors defining the Hodge decomposition and, for real v, under F\ensuremath{_{∞}}; one associates to each subspace the “\ensuremath{Γ}-factor” in Table (5.3) and takes their product. For complex v, the minimal subspaces are one-dimensional, of type (p, q). For real v, they are either two-dimensional of type \{(p, q), (q, p)\}, p \ensuremath{≠} q, or one-dimensional of type (p, p), with F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{±}1. Write \ensuremath{Λ}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) for the product of the L\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s). (b) Let \ensuremath{Ψ} be a nontrivial character of the idele-class group \ensuremath{𝔸} \ensuremath{⊗} k/k, with components \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}. For every place v of k, also choose a Haar measure dx\ensuremath{_{v}} on k\ensuremath{_{v}}. Assume that for almost every v, dx\ensuremath{_{v}} gives mass 1 to the integers of k\ensuremath{_{v}}, and that \ensuremath{⊗} dx\ensuremath{_{v}} is the Tamagawa measure, assigning mass 1 to the idele-class group.\par
Define local constants \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}, dx\ensuremath{_{v}}), almost all equal to 1 and each, as a function of s, a constant times an exponential. Let \ensuremath{ε}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) be their product; it is independent of \ensuremath{Ψ} and the dx\ensuremath{_{v}}. (c) The conjectural functional equation is\par
\ensuremath{Λ}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ε}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, s)\ensuremath{Λ}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{\check{M}}, 1 \ensuremath{−} s).\par
Defining the \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}} requires an additional compatibility hypothesis among the H\ensuremath{_{l}}(M). It assigns to v, \ensuremath{σ}, and M an isomorphism class of complex representations of the Weil group W(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}\ensuremath{_{v}}/k\ensuremath{_{v}}) for infinite v, and of the enlarged Weil group W\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}\ensuremath{_{v}}/k\ensuremath{_{v}}) for finite v; one takes the \ensuremath{ε}-factor of [4, 8.12.4], with t \ensuremath{=} p\ensuremath{^{−s}}.\par
For infinite v, this amounts to decomposing H\ensuremath{_{τ}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E,σ}} \ensuremath{ℂ} as in (a), and associating\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{17}{329}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
a factor \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{v}} to each subspace of the decomposition, then taking their product. The table of \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{v}} for a particular choice of \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} and dx\ensuremath{_{v}} is given in 5.3.\par
For finite v, first restrict the representations H\ensuremath{_{l}}(M) to a decomposition group Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}\ensuremath{_{v}}/k\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{⊂} Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}/k), and then to the Weil group W(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}\ensuremath{_{v}}/k\ensuremath{_{v}}). Applying [4, 8.3, 8.4] gives from H\ensuremath{_{l}}(M) an isomorphism class \ensuremath{ρ}\ensuremath{_{l}} of representations of W\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{\bar{k}}\ensuremath{_{v}}/k\ensuremath{_{v}}) over E\ensuremath{_{l}}. It is permissible, and useful, to replace it by its F-semisimplification [4, 8.6]. These representations, as l varies, are required to be compatible: after extending scalars from E\ensuremath{_{l}} to \ensuremath{ℂ} by \ensuremath{\widetilde{σ}}: E\ensuremath{_{λ}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ} extending \ensuremath{σ}, the isomorphism class obtained must be independent of l and \ensuremath{σ}. This is the required isomorphism class.\par
For the reader, we unpack the internal references to [4]. A representation of W\ensuremath{′} consists of a representation \ensuremath{ρ} of the Weil group in GL(V), together with a nilpotent endomorphism N of V. In terms of the local constant of \ensuremath{ρ} in [4, 4.1], that of (\ensuremath{ρ}, N) is\par
\ensuremath{ε}((\ensuremath{ρ}, N), s, \ensuremath{Ψ}, dx) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ε}(\ensuremath{ρ} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{s}}, \ensuremath{Ψ} dx) \ensuremath{·} det(\ensuremath{−}F Nv\ensuremath{^{−s}}, V\ensuremath{^{ρ(I)}}/Ker(N)\ensuremath{^{ρ(I)}}).\par
REMARK 5.2.1. The function of s\par
\ensuremath{ε}((\ensuremath{ρ}, N), s, \ensuremath{Ψ}, dx)L((\ensuremath{ρ}, N)\ensuremath{^{∨}}, 1 \ensuremath{−} s)L((\ensuremath{ρ}, N), s)\ensuremath{^{-1}}\par
is the same for (\ensuremath{ρ}, N) and (\ensuremath{ρ}, 0). Thus the conjectural functional equation for L-functions can be stated assuming compatibility only among the semisimplifications of the restrictions of H\ensuremath{_{l}}(M) to a decomposition group.\par
5.3. The following table gives the local factors and constants attached to the various types of minimal subspaces in the Hodge realization. For the constants, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} and dx\ensuremath{_{v}} are chosen as follows: real v: \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}(x) \ensuremath{=} exp(2\ensuremath{π}ix), measure dx; complex v: \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}(z) \ensuremath{=} exp(2\ensuremath{π}i Tr\ensuremath{_{ℂ/ℝ}}(z)), measure \ensuremath{|}dz \ensuremath{∧} d \ensuremath{\bar{z}}\ensuremath{|}, so that for z \ensuremath{=} x \ensuremath{+} iy these are exp(4\ensuremath{π}ix) and 2dxdy.\par
Use the notation \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℝ}}(s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{π}\ensuremath{^{−s/2}} \ensuremath{Γ}(s/2), \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℂ}}(s) \ensuremath{=} 2 \ensuremath{·} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{−s}} \ensuremath{Γ}(s).\par
place       type                                      \ensuremath{Γ}-factor          constant (for \ensuremath{Ψ}, dx above) complex     (p, q) or (q, p), p \ensuremath{≤} q                   \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℂ}}(s \ensuremath{−} p)       i\ensuremath{^{q−p}} real        \{(p, q), (q, p)\}, p \ensuremath{<} q                   \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℂ}}(s \ensuremath{−} p)       i\ensuremath{^{q−p+1}} (p, p), F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{p+ε}}, \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} 0 or 1     \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℝ}}(s\ensuremath{+}\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{−}p)       i\ensuremath{^{ε}}\par
The case of interest here is k \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}. One may then take \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{∞}}(x) \ensuremath{=} exp(2\ensuremath{π}ix), \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{p}}(x) \ensuremath{=} exp(\ensuremath{−}2\ensuremath{π}ix), using the identification of \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{p}}/\ensuremath{ℤ}\ensuremath{_{p}} with the p-primary part of \ensuremath{ℚ}/\ensuremath{ℤ}; dx\ensuremath{_{∞}} is Lebesgue measure dx, and dx\ensuremath{_{p}} is Haar measure on \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{p}} giving \ensuremath{ℤ}\ensuremath{_{p}} mass 1.\par
PROPOSITION 5.4. If M is critical of weight w, then, modulo a rational number independent of \ensuremath{σ},\par
L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{\check{M}}(1))L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M)\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{−d⁻(M)}} \ensuremath{·} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{−wd(M)/2}}.\par
By 2.5, the L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, ) are independent of \ensuremath{σ}. It is therefore enough to verify 5.4 for a fixed \ensuremath{σ}. The formula is compatible with the substitution M \ensuremath{↦} \ensuremath{\check{M}}(1): \ensuremath{\check{M}}(1) has\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{18}{330}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
weight \ensuremath{−}2 \ensuremath{−} w, its d\ensuremath{^{-}} is d\ensuremath{^{+}}(M), and abbreviating d(M) and d\ensuremath{^{±}}(M) as d and d\ensuremath{^{±}}, one has d \ensuremath{=} d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{+} d\ensuremath{^{-}} and\par
(\ensuremath{−}d\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{−} wd/2) \ensuremath{+} (\ensuremath{−}d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{−} ((\ensuremath{−}2 \ensuremath{−} w)d)/2) \ensuremath{=} 0.\par
It is therefore enough to verify 5.4 for w \ensuremath{≥} \ensuremath{−}1. For an integer s, modulo \ensuremath{ℚ}*,\par
(5.4.1)    \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℝ}}(s) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{−s/2}}       for even s \ensuremath{>} 0, \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℝ}}(s) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{(1−s)/2}}    for odd s, \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{ℂ}}(s) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{−s}}         for s \ensuremath{>} 0.\par
For w \ensuremath{≥} \ensuremath{−}1, the power of 2\ensuremath{π} contributed by each subspace of H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}, as in 5.2(a), is therefore\par
L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(M)       L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}}(1))       L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}}(1))L\ensuremath{_{∞}}(M)\ensuremath{^{-1}} \{(pq), (qp)\}, p \ensuremath{≤} q                  p             \ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}p                   \ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}w (pp), p even \ensuremath{≥} 0, F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}1          p/2           \ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}p/2                 \ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}w/2 (pp), p odd \ensuremath{≥} 0, F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}1           (1\ensuremath{+}p)/2       (\ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}p)/2               \ensuremath{−}1\ensuremath{−}w/2\par
The proposition follows immediately. Set det M \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∧}\ensuremath{^{d(M)}}M, the exterior power over E.\par
PROPOSITION 5.5. \ensuremath{ε}*(M) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{ε}*(det M).\par
For the dx\ensuremath{_{v}} chosen as suggested in 5.4, we prove more precisely the equivalences\par
(5.5.1)    \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}, dx\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(det M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}, dx\ensuremath{_{v}}).\par
Set \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}, dx\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}}\ensuremath{^{-1}}(\ensuremath{σ}, det M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}, dx\ensuremath{_{v}}). This is equivalent to\par
(5.5.2)    \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}})\par
for every automorphism \ensuremath{τ} of \ensuremath{ℂ}.\par
It follows from [4, 5.4] that, if a \ensuremath{∈} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{v}}* has absolute value 1 and (\ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} \ensuremath{·} a)(x) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}(ax), then\par
(5.5.3)    \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} \ensuremath{·} a)   (for \ensuremath{‖}a\ensuremath{‖}\ensuremath{_{v}} \ensuremath{=} 1).\par
For an automorphism \ensuremath{τ} of \ensuremath{ℂ} and finite v, \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} is of the form \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}} \ensuremath{·} a with \ensuremath{‖}a\ensuremath{‖}\ensuremath{_{v}} \ensuremath{=} 1; likewise, \ensuremath{\bar{Ψ}}\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{·} (\ensuremath{−}1).\par
For finite v, the definition of \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{v}} is purely algebraic, so \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{v}}(\ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{v}}), and (5.5.2) follows from (5.5.3).\par
For v \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∞}, one also has \ensuremath{\bar{η}}\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{\bar{Ψ}}\ensuremath{_{∞}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{\bar{σ}}, M, \ensuremath{\bar{Ψ}}\ensuremath{_{∞}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{\bar{σ}}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{∞}}). If \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{∞}} is chosen as in 5.3, \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{∞}} is a power of i independent of \ensuremath{σ}; hence \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{_{∞}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M, \ensuremath{Ψ}\ensuremath{_{∞}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{±}1, independently of \ensuremath{σ}, which proves (5.5.2).\par
THEOREM 5.6. Subject to Conjecture 6.6 on the nature of rank-one motives, Conjecture 2.8 is compatible with the conjectural functional equation of L-functions: one has\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{19}{331}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
L\ensuremath{_{∞}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(M)c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{*}}(M)L\ensuremath{_{∞}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}}(1))c\ensuremath{^{+}}(\ensuremath{\check{M}}(1)).\par
By 5.1, 5.3, and 5.5, this formula is equivalent to\par
(2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{-d^-(M)}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{-d^-(M)}} \ensuremath{·} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{-wd(M)/2}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{*}}(det M).\par
Set D \ensuremath{=} det M and \ensuremath{ε} \ensuremath{=} d\ensuremath{^{-}}(D). Then \ensuremath{δ}(M) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ}(D), d\ensuremath{^{-}}(M) \ensuremath{≡} \ensuremath{ε} (mod 2), and wd(M) is the weight w(D) of D, so that the formula is again equivalent to\par
(5.6.1)    \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{*}}(D) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{w(D)/2}} \ensuremath{·} i\ensuremath{^{ε}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{δ}(D).\par
In 6.5 we shall prove that (5.6.1) holds for a class of rank-one motives which conjecturally (6.6) includes them all.\par
\SectionLead{6. Example: Artin L-functions.} DEFINITION 6.1. The category of Artin motives is the Karoubian envelope of the dual of the category whose objects are zero-dimensional varieties over \ensuremath{ℚ} and whose morphisms are correspondences defined over \ensuremath{ℚ}.\par
By definition, every zero-dimensional variety X defines an Artin motive H(X); H is a fully faithful contravariant functor,\par
H: (zero-dimensional varieties, correspondences) \ensuremath{⟶} (Artin motives),\par
and every Artin motive is a direct factor of some H(X).\par
6.2. Let us make this definition explicit. Let \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} be an algebraic closure of \ensuremath{ℚ}, and let G be the Galois group Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ}). A zero-dimensional variety is the spectrum of a finite product A of number fields, and Galois theory, in the form given to it by Grothendieck, says that the functor\par
X \ensuremath{=} spec(A) \ensuremath{↦} X(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{=} Hom(A, \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}):\par
(category of zero-dimensional varieties over \ensuremath{ℚ} and morphisms of schemes) \ensuremath{⟶} (category of finite sets with a continuous G-action)\par
is an equivalence of categories. The inverse functor sends I to the spectrum of the ring of G-invariant functions from I to \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}.\par
A correspondence from a zero-dimensional variety X to another Y is a formal rational linear combination of connected components of X \ensuremath{×} Y. The map\par
\ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{i}} Z\ensuremath{_{i}} \ensuremath{↦} \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{i}}(characteristic function of Z\ensuremath{_{i}}(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{⊂} (X \ensuremath{×} Y)(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}))\par
identifies correspondences with rational-valued G-invariant functions on (X \ensuremath{×} Y)(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{=} X(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{×} Y(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}), and composition of correspondences with matrix multiplication.\par
Let H be the contravariant functor sending X to the vector space \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} with its natural G-action; a correspondence F: X \ensuremath{→} Y is sent to the morphism F*: \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{Y(\bar{ℚ})}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} whose matrix is \ensuremath{^{t}}F. This functor is fully faithful and identifies the category of Artin motives with that of rational representations of G.\par
6.3. In this model, if \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} is the algebraic closure of \ensuremath{ℚ} inside \ensuremath{ℂ}, the “Betti realization” functor H\ensuremath{_{B}} is the “underlying vector space” functor. The Hodge structure is purely of type (0, 0), and the involution F\ensuremath{_{∞}} is the action of complex conjugation F\ensuremath{_{∞}} \ensuremath{∈} G. Indeed, there is an isomorphism, functorial for correspondences,\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{20}{332}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
H\ensuremath{^{*}}(X(\ensuremath{ℂ}), \ensuremath{ℚ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(ℂ)}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} \ensuremath{=} H(X).\par
The “l-adic realization” functor H\ensuremath{_{l}} is H\ensuremath{_{l}}(V) \ensuremath{=} V \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{l}}. Indeed, there is an isomorphism, functorial for correspondences,\par
H\ensuremath{^{*}}(X(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}), \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{l}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{l}}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{_{l}}.\par
Let us similarly compute the de Rham realization. For X \ensuremath{=} Spec(A), H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(X) \ensuremath{=} A. Since A \ensuremath{=} Hom\ensuremath{_{G}}(X(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}), \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{ℚ}\ensuremath{^{X(\bar{ℚ})}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}})\ensuremath{^{G}}, we obtain\par
(6.3.1)    H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(V) \ensuremath{=} (V \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}})\ensuremath{^{G}}.\par
Formula (6.3.1) realizes H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(V) as a subspace of V \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}. This subspace is a \ensuremath{ℚ}-structure: (V \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}})\ensuremath{^{G}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} \ensuremath{→}\ensuremath{≃} V \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}. After extending scalars to \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}, H\ensuremath{_{B}}(V) and H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(V) are therefore canonically isomorphic. Extending scalars further to \ensuremath{ℂ} gives the isomorphism (0.4.1); this may be checked for V \ensuremath{=} H(X).\par
6.4. Let E be a finite extension of \ensuremath{ℚ}. The category of Artin motives with coefficients in E is obtained from the category of Artin motives as in 2.1. We identify it with the category of finite-dimensional E-vector spaces endowed with a G-action.\par
Rank-one Artin motives with coefficients in E correspond to characters \ensuremath{ε}: G \ensuremath{→} E*. We now compute their periods. Let \ensuremath{ε}: G \ensuremath{→} E* and let f be its conductor; \ensuremath{ε} factors through a character, again denoted \ensuremath{ε}, of the quotient (\ensuremath{ℤ}/f\ensuremath{ℤ})* \ensuremath{=} Gal(\ensuremath{ℚ}(exp(2\ensuremath{π}i/f))/\ensuremath{ℚ}) of G. Let [\ensuremath{ε}] denote the one-dimensional E-vector space E\ensuremath{_{ε}} on which G acts through \ensuremath{ε}. The Gauss sum\par
g \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} \ensuremath{ε}(u) \ensuremath{⊗} exp(2\ensuremath{π}iu/f) \ensuremath{∈} [\ensuremath{ε}] \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}\par
is nonzero and G-invariant; it is an E-basis of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}([\ensuremath{ε}]). The determinant of I: H\ensuremath{_{B}}([\ensuremath{ε}]) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{→}\ensuremath{≃} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}([\ensuremath{ε}]) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}, computed in the bases 1 and g, is g\ensuremath{^{-1}}. For every complex embedding \ensuremath{σ} of E one knows that \ensuremath{σ}g \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{\bar{σ}}g \ensuremath{=} f, a rational number independent of \ensuremath{σ}. Hence\par
(6.4.1)    \ensuremath{δ}([\ensuremath{ε}]) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{∑} \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{-1}}(u) \ensuremath{⊗} exp(\ensuremath{−}2\ensuremath{π}iu/f) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*.\par
PROPOSITION 6.5. Let D be the motive [\ensuremath{ε}](n). It is a rank-one motive over \ensuremath{ℚ} with coefficients in E and weight \ensuremath{−}2n. Write \ensuremath{ε}(\ensuremath{−}1) \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{η}}, with \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{=} 0 or 1. Then\par
\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{*}}(D) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{-n}} i\ensuremath{^{η−n}} \ensuremath{δ}(D).\par
The constant in the functional equation of the Dirichlet L-function\par
L(\ensuremath{σ}, [\ensuremath{ε}], s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} \ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{-1}}(n) \ensuremath{·} n\ensuremath{^{-s}},\par
where \ensuremath{σ} is a complex embedding of E, is known to be\par
\ensuremath{ε}(\ensuremath{σ}, [\ensuremath{ε}], s) \ensuremath{=} i\ensuremath{^{η}} \ensuremath{·} f\ensuremath{^{s}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{∑} \ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{ε}(u)\ensuremath{^{-1}} exp(\ensuremath{−}2\ensuremath{π}iu/f).\par
On the other hand, (5.1.9) gives \ensuremath{δ}(D) \ensuremath{=} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{δ}([\ensuremath{ε}]). Applying (6.4.1), and observing that for integral s \ensuremath{=} n the number f\ensuremath{^{n}} is rational and independent of \ensuremath{σ}, proves the proposition.\par
This proposition verifies (5.6.1) for the motives [\ensuremath{ε}](n). To complete the proof of 5.6, it remains only to state:\par
Conjecture 6.6. Every rank-one motive over \ensuremath{ℚ} with coefficients in E is of the form [\ensuremath{ε}](n), where \ensuremath{ε} is a character of G \ensuremath{=} Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ}) with values among the roots of unity in E, and n is an integer.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{21}{333}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
PROPOSITION 6.7. Conjecture 2.8 is true for Artin L-functions.\par
For Artin motives, the functional equation of the L-functions is available. Moreover, the determinant of an Artin motive, after a Tate twist, is of the type predicted in 6.6. The arguments of Sections 5 and 6 therefore show the compatibility of 2.8 with the functional equation, and it is enough to prove 2.8 for motives V(n), where V is an Artin motive and n \ensuremath{≤} 0 is an integer. If V(n) is critical, F\ensuremath{_{∞}} acts on V by multiplication by \ensuremath{−}(\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{n}} and c\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} 1 (cf. 3.1); one must prove that for every embedding \ensuremath{σ}: E \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ} and every automorphism \ensuremath{τ} of \ensuremath{ℂ},\par
\ensuremath{τ}L(\ensuremath{σ}, V(n)) \ensuremath{=} L(\ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{σ}, V(n)).\par
This follows from Siegel’s results [14]. See [2, 1.2].\par
\SectionLead{7. L-functions attached to modular forms.} 7.1. Put q \ensuremath{=} e\ensuremath{^{2πiz}}, and let f \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{nq}}}\ensuremath{^{n}} be a primitive holomorphic cuspidal modular form (new form) of weight k \ensuremath{≥} 2, conductor N, and character \ensuremath{ε}. The Dirichlet series \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{nn}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}} has an Euler-product expansion whose local factor at p \ensuremath{∤} N is\par
(1 \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{pp}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{ε}(p)p\ensuremath{^{k−1}}p\ensuremath{^{-2s}})\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
Let E be the subfield of \ensuremath{ℂ} generated by the a\ensuremath{_{n}}. The form f should give rise to a rank-two motive M(f) with coefficients in E, of Hodge type \{(k \ensuremath{−} 1, 0), (0, k \ensuremath{−} 1)\}, determinant [\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{-1}}](1 \ensuremath{−} k) in the notation of 6.4, and L-function given by the Dirichlet series \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{nn}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}}.\par
I have not tried to define M(f) as a motive in Grothendieck’s sense. One difficulty is that M(f) appears naturally as a direct factor in the cohomology of a noncompact variety, or as a direct factor in the cohomology of a complete modular curve with coefficients in the direct image of a locally constant sheaf—more properly, a local system of motives—on the finite part of that modular curve. This lies outside Grothendieck’s formalism, but it permits the realizations of M(f) to be defined.\par
7.2. First suppose that k \ensuremath{=} 2 and \ensuremath{ε} is trivial. Let X be the Poincaré upper half-plane, let N be the conductor of f, and let \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N) be the subgroup of SL(2, \ensuremath{ℤ}) consisting of matrices whose reduction modulo N has the form ((*, *), (0, *)). Put\par
\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{nq}}}\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{·} dq/q \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{nq}}}\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{·} 2\ensuremath{π}i dz.\par
The form \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} is a holomorphic differential on the completed curve \ensuremath{\bar{M}}(\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N)) associated with M(\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N)) \ensuremath{=} X/\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N). It is an eigenvector for the Hecke correspondences:\par
(7.2.1)    T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} \ensuremath{=} a\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}}    (for n prime to N),\par
and is characterized up to a factor by (7.2.1). This follows from strong multiplicity one and the theory of primitive forms. The reader may instead supplement (7.2.1) by the analogous condition for n not prime to N, and do the same below; the assertion then becomes elementary, since the completed condition (7.2.1) determines the Taylor expansion of \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} at the cusp i\ensuremath{∞} up to a factor.\par
Abbreviate M(\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N)) to M and \ensuremath{\bar{M}}(\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N)) to \ensuremath{\bar{M}}. These curves have a natural \ensuremath{ℚ}-structure for which the Hecke correspondences are defined over \ensuremath{ℚ}. The form \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} is defined over E, and its conjugate by an automorphism \ensuremath{σ} of \ensuremath{ℂ} is \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σf}}, obtained by applying \ensuremath{σ} to the coefficients.\par
In the language of 2.1(B), define M(f) to be the submotive of H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}})\ensuremath{_{E}} that is the kernel of the endomorphisms T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}} \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{n}}—if one wishes to use only\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{22}{334}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
kernels of projectors, replace T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}} \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{n}} by P(T\ensuremath{_{n}} \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{Δ})\ensuremath{^{*}} for a suitable polynomial P. The motive M(f) has the properties stated in 7.1.\par
In each cohomology theory \ensuremath{ℋ} under consideration, the map\par
(7.2.2)    \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M) \ensuremath{⟶} \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}})\par
is surjective, and the systems of eigenvalues of the T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}} on its kernel do not occur in \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}). The \ensuremath{ℋ}-realization of M(f) is therefore still the common kernel, inside \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} E, of the T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}} \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{n}}.\par
The cohomology group H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M, \ensuremath{ℚ}) carries a mixed Hodge structure of type \{(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0)\}, with H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}, \ensuremath{ℚ}) as its quotient of type \{(0, 1), (1, 0)\}. In particular, (7.2.2) induces an isomorphism on the F\ensuremath{^{1}}-subspaces of the Hodge filtration; every holomorphic differential \ensuremath{ω} on \ensuremath{\bar{M}} therefore defines a compactly supported cohomology class on M. This can be seen directly. If \ensuremath{𝒥} \ensuremath{⊂} \ensuremath{𝒪} is the ideal of the cusps, de Rham cohomology H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{*}}(M) is the hypercohomology on \ensuremath{\bar{M}} of the complex \ensuremath{𝒥} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{Ω}\ensuremath{^{1}}; analytically this complex resolves the constant sheaf \ensuremath{ℂ} on M extended by zero to \ensuremath{\bar{M}}, and H\ensuremath{^{1}} receives H\ensuremath{^{0}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}, \ensuremath{Ω}\ensuremath{^{1}}).\par
For simplicity suppose E \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}, and compute c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M(f)(1)). The motive M(f)(1) is dual to M(f), so c\ensuremath{^{+}} is a period of M(f) by 1.7: one integrates \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} against a rational homology class of \ensuremath{\bar{M}} fixed by F\ensuremath{_{∞}}. Lifting M(f) to \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M) shows that one may instead integrate \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} against a homology class without compact support on M fixed by F\ensuremath{_{∞}}. All nonzero integrals of this type are commensurable.\par
To compute F\ensuremath{_{∞}}, it is useful to write M as the quotient of X\ensuremath{^{±}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{ℝ} by the subgroup of GL(2, \ensuremath{ℤ}) whose reduction modulo N has the form ((*, *), (0, *)). Complex conjugation is induced by z \ensuremath{↦} \ensuremath{\bar{z}}, and the image of i\ensuremath{ℝ}\ensuremath{^{+}} in M(\ensuremath{ℂ}) is a noncompact cycle fixed by F\ensuremath{_{∞}}. The formula\par
L(M(f), 1) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}\ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{0}}\ensuremath{^{i∞}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}}\par
therefore verifies 1.8 for M(f)(1): the right-hand side is either zero or equivalent to c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M(f)(1)).\par
REMARK 7.3. One also has\par
c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M(f)(1)) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{a/b}}\ensuremath{^{i∞}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} \ensuremath{±} \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{−a/b}}\ensuremath{^{i∞}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}}.\par
7.4. For arbitrary \ensuremath{ε} and E, \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{0}}(N) must be replaced by \ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{1}}(N), the subgroup of SL(2, \ensuremath{ℤ}) consisting of matrices whose reduction modulo N has the form ((1, *), (0, 1)). As above, for computing F\ensuremath{_{∞}} it is more convenient to work with X\ensuremath{^{±}} and the subgroup of GL(2, \ensuremath{ℤ}) whose reduction modulo N has the form ((1, *), (0, *)). A dualization also appears, hidden in 7.2 by the symmetry of the correspondence T\ensuremath{_{n}}. For a suitable definition of T\ensuremath{_{n}} one has:\par
(a) M(f) is the common kernel of the T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}} \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{n}} in H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}), where \ensuremath{\bar{M}} \ensuremath{=} X/\ensuremath{Γ}\ensuremath{_{1}}(N).\par
(b) One has \ensuremath{^{t}}T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} \ensuremath{=} a\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} and T\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{*}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} \ensuremath{=} ā\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}}, where ā\ensuremath{_{n}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ε}(n)\ensuremath{^{-1}}a\ensuremath{_{n}}. Thus \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{f}} belongs to the de Rham realization of M(f) \ensuremath{=} M(f)\ensuremath{^{∨}}(\ensuremath{−}1).\par
It follows that c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M(f)(1)) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*/E* \ensuremath{≅} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{Hom(E,ℂ)}}/E* is given by the system of periods\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M(f)(1)) \ensuremath{∼} (\ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{0}}\ensuremath{^{i∞}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σf}})\ensuremath{_{σ}},\par
provided this system is nonzero. If one of these integrals vanishes, they all vanish. This happens exactly when, in the part of noncompact homology\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{23}{335}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
spanned by the cycle i\ensuremath{ℝ}\ensuremath{^{+}} and its transforms under the T\ensuremath{_{n}}, the system of eigenvalues a\ensuremath{_{n}} for the T\ensuremath{_{n}} does not occur. This proves 2.8, and partly 2.7, for M(f)(1).\par
REMARK 7.5. The systems of T\ensuremath{_{n}}-eigenvalues in Ker(\ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M) \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}})) are associated with Eisenstein series, whereas those occurring in \ensuremath{ℋ}\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}) are associated with cusp forms. The two sets are therefore disjoint. It follows that the mixed Hodge structure on H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M, \ensuremath{ℚ}) is a direct sum of Hodge structures: the extension of H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}, \ensuremath{ℚ}) by Ker(H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M, \ensuremath{ℚ}) \ensuremath{→} H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}, \ensuremath{ℚ})) splits. Generalized to any congruence subgroup of SL(2, \ensuremath{ℤ}), this is equivalent to Manin’s theorem [9] that the difference of two cusps always has finite order in the Jacobian (cf. [6, 10.3.4, 10.3.8, and 10.1.3]). The proof just given does not differ in substance from Manin’s.\par
7.6. For arbitrary weight k, the cohomology of \ensuremath{\bar{M}} must be replaced by cohomology with coefficients in a suitable sheaf. To describe the construction, replace M and \ensuremath{\bar{M}} by M\ensuremath{_{n}} and \ensuremath{\bar{M}}\ensuremath{_{n}} for the congruence subgroup \ensuremath{Γ}(n), where n is a multiple of N and n \ensuremath{≥} 3. One then descends to M and \ensuremath{\bar{M}} by taking invariants under a suitable finite group. Let g: \ensuremath{ℰ} \ensuremath{→} M\ensuremath{_{n}} be the universal elliptic curve and j the inclusion M\ensuremath{_{n}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{\bar{M}}\ensuremath{_{n}}. The relevant cohomology is\par
H\ensuremath{^{1}}(\ensuremath{\bar{M}}\ensuremath{_{n}}, j\ensuremath{_{*}}Sym\ensuremath{^{k−2}}(R\ensuremath{^{1}}g\ensuremath{_{*}}\ensuremath{ℚ})).\par
The realizations of M(f) are direct factors of this group, computed in the corresponding cohomology theory. As before they may be lifted to\par
H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}}(M\ensuremath{_{n}}, Sym\ensuremath{^{k−2}}(R\ensuremath{^{1}}g\ensuremath{_{*}}\ensuremath{ℚ})).\par
To compute c\ensuremath{^{±}} of the dual of M(f), one integrates the class in H\ensuremath{_{c}}\ensuremath{^{1}} defined by f against noncompact homology classes on M\ensuremath{_{n}} with coefficients in the local system dual to Sym\ensuremath{^{k−2}}(R\ensuremath{^{1}}g\ensuremath{_{*}}\ensuremath{ℚ}). Taking the cycle that is the image of i\ensuremath{ℝ}\ensuremath{^{+}}, together with various sections of the dual local system forming a basis, gives the Eichler integrals\par
\ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{0}}\ensuremath{^{i∞}} f(q) \ensuremath{·} dq/q \ensuremath{·} (2\ensuremath{π}iz)\ensuremath{^{l}}    (0 \ensuremath{≤} l \ensuremath{≤} k \ensuremath{−} 2),\par
even periods for even l and odd periods for odd l. Critical values L(M(f), n) can be expressed in terms of these periods.\par
PROPOSITION 7.7. Let M be a rank-two motive with coefficients in E and Hodge type \{(a, b), (b, a)\}, where a \ensuremath{≠} b. Then d\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{n}}(M) and c\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} are given by the following formulas:\par
(1) if n \ensuremath{=} 2l \ensuremath{+} 1, then d\ensuremath{^{±}} \ensuremath{=} l \ensuremath{+} 1 and\par
c\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} \ensuremath{=} c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M)\ensuremath{^{(l+1)(l+2)/2}} c\ensuremath{^{∓}}(M)\ensuremath{^{l(l+1)/2}} \ensuremath{δ}(M)\ensuremath{^{l(l+1)/2}};\par
(2) if n \ensuremath{=} 2l, then d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} l \ensuremath{+} 1, d\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} l, and\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} \ensuremath{=} (c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)c\ensuremath{^{-}}(M))\ensuremath{^{l(l+1)/2}} \ensuremath{δ}(M)\ensuremath{^{l(l+1)/2}}, c\ensuremath{^{-}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} \ensuremath{=} (c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)c\ensuremath{^{-}}(M))\ensuremath{^{l(l+1)/2}} \ensuremath{δ}(M)\ensuremath{^{l(l−1)/2}}.\par
This is a question of elementary linear algebra, which we treat by “dimensional analysis.”\par
(a) H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) is a rank-two E-vector space with an involution F\ensuremath{_{∞}} having matrix ((0, 1), (1, 0)) in a suitable basis e\ensuremath{^{+}}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}. The quantities d\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} are the dimensions of the plus and minus parts of the nth symmetric power, with respective bases\par
\{(e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n}}, (e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−2}}(e\ensuremath{^{-}})\ensuremath{^{2}}, …\} and \{(e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−1}}e\ensuremath{^{-}}, (e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−3}}(e\ensuremath{^{-}})\ensuremath{^{3}}, …\}.\par
The stated dimensions follow.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{24}{336}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
(b) Let \ensuremath{ω}, \ensuremath{η} be a basis of the dual of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M), with \ensuremath{ω} annihilating F\ensuremath{^{+}}H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M). The subspace F\ensuremath{^{±}} of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}})\ensuremath{^{∨}} \ensuremath{∼} Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nH}}}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M)\ensuremath{^{∨}} has basis\par
\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n}}, \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n−1}}\ensuremath{η}, …, \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n−d^±+1}}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{^{d^±−1}},\par
and\par
(7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}}    c\ensuremath{^{+}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{∧} (\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n−1}}\ensuremath{η}) \ensuremath{∧} …, (e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{∧} ((e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−2}}(e\ensuremath{^{-}})\ensuremath{^{2}}) \ensuremath{∧} …\ensuremath{⟩},\par
(7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{−}}    c\ensuremath{^{-}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{∧} (\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{n−1}}\ensuremath{η}) \ensuremath{∧} …, ((e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−1}}e\ensuremath{^{-}}) \ensuremath{∧} ((e\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{^{n−3}}(e\ensuremath{^{-}})\ensuremath{^{3}}) \ensuremath{∧} …\ensuremath{⟩}.\par
(c) Put V \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{B}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{∼} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}; this is an E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-module. The formulas above show that c\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} depends only on V as an E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-module, on its basis e\ensuremath{^{+}}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}, on \ensuremath{ω} \ensuremath{∈} V*, and on the image \ensuremath{\bar{η}} of \ensuremath{η} in V*/\ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{⟩}. The d\ensuremath{^{±}}-vector on the left of the pairing in (7.7.1) does not change when \ensuremath{η} is replaced by \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{λ}\ensuremath{ω}. Moreover, \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}, e\ensuremath{^{+}}\ensuremath{⟩} and \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}\ensuremath{⟩} are invertible and \ensuremath{\bar{η}} is a basis of V*/\ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{⟩}. Up to isomorphism, the system (V, e\ensuremath{^{+}}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}, \ensuremath{ω}, \ensuremath{\bar{η}}) is therefore described by\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}, e\ensuremath{^{+}}\ensuremath{⟩},   c\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}\ensuremath{⟩},   \ensuremath{δ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ω} \ensuremath{∧} \ensuremath{η}, e\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{∧} e\ensuremath{^{-}}\ensuremath{⟩}\par
in (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*. Replacing e\ensuremath{^{+}}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}, \ensuremath{ω}, \ensuremath{\bar{η}} by \ensuremath{λ}e\ensuremath{^{+}}, \ensuremath{μ}e\ensuremath{^{-}}, \ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{ω}, \ensuremath{ν}\ensuremath{\bar{η}}/\ensuremath{λ}\ensuremath{μ} replaces c\ensuremath{^{+}}, c\ensuremath{^{-}}, and \ensuremath{δ} by \ensuremath{λ}\ensuremath{α}c\ensuremath{^{+}}, \ensuremath{μ}\ensuremath{α}c\ensuremath{^{-}}, and \ensuremath{ν}\ensuremath{δ}. When c\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} c\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{δ} \ensuremath{=} 1, the right-hand side of (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{±}} lies in \ensuremath{ℚ}*. In general, c\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}} is therefore a rational multiple of the product of c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M), c\ensuremath{^{-}}(M), and \ensuremath{δ}(M)/c\ensuremath{^{+}}(M)c\ensuremath{^{-}}(M), raised to the respective degrees with which e\ensuremath{^{+}}, e\ensuremath{^{-}}, and \ensuremath{\bar{η}} occur in (7.7.1). Half the calculation may be avoided by observing that replacing F\ensuremath{_{∞}} by \ensuremath{−}F\ensuremath{_{∞}} exchanges e\ensuremath{^{+}} and e\ensuremath{^{-}}, hence c\ensuremath{^{+}} and c\ensuremath{^{-}}, preserves \ensuremath{δ}, and exchanges (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}} and (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{−}} when n is odd while preserving them when n is even.\par
For n \ensuremath{=} 2l \ensuremath{+} 1, d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} d\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} l \ensuremath{+} 1:\par
deg \ensuremath{\bar{η}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{±}} \ensuremath{=} 0 \ensuremath{+} 1 \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} l \ensuremath{=} l(l \ensuremath{+} 1)/2, deg e\ensuremath{^{+}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} (2l \ensuremath{+} 1) \ensuremath{+} (2l \ensuremath{−} 1) \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} 1 \ensuremath{=} (l \ensuremath{+} 1)\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{=} deg e\ensuremath{^{-}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{-}}, deg e\ensuremath{^{+}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} 2l \ensuremath{+} (2l \ensuremath{−} 2) \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} 0 \ensuremath{=} l(l \ensuremath{+} 1) \ensuremath{=} deg e\ensuremath{^{-}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}}.\par
For n \ensuremath{=} 2l, d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} l \ensuremath{+} 1 and d\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} l:\par
deg \ensuremath{\bar{η}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} 0 \ensuremath{+} 1 \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} l \ensuremath{=} l(l \ensuremath{+} 1)/2, deg \ensuremath{\bar{η}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} 0 \ensuremath{+} 1 \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} (l \ensuremath{−} 1) \ensuremath{=} l(l \ensuremath{−} 1)/2, deg e\ensuremath{^{±}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} 2l \ensuremath{+} (2l \ensuremath{−} 2) \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} 0 \ensuremath{=} l(l \ensuremath{+} 1), deg e\ensuremath{^{±}} in (7.7.1)\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} (2l \ensuremath{−} 1) \ensuremath{+} (2l \ensuremath{−} 3) \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{⋯} \ensuremath{+} 1 \ensuremath{=} l\ensuremath{^{2}}.\par
7.8. This proposition gives a conjecture for the values at critical integers of L(Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f), s). The formulas are as follows:\par
(7.8.1)    L(\ensuremath{σ}, M(f), s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} \ensuremath{σ}a\ensuremath{_{n}} n\ensuremath{^{-s}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{p}} L\ensuremath{_{p}}(\ensuremath{σ}, M(f), s),\par
where for almost every p,\par
L\ensuremath{_{p}}(M(f), s) \ensuremath{=} (1 \ensuremath{−} a\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{pp}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{ε}(p)p\ensuremath{^{k−1−2s}})\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{=} ((1 \ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{α}'\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{pp}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}})(1 \ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{α}''\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{pp}}}\ensuremath{^{-s}}))\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
Here \ensuremath{ε} is a Dirichlet character. Since \ensuremath{∧}\ensuremath{^{2}}M(f) \ensuremath{=} [\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{^{-1}}](1 \ensuremath{−} k), one obtains\par
(7.8.2)    \ensuremath{δ}(M(f)) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{1−k}} \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u\,mod\,F}} \ensuremath{ε}(u) \ensuremath{⊗} exp(\ensuremath{−}2\ensuremath{π}iu/F),\par
if \ensuremath{ε} has conductor F, and\par
(7.8.3)    L\ensuremath{^{*}}(M(f), m) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{m}} c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M(f)),    \ensuremath{±} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{m}}, for 1 \ensuremath{≤} m \ensuremath{≤} k \ensuremath{−} 1.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{25}{337}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
(7.8.4)    L(\ensuremath{σ}, Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f), s) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{p}} L\ensuremath{_{p}}(\ensuremath{σ}, Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f), s),\par
where for almost every p,\par
L\ensuremath{_{p}}(Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f), s)\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{i=0}}\ensuremath{^{n}} (1 \ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{p}}\{\}\ensuremath{^{i}} \ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{″}\ensuremath{_{p}}\{\}\ensuremath{^{n−i}} p\ensuremath{^{-s}}).\par
Conjecturally, for critical m,\par
L\ensuremath{^{*}}(Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f), m) \ensuremath{∼} (2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{m\,d^±Sym^nM(f)}} \ensuremath{·} c\ensuremath{^{±}}Sym\ensuremath{^{\mathrm{nM}}}(f),    \ensuremath{±} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{−}1)\ensuremath{^{m}},\par
where c\ensuremath{^{±}} and d\ensuremath{^{±}} are given in terms of c\ensuremath{^{±}}(M) and \ensuremath{δ}(M), characterized by (7.8.2) and (7.8.3), through the formulas of 7.7.\par
For numerical evidence supporting this conjecture, see [18].\par
\SectionLead{8. Algebraic Hecke characters.} In [3, paragraph 5], whose notation we shall use, the reader will find the essential definitions concerning algebraic Hecke characters (\ensuremath{=} Grössencharaktere of type A\ensuremath{_{0}}).\par
Conjecture 8.1. Let k and E be two finite extensions of \ensuremath{ℚ}, and let \ensuremath{χ} be an algebraic Hecke character of k with values in E.\par
(i) There exists a rank-one motive M(\ensuremath{χ}) over k, with coefficients in E, such that, for every place \ensuremath{λ} of E, the \ensuremath{λ}-adic representation H\ensuremath{_{λ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) is the one defined by \ensuremath{χ}: geometric Frobenius at a prime \ensuremath{𝔓} prime to the conductor of \ensuremath{χ} and to the residue characteristic l of \ensuremath{λ} acts by multiplication by \ensuremath{χ}(\ensuremath{𝔓}).\par
(ii) This motive is characterized up to isomorphism by this property.\par
(iii) Every rank-one motive is of the form M(\ensuremath{χ}).\par
(iv) Decompose k \ensuremath{⊗} E as a product of fields, k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏} K\ensuremath{_{i}}, and write the algebraic part \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}: k* \ensuremath{→} E* of \ensuremath{χ} in the form\par
\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}(x) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏} N\ensuremath{_{K_i/E}}(x)\ensuremath{^{n_i}}.\par
The decomposition of k \ensuremath{⊗} E induces a decomposition of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) into\par
H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ}))\ensuremath{_{i}} :\ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{k⊗E}} K\ensuremath{_{i}};\par
with this notation, the Hodge filtration is the filtration by\par
\ensuremath{⊕}\ensuremath{_{n_i\,≥\,p}} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ}))\ensuremath{_{i}}.\par
The uniqueness in 8.1(ii) imposes the following formalism on the M(\ensuremath{χ}):\par
(8.1.1)    M(\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{″}) \ensuremath{∼} M(\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{′}) \ensuremath{⊗} M(\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{″}).\par
(8.1.2) If \ensuremath{ι}: E \ensuremath{→} E\ensuremath{′} is a finite extension of E, then M(\ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{χ}) is obtained from M(\ensuremath{χ}) by extension of coefficients from E to E\ensuremath{′}.\par
(8.1.3) If k\ensuremath{′} is a finite extension of k, then M(\ensuremath{χ} \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{k′/k}}) is obtained from M(\ensuremath{χ}) by extension of scalars from k to k\ensuremath{′}.\par
REMARK 8.2. Introduce the notation c \ensuremath{=} complex conjugation, \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} \ensuremath{=} the algebraic closure of \ensuremath{ℚ} in \ensuremath{ℂ}, S \ensuremath{=} Hom(k, \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{=} Hom(k, \ensuremath{ℂ}), and J \ensuremath{=} Hom(E, \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}) \ensuremath{=} Hom(E, \ensuremath{ℂ}). The decomposition of k \ensuremath{⊗} E into the fields K\ensuremath{_{i}} corresponds to the partition of S \ensuremath{×} J into Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ})-orbits.\par
Every algebraic homomorphism \ensuremath{η}: k* \ensuremath{→} E* can be written in the form \ensuremath{∏} N\ensuremath{_{K_i/E}}(x)\ensuremath{^{n_i}}. If the Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ})-orbit of (\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{∈} S \ensuremath{×} J corresponds to K\ensuremath{_{i}}, that is, if \ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{τ}: k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ} factors through K\ensuremath{_{i}}, write n(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}), or simply n(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}), for the integer n\ensuremath{_{i}}. The function n(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is constant on Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/\ensuremath{ℚ})-orbits. If \ensuremath{η} is the algebraic part of a Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}, then in addition\par
(8.2.1)    The integer w \ensuremath{=} n(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{+} n(\ensuremath{η}; c\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is independent of \ensuremath{σ} and \ensuremath{τ}.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{26}{338}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
This is the weight of \ensuremath{χ}, and of M(\ensuremath{χ}). We shall sometimes write n(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) for n(\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}).\par
Conversely, a homomorphism \ensuremath{η} satisfying (8.2.1) is nearly of the form \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}} for a suitable Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}: (a) some power of it is of this form; (b) there is a finite extension \ensuremath{ι}: E \ensuremath{→} E\ensuremath{′} of E such that \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{η} is of this form; (c) there is a finite extension k\ensuremath{′} of k such that \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{k′/k}} is of this form.\par
Rule 8.1(iv) determines the Hodge bigrading of H\ensuremath{_{σ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) from its E-module structure: the direct factor H\ensuremath{_{σ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{E,τ}} \ensuremath{ℂ} of H\ensuremath{_{σ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} has Hodge type (p, q), where p \ensuremath{=} n(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) and q \ensuremath{=} w \ensuremath{−} p \ensuremath{=} n(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, c\ensuremath{τ}).\par
EXAMPLE 8.3. Let A be an abelian variety over k with complex multiplication by E. Suppose H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A) has rank one over E (CM type). It follows from the theory of Shimura and Taniyama that H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A) satisfies condition 8.1(i) for an algebraic Hecke character \ensuremath{χ} of k with values in E, and that the algebraic part \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}} of \ensuremath{χ} is read from the k \ensuremath{⊗} E-module Lie(A):\par
\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}(x) \ensuremath{=} det\ensuremath{_{E}}(x \ensuremath{⊗} 1, Lie(A))\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
EXAMPLE 8.4. Let k be the field of n-th roots of unity, let V be the Fermat hypersurface with projective equation \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{i=0}}\ensuremath{^{m}} X\ensuremath{_{i}}\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{=} 0, and let M be the motive “primitive cohomology in the middle dimension of V\ensuremath{^{m}}.” Let G be the quotient of \ensuremath{μ}\ensuremath{_{n}}\ensuremath{^{m+1}} by its diagonal subgroup. This group acts on V by (\ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{_{i}}) * (X\ensuremath{_{i}}) \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{iX}}}\ensuremath{_{i}}), and on M by transport of structure. Decomposing M by means of the product decomposition of the group algebra \ensuremath{ℚ}[G], one obtains motives satisfying 8.1(i) for suitable algebraic Hecke characters, namely those introduced by Weil in his study of Jacobi sums.\par
EXAMPLE 8.5. The motive \ensuremath{ℤ}(\ensuremath{−}1) satisfies 8.1(i) for \ensuremath{χ} equal to the norm. For \ensuremath{χ} of finite order, a suitable Artin motive satisfies 8.1(i).\par
8.6. For every \ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{∈} S, H\ensuremath{_{σ}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) has rank one over E. Choose a basis e\ensuremath{_{σ}} of each H\ensuremath{_{σ}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})). Besides its E-module structure, the sum of the H\ensuremath{_{σ}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} has a natural k \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{S}}-module structure; altogether it is a free rank-one k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-module, for which e \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} e\ensuremath{_{σ}} is a basis.\par
8.7. The de Rham realization H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) is a free rank-one k \ensuremath{⊗} E-module. Choose a basis \ensuremath{ω}. The sum of the maps I\ensuremath{_{σ}}: H\ensuremath{_{σ}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{k,σ}} \ensuremath{ℂ} is the isomorphism (0.4) of k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-modules\par
I: \ensuremath{⊕}\ensuremath{_{σ}} H\ensuremath{_{σ}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}  \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}}  H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}(M(\ensuremath{χ})) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{ℚ}} \ensuremath{ℂ}.\par
Put p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ω}/I(e) \ensuremath{∈} (k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*. This period depends on \ensuremath{χ}, \ensuremath{ω}, and e. Modulo (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)* and E\ensuremath{^{*S}}, it depends only on \ensuremath{χ}. Write p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}), or simply p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}), for the component indexed by (\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) of its image under the isomorphism k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{S×J}}.\par
8.8. Let A be as in 8.3 and calculate the periods p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}), modulo \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}*, for the motive H\ensuremath{^{1}}(A). First extend scalars from k to \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} using \ensuremath{σ}. If n(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} 1, there is a holomorphic 1-form \ensuremath{ω} defined over \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}} such that u*\ensuremath{ω} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{τ}(u)\ensuremath{ω} for u \ensuremath{∈} E, and, for Z \ensuremath{∈} H\ensuremath{_{1}}(A(\ensuremath{ℂ})), one has p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{∫}\ensuremath{_{Z}} \ensuremath{ω}. The general case follows from\par
p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{·} p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, c\ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{∼} 2\ensuremath{π}i.\par
8.9. Conjecture 8.1(ii) asserts in particular that two motives satisfying 8.1(i) have the same period p. For the motives of 8.4, the periods are expressed\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{27}{339}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
in terms of values of the \ensuremath{Γ} function and, when working modulo \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}*, 8.1 suggests B. Gross’s conjecture [7] relating certain periods to products of \ensuremath{Γ}-values.\par
Comparison of 8.4 and 8.5 leads to Conjectures 8.11 and 8.13 below. The result announced after 0.10 proves them.\par
8.10. Let N be an integer, k \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}(exp(2\ensuremath{π}i/N)), \ensuremath{𝔓} a prime ideal of k prime to N, k\ensuremath{_{𝔓}} its residue field, and q \ensuremath{=} N\ensuremath{𝔓} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{|}k\ensuremath{_{𝔓}}\ensuremath{|}. Let t denote the inverse of reduction modulo \ensuremath{𝔓}, from the N-th roots of unity in k\ensuremath{_{𝔓}} to those in k.\par
For a \ensuremath{∈} N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ}, a \ensuremath{≠} 0, consider the Gauss sum\par
g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{x∈k_𝔓*}} t(x\ensuremath{^{−a(q−1)}}) \ensuremath{Ψ}(x).\par
The sum is over k\ensuremath{_{𝔓}}*, and \ensuremath{Ψ}: k\ensuremath{_{𝔓}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ}* is a nontrivial additive character.\par
Let \ensuremath{𝐚} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} n(a)\ensuremath{δ}\ensuremath{_{a}} in the free abelian group with basis N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ} \ensuremath{−} \{0\}. If \ensuremath{∑} n(a)a \ensuremath{=} 0, the product of the g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ})\ensuremath{^{n(a)}} is independent of \ensuremath{Ψ}, and set\par
g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{a}} g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ})\ensuremath{^{n(a)}}.\par
Weil [16] proved that, as a function of \ensuremath{𝔓}, g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) is an algebraic Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} of k with values in k. Let \ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩} be the representative between 0 and 1 of a in \ensuremath{ℤ}/N. If \ensuremath{𝐚} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} n(a)\ensuremath{δ}\ensuremath{_{a}} satisfies\par
(*)    For every u \ensuremath{∈} (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N)*, \ensuremath{∑} n(a)\ensuremath{⟨}ua\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} 0,\par
