Weil’s determination of the algebraic part of \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} implies that \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} has finite order; write \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} also for the character of Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/k) whose value at geometric Frobenius at \ensuremath{𝔓} is \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}}(\ensuremath{𝔓}).\par
Put \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩})\ensuremath{^{n(a)}}. A first part of the conjecture, the algebraicity of \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}) when \ensuremath{𝐚} satisfies (*), was proved by Koblitz and Ogus; see the appendix. More precisely, one would like:\par
Conjecture 8.11. If \ensuremath{𝐚} satisfies (*), then \ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}}(\ensuremath{σ}) \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}) for every \ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{∈} Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/k).\par
If \ensuremath{𝐚} is invariant under a subgroup H of (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N)*, 8.11 can be sharpened by replacing Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/k) with Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/k\ensuremath{^{H}}), and by using SGA 4\ensuremath{^{1/2}} 6.5 to define a character of this group with values in the roots of unity of k\ensuremath{^{H}}. This is done below.\par
8.12. Let H be a subgroup of (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N)*, \ensuremath{𝔓} a prime ideal of k\ensuremath{^{H}} prime to N, \ensuremath{κ} its residue field, and \ensuremath{Ψ}: \ensuremath{κ} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ}* a nontrivial additive character. For a \ensuremath{∈} N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ} \ensuremath{−} \{0\}, let \ensuremath{𝔓}\ensuremath{_{a,i}} be the prime ideals of k\ensuremath{^{H}}(exp(2\ensuremath{π}ia)) above \ensuremath{𝔓}. If \ensuremath{κ}\ensuremath{′} is the residue field at \ensuremath{𝔓}\ensuremath{_{a,i}} and \ensuremath{|}\ensuremath{κ}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{=} q\ensuremath{′}, write g(\ensuremath{𝔓}\ensuremath{_{a,i}}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ}) for the Gauss sum\par
\ensuremath{−} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{x∈κ′*}} t(x\ensuremath{^{−a(q′−1)}}) \ensuremath{Ψ}(Tr\ensuremath{_{κ′/κ}}x).\par
The product g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{i}} g(\ensuremath{𝔓}\ensuremath{_{a,i}}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ}) depends only on the H-orbit of a.\par
Let \ensuremath{𝐚} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} n(a)\ensuremath{δ}\ensuremath{_{a}} be H-invariant and satisfy \ensuremath{∑} n(a)a \ensuremath{=} 0. For every H-orbit O in N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ} \ensuremath{−} \{0\}, write n(O) for the constant value of n(a) on O, and put\par
g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{a\,mod\,H}} g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, a, \ensuremath{Ψ})\ensuremath{^{n(a)}}.\par
As a function of \ensuremath{𝔓}, g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) is an algebraic Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} of k\ensuremath{^{H}} with values in k\ensuremath{^{H}}. To prove this, by additivity one reduces to n(a) \ensuremath{≥} 0. Apply [3, 6.5] with F \ensuremath{=} k\ensuremath{^{H}}, \ensuremath{\bar{F}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}, k equal to the present k, and I a disjoint union of H-orbits, with n(O) copies of O. For i \ensuremath{∈} I whose image in N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ} is a/N, take \ensuremath{λ}\ensuremath{_{i}} to be the composite\par
\ensuremath{\widehat{ℤ}}(1)\ensuremath{_{F}} \ensuremath{→} (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N)(1)\ensuremath{_{F}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{μ}\ensuremath{_{N}}(k) \ensuremath{→}\ensuremath{^{x↦x^a}} k*.\par
The resulting Hecke character is the product of \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} with the “signature” character of the\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{28}{340}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
permutation representation of H on I\ensuremath{″}. A special case of this result already appears in Weil [17]. The character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} of 8.10 is the composite of the \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{𝐚}} above with the norm N\ensuremath{_{k/k^H}}.\par
Conjecture 8.13. Let \ensuremath{𝔓} be a prime ideal of k\ensuremath{^{H}} prime to N, and let F\ensuremath{_{𝔓}} be a geometric Frobenius at \ensuremath{𝔓}. If the H-invariant \ensuremath{𝐚} satisfies (*), then\par
F\ensuremath{_{𝔓}}\ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{=} g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) \ensuremath{·} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚}).\par
In particular, if the group of roots of unity of k\ensuremath{^{H}} has order N\ensuremath{′}, then \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚})\ensuremath{^{N′}} \ensuremath{∈} k\ensuremath{^{H}}.\par
One can deduce from 8.13 the following, apparently more general, variant. Replace condition (*) by\par
(*\ensuremath{′})    \ensuremath{∑} n(a)\ensuremath{⟨}ua\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} k,    an integer independent of u \ensuremath{∈} (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N)*.\par
The Hecke character N\ensuremath{𝔓}\ensuremath{^{−k}} \ensuremath{·} g(\ensuremath{𝔓}, \ensuremath{𝐚}) then has finite order. Identify it with a character \ensuremath{χ} of Gal(\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}/k\ensuremath{^{H}}); one expects\par
\ensuremath{σ}((2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{−k}} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚})) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}(\ensuremath{σ}) \ensuremath{·} ((2\ensuremath{π}i)\ensuremath{^{−k}} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{𝐚})).\par
8.14. If k is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field—that is, in the terminology used here, a field of CM type—Shimura [13] determined the critical values of the L-functions of algebraic Hecke characters of k up to multiplication by an algebraic number. He expresses them in terms of periods of CM abelian varieties with complex multiplication by k. In the remainder of the section, we show that his theorem is compatible with Conjecture 2.8, which expresses them in terms of periods of rank-one motives over k.\par
8.15. Let \ensuremath{χ} and M(\ensuremath{χ}) be as in 8.1. Exclude the case 8.5 and suppose R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) satisfies 1.7. Then k is totally imaginary, and the Hodge numbers h\ensuremath{^{p,p}} vanish: with the notation of 8.1 and 8.2, no n\ensuremath{_{i}} equals w/2. Our first task is to compute c\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) in terms of the periods p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}). Recall that it is the determinant of the isomorphism of E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-modules\par
I\ensuremath{^{+}}: H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}  \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}}  H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ},\par
calculated in bases defined over E.\par
Choose the e\ensuremath{_{σ}} of 8.6 so that F\ensuremath{_{∞}}e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{=} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}}. The vectors e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{±} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}} then form a basis of H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{±}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊂} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{BR}}}\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M\ensuremath{_{χ}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{⊕}\ensuremath{_{σ∈S}}H\ensuremath{_{σ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}). Note that d\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} d\ensuremath{^{-}} \ensuremath{=} ½[k:\ensuremath{ℚ}]. Let \ensuremath{\bar{S}} be the quotient of S by Gal(\ensuremath{ℂ}/\ensuremath{ℝ}). To calculate c\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} det(I\ensuremath{^{+}}), use the basis (e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{+} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}}) of H\ensuremath{_{B}}\ensuremath{^{+}}, indexed by \ensuremath{\bar{S}}.\par
By 8.1(iv), the Hodge filtration of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DRR}}}\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DRM}}}(\ensuremath{χ}) is read from its k \ensuremath{⊗} E-module structure. Let (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}} be the direct factor of k \ensuremath{⊗} E that is the product of the K\ensuremath{_{i}} with n\ensuremath{_{i}} \ensuremath{<} w/2. The quotient H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) is the corresponding direct factor:\par
H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DRM}}}(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{⊗}\ensuremath{_{k⊗E}} (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}}.\par
Let \ensuremath{ω} be as in 8.7, and use the k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{S×J}}-module structure of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DRM}}}(\ensuremath{χ}) to decompose \ensuremath{ω} as \ensuremath{ω} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σ,τ}}. By definition I(e\ensuremath{_{σ}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{τ}} p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ},\ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σ,τ}}, hence\par
I\ensuremath{^{+}}(e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{+} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,τ)<w/2}} p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ},\ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σ,τ}} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(cσ,τ)<w/2}} p\ensuremath{′}(c\ensuremath{σ},\ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{cσ,τ}}.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{29}{341}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
This is the sum, indexed by \ensuremath{τ} \ensuremath{∈} J, of terms p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σ,τ}} when n(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{<} w/2, and p\ensuremath{′}(c\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{cσ,τ}} when n(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{>} w/2. For \ensuremath{\bar{σ}} \ensuremath{∈} \ensuremath{\bar{S}} represented by \ensuremath{σ}, put\par
\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,τ)<w/2}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{σ,τ}} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(cσ,τ)<w/2}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{cσ,τ}}.\par
The vectors I\ensuremath{^{+}}(e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{+} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}}) are multiples of the \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}} by elements of E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}; thus the \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}} form a basis of H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}}. In the bases e\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{+} e\ensuremath{_{cσ}} and \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}}, the matrix of I\ensuremath{^{+}} is diagonal, and its determinant det\ensuremath{′}(I\ensuremath{^{+}}) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})* \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{*J}} has coordinates\par
det\ensuremath{′}(I\ensuremath{^{+}})\ensuremath{_{τ}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,τ)<w/2}} p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}}.\par
Consider the maps E\ensuremath{^{\bar{S}}} \ensuremath{→} E\ensuremath{^{S}} given by 1\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}} \ensuremath{↦} 1\ensuremath{_{σ}} \ensuremath{+} 1\ensuremath{_{cσ}}, for \ensuremath{\bar{σ}} the image of \ensuremath{σ}; the isomorphism E\ensuremath{^{S}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} k \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} induced by k \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{≅} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{S}}; and the projection of k \ensuremath{⊗} E onto (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}}. Their composite is an isomorphism of E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}-modules\par
E\ensuremath{^{\bar{S}}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}  \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}}  (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}.\par
Let D(\ensuremath{χ}) be its determinant, calculated in bases defined over E on both sides. Identifying H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}} with k \ensuremath{⊗} E by means of the basis \ensuremath{ω}, this is the determinant of the identity map on H\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{DR}}}\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}, calculated in the basis \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{\bar{σ}}} at the source and in a basis defined over E at the target. Let D\ensuremath{_{τ}}(\ensuremath{χ}) denote its components in \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{J}}. Since c\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{=} det\ensuremath{′}(I\ensuremath{^{+}}) \ensuremath{·} D(\ensuremath{χ}), one obtains:\par
PROPOSITION 8.16. One has\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}}R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}}M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} ( \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,τ)<w/2}} p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{·} D\ensuremath{_{τ}}(\ensuremath{χ}) )\ensuremath{_{τ∈J}}.\par
REMARK 8.17. Suppose k is of CM type, a quadratic extension of the totally real field k\ensuremath{_{0}}. Then \ensuremath{\bar{S}} identifies with the set of complex embeddings of k\ensuremath{_{0}}, and the diagram\par
\begin{D030Diagram}
E^{S̄} ⊗ ℂ  ──∼──▶  k₀ ⊗ E ⊗ ℂ
     │                         │
     ▼                         ▼
E^S ⊗ ℂ     ──∼──▶  k ⊗ E ⊗ ℂ  ──▶  (k ⊗ E)^+ ⊗ ℂ
\end{D030Diagram}
commutes. The composite k\ensuremath{_{0}} \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{→} (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}} is therefore an isomorphism, and D(\ensuremath{χ}) is also the determinant of E\ensuremath{^{\bar{S}}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} k\ensuremath{_{0}} \ensuremath{⊗} E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} obtained by extending scalars from \ensuremath{ℚ} to E in the isomorphism \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{\bar{S}}} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} k\ensuremath{_{0}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ}. Thus D(\ensuremath{χ}), well defined modulo E*, has a representative in (\ensuremath{ℚ} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})* \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ}* \ensuremath{⊂} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*, namely the determinant of the inverse of the matrix (\ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{α}), where \ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{∈} \ensuremath{\bar{S}} and \ensuremath{α} runs through a basis of k\ensuremath{_{0}} over \ensuremath{ℚ}. The isomorphism \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{\bar{S}}} \ensuremath{\widetilde{→}} k\ensuremath{_{0}} \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ} transforms the quadratic form \ensuremath{∑}x\ensuremath{_{σ}}\ensuremath{^{2}} into Tr(xy). Hence (det(\ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{α}))\ensuremath{^{2}} identifies with the discriminant of k\ensuremath{_{0}}:\par
D(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{∼} a square root of the discriminant of k\ensuremath{_{0}}.\par
8.18. Let p\ensuremath{″}(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) denote the image of p\ensuremath{′}(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) in \ensuremath{ℂ}*/\ensuremath{\bar{ℚ}}*. It depends only on \ensuremath{χ}, \ensuremath{σ}, and \ensuremath{τ}. If an algebraic homomorphism \ensuremath{η}: k* \ensuremath{→} E* satisfies (8.2.1), some power of it is the algebraic part of a Hecke character: \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{^{N}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}. Moreover, if \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{″}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}, then \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{′} and \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{″} differ only by a finite-order character, and \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{^{M}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{″}\ensuremath{^{M}} for a suitable M. It follows from (8.1.1) that p\ensuremath{″}(\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{^{M}}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p\ensuremath{″}(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{M}}, which permits the following unambiguous definition:\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{30}{342}{FRENCH MAIN BODY}
p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{χ}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})\ensuremath{^{1/N}},    when \ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{^{N}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}.\par
These periods satisfy the following formalism:\par
(8.18.1) p(\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{″}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{′}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ})p(\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{″}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}).\par
(8.18.2) p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is unchanged when E is replaced by an extension E\ensuremath{′} and \ensuremath{τ} by one of its extensions to E\ensuremath{′}.\par
(8.18.3) p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is unchanged when k is replaced by an extension k\ensuremath{′}, \ensuremath{σ} by one of its extensions to k\ensuremath{′}, and \ensuremath{χ} by \ensuremath{χ} \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{k′/k}}.\par
(8.18.4) If \ensuremath{α} is an automorphism of k and \ensuremath{β} an automorphism of E, then\par
p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{β}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{^{-1}}; \ensuremath{σ}\ensuremath{α}\ensuremath{^{-1}}, \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{β}\ensuremath{^{-1}}).\par
(8.18.5) The complex conjugate of p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{\bar{σ}}, \ensuremath{\bar{τ}}).\par
(8.18.6) For k \ensuremath{=} F \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℚ}, p(Id; Id, Id) \ensuremath{=} 2\ensuremath{π}i.\par
Formulas (8.15.1)–(8.15.3) follow from (8.1.1)–(8.1.3); (8.18.4) and (8.18.5) follow by transport of structure; and (8.18.6) follows from (8.5).\par
8.19. Let \ensuremath{η}: k* \ensuremath{→} E* be a homomorphism satisfying (8.2.1). Suppose also that n(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) is never w/2, which makes it possible to define (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}} as in 8.15. Define \ensuremath{η}*: E* \ensuremath{→} k* by\par
\ensuremath{η}*(y) \ensuremath{=} det\ensuremath{_{k}}(1 \ensuremath{⊗} y, (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}}).\par
This homomorphism again satisfies (8.2.1), and\par
n(\ensuremath{η}*; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} 1    if n(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{<} w/2, 0    if n(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{>} w/2.\par
If \ensuremath{η}* is the algebraic part of a Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}*, then M(\ensuremath{χ}*) is the H\ensuremath{^{1}} of an abelian variety over E with complex multiplication by k, whose Lie algebra, as a k \ensuremath{⊗} E-module, is isomorphic to (k \ensuremath{⊗} E)\ensuremath{^{+}}.\par
PROPOSITION 8.20. Under the hypotheses and notation of 8.19, regard E as a subfield of \ensuremath{ℂ} and write 1 for the identity embedding E \ensuremath{↪} \ensuremath{ℂ}. Then\par
\ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,1)<w/2}} p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, 1) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{σ}} p(\ensuremath{η}*; 1, \ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{^{n(η;σ,1)}}.\par
If \ensuremath{ι}: E \ensuremath{→} E\ensuremath{′} \ensuremath{⊂} \ensuremath{ℂ} is a finite extension of E, the left-hand side does not change when \ensuremath{η} is replaced by \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{η}, by (8.18.2). One has (\ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{η})* \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{η}* \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{E′/E}}; by (8.18.3), the right-hand side is likewise unchanged.\par
If \ensuremath{ι}: k \ensuremath{→} k\ensuremath{′} is a finite extension of degree d, the left-hand side is raised to the d-th power when k is replaced by k\ensuremath{′} and \ensuremath{η} by \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{k′/k}}: a complex embedding of k is induced by d embeddings of k\ensuremath{′}, and (8.18.3) applies. The same holds for the right-hand side, by (8.18.2) and the equality (\ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} N\ensuremath{_{k′/k}})* \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{η}*.\par
These compatibilities reduce us to the case in which E is Galois and k is isomorphic to E. For each isomorphism \ensuremath{ω} from k to E, put n(\ensuremath{ω}) \ensuremath{=} n(\ensuremath{η}; 1 \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}, 1). Writing the group of homomorphisms k* \ensuremath{→} E* additively, \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑} n(\ensuremath{ω})\ensuremath{ω}. Since p(\ensuremath{η}; 1 \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}, 1) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{-1}}; 1, 1), by (8.15.4), one obtains\par
(8.20.1)    \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{n(σ,1)<w/2}} p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, 1) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{n(ω)<w/2}} p(\ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{-1}}; 1, 1) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(ω)<w/2}} \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{-1}}; 1, 1).\par
On the other hand,\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{31}{343}{SOURCE ENGLISH KOBLITZ OGUS APPENDIX}
\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(ω)<w/2}} \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(ω₁)<w/2;\,ω₂}} n(\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}}) \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{1}}\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{ω₂}} n(\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}}) \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{n(ω₁)<w/2}} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{1}}\ensuremath{^{-1}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{ω₂}} n(\ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}}) \ensuremath{ω}\ensuremath{_{2}} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{η}*.\par
This permits (8.20.1) to be continued as\par
\ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{ω}} p(\ensuremath{ω} \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{η}*; 1, 1)\ensuremath{^{n(ω)}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{ω}} p(\ensuremath{η}*; 1, 1 \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{ω})\ensuremath{^{n(ω)}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{σ}} p(\ensuremath{η}*; 1, \ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{^{n(η;σ,1)}},\par
(a new application of 8.15.4), and proves 8.20.\par
8.21. Combining 8.16 and 8.20, one obtains, for the component of index 1 of\par
c\ensuremath{^{+}} R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}} M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{∈} (E \ensuremath{⊗} \ensuremath{ℂ})*/E* \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ℂ}\ensuremath{^{*J}}/E*,\par
the following expression, modulo \ensuremath{\bar{Q}}*:\par
c\ensuremath{_{1}}\ensuremath{^{+}} R\ensuremath{_{k/ℚ}} M(\ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{σ}} p(\ensuremath{χ}*\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}; 1, \ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{^{−n(χ;σ,1)}}.\par
If \ensuremath{χ} (i.e., M(\ensuremath{χ})) is critical, Conjecture 2.8 therefore asserts that\par
L(1 \ensuremath{∘} \ensuremath{χ}, 0) \ensuremath{∼} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{σ}} p(\ensuremath{χ}*\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}}; 1, \ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{^{−n(χ;σ,1)}}    (mod \ensuremath{\bar{Q}}*).\par
For E sufficiently large, \ensuremath{χ}*\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{alg}}} is the algebraic part of a Hecke character \ensuremath{χ}*, and the periods are interpreted as periods of abelian integrals (8.19), (8.3). The resulting statement is the one Shimura proved when k is of CM type, or is abelian over a field of CM type (with a restriction on the weight).\par
REMARK 8.22. If \ensuremath{η} : k* \ensuremath{→} E* satisfies (8.2.1), there are subfields k\ensuremath{′} of k and E\ensuremath{′} of E, each either of CM type or equal to \ensuremath{ℚ}, an inclusion \ensuremath{ι} : E\ensuremath{′} \ensuremath{→} E, and a factorization \ensuremath{η} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{ι}\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{′}N\ensuremath{_{k/k′}}. One then has p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η}\ensuremath{′}; \ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{|} k\ensuremath{′}, \ensuremath{τ} \ensuremath{|} E\ensuremath{′}).\par
If now k and E are of CM type (or \ensuremath{ℚ}), and c again denotes their complex conjugation, then c\ensuremath{σ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{σ}c, c\ensuremath{τ} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{τ}c, and \ensuremath{η}c \ensuremath{=} c\ensuremath{η}; hence\par
p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}\ensuremath{\bar{)}} \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η}; c\ensuremath{σ}, c\ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}c, \ensuremath{τ}c) \ensuremath{=} p(c\ensuremath{η}c\ensuremath{^{-1}}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{η}; \ensuremath{σ}, \ensuremath{τ}).\par
Thus the periods, a priori in \ensuremath{ℂ}*/\ensuremath{\bar{Q}}*, are real, i.e., lie in \ensuremath{ℝ}*/(\ensuremath{\bar{Q}}* \ensuremath{∩} \ensuremath{ℝ}*).\par
REMARK 8.23. Let G be the Galois group of the union of the CM-type extensions of \ensuremath{ℚ} in \ensuremath{\bar{Q}} \ensuremath{⊂} \ensuremath{ℂ}, and let c \ensuremath{∈} G be complex conjugation. It is a central element of G. If \ensuremath{φ} is a locally constant integer-valued function on G, put \ensuremath{φ}*(x) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{φ}(xc). Suppose that \ensuremath{φ} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{φ}* is constant. Let G\ensuremath{_{1}} be a finite quotient of G through which \ensuremath{φ} factors as a function \ensuremath{φ}\ensuremath{_{1}} on G\ensuremath{_{1}}, and let k be the corresponding field. The hypothesis means that the endomorphism \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{φ}\ensuremath{_{1}}(\ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{σ} of k* satisfies (8.2.1). The period p(\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{φ}\ensuremath{_{1}}(\ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{σ}; 1, 1) is independent of the choice of G\ensuremath{_{1}}; put P(\ensuremath{φ}) \ensuremath{=} p(\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{φ}\ensuremath{_{1}}(\ensuremath{σ})\ensuremath{σ}; 1, 1). The functional P is a homomorphism into \ensuremath{ℂ}*/\ensuremath{\bar{Q}}* from the group of locally constant integer-valued functions on G satisfying \ensuremath{φ} \ensuremath{+} \ensuremath{φ}* \ensuremath{=} constant.\par
Appendix by N. Koblitz and A. Ogus. Algebraicity of some products of values of the \ensuremath{Γ} function. Let A\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{=} N\ensuremath{^{-1}}\ensuremath{ℤ}/\ensuremath{ℤ} \ensuremath{−} \{0\}, and let U\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{ℤ}/N\ensuremath{ℤ})* operate on A\ensuremath{_{N}} in the obvious way. If f : A\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ}, define \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} : U\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ} by\par
\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩}(u) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{a∈A_N}} \ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩}f(ua),\par
where \ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩} denotes the representative of a between 0 and 1.\par
We first compute H\ensuremath{_{Q}} \ensuremath{=} \{f : A\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℚ} : \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} is constant\}.\par
EXAMPLE. If n is a divisor of N and a \ensuremath{∈} A\ensuremath{_{N}}, consider the set\par
S\ensuremath{_{n,a}} \ensuremath{=} [\{a \ensuremath{+} k/n : k \ensuremath{=} 0, 1, …, n \ensuremath{−} 1\} \ensuremath{∪} \{\ensuremath{−}na\}] \ensuremath{∩} A\ensuremath{_{N}}.\par
It is easy to see that its characteristic function \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{n,a}} is in H\ensuremath{_{Q}}. Note that S\ensuremath{_{1,a}} \ensuremath{=} \{a, \ensuremath{−}a\}.\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{32}{344}{SOURCE ENGLISH KOBLITZ OGUS APPENDIX}
PROPOSITION. H\ensuremath{_{Q}} is generated by \{\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{n,a}} : n \ensuremath{=} 1 or n is prime and na \ensuremath{≠} 0\}.\par
PROOF. The orbits of A\ensuremath{_{N}} under the action of U\ensuremath{_{N}} correspond to the divisors d of N with 1 \ensuremath{<} d \ensuremath{≤} N: each orbit can be written uniquely in the form U\ensuremath{_{N}}(1/d). The stabilizer subgroup I\ensuremath{_{d}} of 1/d is \{u \ensuremath{∈} U\ensuremath{_{N}} : u \ensuremath{≡} 1 mod d\} and the orbit of 1/d is canonically isomorphic to U\ensuremath{_{d}}. Thus, a function f on A\ensuremath{_{N}} is determined by the collection of functions f\ensuremath{_{d}} : U\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℚ} defined by f\ensuremath{_{d}}(v) \ensuremath{=} f(v/d).\par
To prove the proposition, we first complexify, so as to be able to work with characters of U\ensuremath{_{N}}.\par
LEMMA. If f : A\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℂ} and if \ensuremath{χ} is a character of U\ensuremath{_{N}}, then the inner product of \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} and \ensuremath{χ} is given by:\par
(\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{d}} L(0, \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}})\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{·} (f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}),\par
where the sum is taken over those divisors d of N such that \ensuremath{χ} is pulled back from a character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}} of U\ensuremath{_{d}}.\par
PROOF. We have\par
(\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈U_N}} \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩}(u)\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{a∈A_N}} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈U_N}} \ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩}f(ua)\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{d∣N}} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{v∈U_d}} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈U_N}} \ensuremath{⟨}v/d\ensuremath{⟩}f\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dv}}})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u),\par
where u\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{∈} U\ensuremath{_{d}} is the image of u.\par
Now if we choose a set U\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{⊆} U\ensuremath{_{N}} of coset representatives for U\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} U\ensuremath{_{d}}, we can write:\par
\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈U_N}} f\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dv}}})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u′∈U′_d}} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈I_d}} f\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dv}}})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u\ensuremath{′})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u′∈U′_d}} f\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dv}}})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u\ensuremath{′}) \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u∈I_d}} \ensuremath{\bar{χ}}(u).\par
Of course, this sum is zero unless \ensuremath{χ} is trivial on I\ensuremath{_{d}}, i.e., unless \ensuremath{χ} is pulled back from a character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}} of U\ensuremath{_{d}}, in which case it is\par
\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{u′∈U′_d}} f\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{′}\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dv}}})\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}\ensuremath{_{d}}(u\ensuremath{′})\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{w∈U_d}} f\ensuremath{_{d}}(wv)\ensuremath{\bar{χ}}\ensuremath{_{d}}(w)\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}(v)\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}(v)\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|}(f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}).\par
If we substitute this into the above expression for (\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) and note that \ensuremath{⟨}v/d\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{|}v\ensuremath{|}/d, where \ensuremath{|}v\ensuremath{|} is the smallest positive representative of v \ensuremath{∈} U\ensuremath{_{d}}, we find:\par
(\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{v∈U_d}} \ensuremath{|}v\ensuremath{|}\ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}(v)\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|}d\ensuremath{^{-1}}(f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{d}} L(0, \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}})\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|}(f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}),\par
as claimed. \ensuremath{□}\par
To prove the proposition, we let d\ensuremath{_{f}} be the largest divisor of N such that f\ensuremath{_{d_f}} \ensuremath{≠} 0; it suffices to prove that any f in H\ensuremath{_{Q}} can be written as g \ensuremath{+} f\ensuremath{′}, with g a linear combination of the \ensuremath{ε}’s and d\ensuremath{_{f′}} \ensuremath{<} d\ensuremath{_{f}}. Let d \ensuremath{=} d\ensuremath{_{f}}; we shall show below that f\ensuremath{_{d}} is a linear combination of functions h\ensuremath{_{1}} which factor through U\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{→} U\ensuremath{_{d}}/\{\ensuremath{±}1\}, and functions h\ensuremath{_{p}} which factor through U\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{→} U\ensuremath{_{d/p}} for some prime divisor p of d, p \ensuremath{≠} d. Any function of the first type is invariant under \ensuremath{±}1, and hence the corresponding function on the orbit U\ensuremath{_{N}}(1/d) is a linear combination of \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{1,a}}’s. A function of the second type is invariant under the kernel K of U\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{→} U\ensuremath{_{d/p}}, which has order p if p divides d/p and order p \ensuremath{−} 1 otherwise. In the first case, K \ensuremath{=} \{1 \ensuremath{+} kd/p : k \ensuremath{=} 0, …, p \ensuremath{−} 1\}, and in\par
\clearpage
\PageUnit{33}{345}{SOURCE ENGLISH KOBLITZ OGUS APPENDIX}
the second, it is this same set with one element deleted, namely, the value of 1 \ensuremath{+} kd/p which is divisible by p. Thus, the set S\ensuremath{_{p,w/d}} \ensuremath{=} (Kw)/d, with the addition of one or two elements in the orbit U\ensuremath{_{N}}(p/d). Hence it is clear that the corresponding function on the orbit U\ensuremath{_{N}}(1/d) can be written as a linear combination of \ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{p,a}}’s and functions supported on the orbit of p/d, and we have obtained our desired decomposition f \ensuremath{=} g \ensuremath{+} f\ensuremath{′}.\par
It remains for us to prove the claim about f\ensuremath{_{d}}. If d is twice an odd number the map U\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{→} U\ensuremath{_{d/2}} is an isomorphism, and the claim is trivial. In the other cases, choose a primitive odd character \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}} of U\ensuremath{_{d}}, and let \ensuremath{χ} be the pull-back of \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}} to U\ensuremath{_{N}}. Since \ensuremath{χ} is nontrivial and \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} is constant, (\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} 0. Let us look at the expression for this inner product provided by the lemma; the only nonzero terms come from those f\ensuremath{_{e}} such that f\ensuremath{_{e}} \ensuremath{≠} 0 and I\ensuremath{_{e}} \ensuremath{⊆} Ker(\ensuremath{χ}). But then Ker(\ensuremath{χ}) contains I\ensuremath{_{e}} and I\ensuremath{_{d}}, hence also I\ensuremath{_{\mathrm{dI}}}\ensuremath{_{e}} \ensuremath{=} I\ensuremath{_{m}}, where m \ensuremath{=} g.c.d.(d, e). Since \ensuremath{χ} is primitive, m \ensuremath{=} d and d divides e, and since f\ensuremath{_{e}} \ensuremath{=} 0 for e \ensuremath{>} d,\par
0 \ensuremath{=} (\ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{−}L(0, \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}})\ensuremath{|}I\ensuremath{_{d}}\ensuremath{|}(f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}).\par
Since \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}} is odd and primitive, we conclude that (f\ensuremath{_{d}} \ensuremath{|} \ensuremath{χ}\ensuremath{_{d}}) \ensuremath{=} 0, i.e., f\ensuremath{_{d}} is orthogonal to every odd primitive character of U\ensuremath{_{d}}. It follows that f\ensuremath{_{d}} can be written as a linear combination of characters which are even (factor through U\ensuremath{_{d}}/\{\ensuremath{±}1\}) or imprimitive (factor through some U\ensuremath{_{d/p}}). When d \ensuremath{=} p, we should also remark that the constant functions on U\ensuremath{_{p}} are also invariant under \ensuremath{±}1, and hence are already covered by the first case. \ensuremath{□}\par
THEOREM. Suppose that f : A\ensuremath{_{N}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℚ} is such that \ensuremath{⟨}f\ensuremath{⟩} is constant: \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{a}}\ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩}f(ua) \ensuremath{=} k for all u \ensuremath{∈} U\ensuremath{_{N}}. Then\par
\ensuremath{Γ}(f) \ensuremath{≔} \ensuremath{π}\ensuremath{^{-k}} \ensuremath{∏}\ensuremath{_{a}} \ensuremath{Γ}(\ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩})\ensuremath{^{f(a)}}\par
is an algebraic number.\par
PROOF. The map \ensuremath{⟨} \ensuremath{⟩} : H\ensuremath{_{Q}} \ensuremath{→} \ensuremath{ℚ} sending any f to \ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{a}}\ensuremath{⟨}a\ensuremath{⟩}f(a) is evidently linear, and hence \ensuremath{Γ}(f \ensuremath{+} g) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{Γ}(f)\ensuremath{Γ}(g), for f and g in H\ensuremath{_{Q}}. By the proposition, any f in H\ensuremath{_{Q}} is a \ensuremath{ℚ}-linear combination of the \ensuremath{ε}’s; hence nf is a sum of \ensuremath{ε}’s for some n. Since \ensuremath{Γ}(f)\ensuremath{^{n}} \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{Γ}(nf), we are reduced to checking the theorem for the \ensuremath{ε}’s described in the proposition. Noting that \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{1,a}}\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} 1 and that \ensuremath{⟨}\ensuremath{ε}\ensuremath{_{p,a}}\ensuremath{⟩} \ensuremath{=} (p \ensuremath{+} 1)/2 if pa \ensuremath{≠} 0, one has only to appeal to the identities:\par
\ensuremath{Γ}(x)\ensuremath{Γ}(1 \ensuremath{−} x) \ensuremath{=} \ensuremath{π}(sin \ensuremath{π}x)\ensuremath{^{-1}},\par
\ensuremath{∑}\ensuremath{_{k=1}}\ensuremath{^{p−1}} \ensuremath{Γ}(x \ensuremath{+} k/p) \ensuremath{=} p\ensuremath{^{1/2−x}}(2\ensuremath{π})\ensuremath{^{(p−1)/2}} \ensuremath{Γ}(px). \ensuremath{□}\par
REMARK. Kubert has recently obtained a much more precise result expressed in a different terminology from which it follows that, if H\ensuremath{_{Q}} is \ensuremath{ℤ}-valued, then 2f is a \ensuremath{ℤ}-linear combination of the \ensuremath{ε}’s (to appear).\par

\SourcePage{1}{247}
\section{SHIMURA VARIETIES: MODULAR INTERPRETATION AND TECHNIQUES FOR CONSTRUCTING CANONICAL MODELS}

PIERRE DELIGNE

\subsubsection{CONTENTS}
